the rapporteur. mr president, it is a pleasure to open this debate, to welcome the president of the european central bank, mario draghi, the vice-president of the commission, mr dombrovskis, and all the colleagues who are going to take part in this discussion on the execution of monetary policy by the ecb. it is true that the ecb is an independent institution which, within the framework of its mandate, implements the objective of achieving an inflation rate close to 2%, but it is true that, in recent times, we have had serious problems in situating the inflation target at that long-term reference. just a few days ago we knew the data of last month that showed a further reduction in inflation, up to 1.3%, and it is true that the forecasts place that 2% well into the year 2019. in turn, according to the growth data, it is true that the euro area is regaining capacity, but we have an excess of potential ahead, an excess of sufficient growth capacity: the monetary fund, the european commission itself, in their estimates of the output gap, show a very wide margin for further growth without inflationary tensions. so this house, in that report, respecting - as i say - the clear independence of the ecb, i think it puts the debate where it should be in order to guide that work over the next year as well. as i said, it is true that the euro area is growing better, but monetary policy is not enough: we need a coherent fiscal policy, which makes it possible to diversify the positions of each of the governments in the economic cycle in order to provide the whole of the euro area with a consistent fiscal policy. it is true that we also need reforms that activate, that improve productivity throughout the union: reforms that are socially responsible, socially forward-looking policies. but the report also points to the need to consolidate the internal market. we need to improve the consolidation of the capital markets union - which the commission is pushing forward with the support of this parliament - and we also need to consolidate the banking union. it is an agenda of reforms, some of which are already legislative proposals, which are on the table in the european parliament and which need the cooperation and debate of all our colleagues. we therefore call for an accommodative monetary policy in the right direction, in the right direction, reforms that are still pending. and then, of course, the report also mentions some of the side effects of this monetary policy, and calls on the ecb to monitor them closely. i am referring to the problems of redistribution of income and wealth; i am referring to the problems for financial stability of maintaining a flat rate curve for a long time; i am also referring to the control and monitoring of potential bubbles that may be emerging in some segments of the financial markets and of the real estate markets as well. and so we ask the ecb to monitor these side effects of its own monetary policy. but the report clearly points to new transparency instruments, to the need for the cspp to have clear eligibility criteria to avoid problems of discrimination between large and small enterprises. we need to improve the implementation of the ela, to give it credibility and robustness throughout the euro area, and we need to improve the monetary dialogue, the control that this house exercises over the work of the european central bank - which is an institution, as the report acknowledges, which is also bound by the paris agreement, which the whole of the european union has signed. i think it is a comprehensive and important report and i hope that this debate will yield new contributions.
mr president, mr draghi, the european union has reached one of the key moments in its history. we have seen a situation of credit shortages, particularly for smes, which hampered economic recovery, and low inflation which prevented the member states of the union from easing their debt levels. the european central bank has played a very important role in the economic recovery, but it has become clear that monetary policy alone is not enough to achieve a sustainable and more balanced and inclusive economic recovery. you said it yourself, structural reforms are needed. and spain is a good example of that. it has now done so and is growing by over 3% and has created over half a million jobs annually over the last three years. we can take a positive view of the performance of the european central bank, with a recent improvement in expectations for both 2018 and 2019. we are now entering a scenario of gradual withdrawal of stimulus in time and quantity, ensuring that at no time is the economic recovery put at risk. in conclusion, i would like to congratulate the author of the report. and i would like to call, in line with the opinion of the european central bank, for the continuation of the negotiations for the establishment of the european deposit guarantee scheme as the third pillar of a genuine banking union, which will help to strengthen and safeguard the financial stability of the european union.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, first of all i would like to thank honourable members and president draghi for the fruitful discussion. let me conclude by mentioning a point which directly concerns the commission. the report encourages the commission to study schemes such as a central bank digital currency and digital base money with a view to improving public access to payment systems. we agree that further study of the potential challenges associated with these schemes to access payment systems is needed. to this end, we will liaise closely with the ecb, as the report invites us to do. we count on your continued support in building the foundations for sustainable growth and job creation in europe.
president of the european central bank. – mr president, let me first thank mr fernández and his colleagues for the report. it is very encouraging for our work that you stress how our measures have contributed to the recovery and to financial stability. you noted in the report that the institutional framework enshrined in the treaties allowed us to take decisive action in line with our price stability mandate, and this has been the objective of our monetary policy throughout. it still is the objective of our monetary policy. in the course of exchanges we are often told that our monetary policy affects one category or another, but our objective is price stability, defined as an inflation rate which is close to, but below, 2% for the whole of the euro area, not necessarily for one specific country. that is how our monetary policy should be judged: whether in the medium term we reach this objective. i would like to thank commission vice—president dombrovskis, and all of you, for this very relevant and useful debate. the debate shows that, while we are now seeing the positive results of our policies, we should not be complacent, but should rather strive for continued improvement. i apologise in advance that, given the short time i have, i cannot comment on each and every statement, but let me touch on some of the issues that you raised. one issue raised by several honourable members concerns the effects that our monetary policy has on the distribution of income and wealth. so let me say a few words about the effects of quantitative easing (qe). it is quite clear that qe raises asset prices. the holders of assets are generally wealthy institutions or wealthy people, so in the short run you have a worsening of distribution. at the same time, to the extent that qe is successful, it increases employment – as i have said, and i am going to say it again – and it is by far the most powerful measure for decreasing inequality in any economic system. from this viewpoint, even though in the short run one has some negative consequences, in the medium and long term the positive consequences outweigh, very consistently and significantly, any short-term negative concerns. this has been shown, by the way, in several studies. the best way to decrease inequality is to increase employment, and that is what we have done, contributing to increasing employment by 7.5 million jobs over three-and-a-half years. when we look at wage growth – and that is very important for us because it is, in a sense, what tells us whether inflation is moving towards our objective in the medium term – annual growth in terms of compensation per employee increased has gradually from 1.1% in the second quarter of 2016 to 1.7% now. it is still below its historical average, which is 2.1%, so we have to be more patient, but looking at what happens in other jurisdictions – for example the united states which is, by the way, far advanced in the business cycle – we see that wage growth picks up in the end. the recent data in the usa show exactly this. we have to be aware that we have weak productivity growth, ongoing impacts of labour market reforms implemented in some countries during the crisis and certainly a much bigger labour supply coming from stronger migration flows and higher participation rates. participation rates of women and older people especially have increased considerably. also, the low-inflation environment that has prevailed for a long time is now influencing current negotiations. and, by the way, one thing that is quite important in explaining this light response by wages is that even though we had a significant increase in employment, when we go and look at the quality of this increase in employment we see a lot of part-time and temporary arrangements. i am listing all these factors, because they are explanations of why the nominal wage-growth response is going to be lower than we had expected. but we know by looking at other jurisdictions which had, by and large, the same problems that, in the end, nominal wages are going to go up, and they are going up, albeit at a subdued rate. as regards the effects of our monetary policy, some speakers questioned the effectiveness of this policy. we have estimated that our measures have made a substantial impact on the economic performance of the euro area. considering all the measures taken between 2014 (and even before, in 2013) and october 2017, the overall impact on eu area real gdp growth is 1.9%: 1.9 percentage points over three years. one member pointed out that investment is still low. we are coming from very, very low levels of private investment but, if anything, over the past three or four quarters, private investment has picked up and it is actually increasing at a much more satisfactory rate than in the past. since the end of may 2014, lending rates for households and non-financial firms have declined significantly. there is one thing i said in the introductory statement which is very important: during the crisis we observed widely differing lending rates by banks in different parts of the euro area, but this difference has now shrunk and rates are very close nowadays, as are growth rates, by the way. one measure we often look at to determine the strength of the growth process and expansion is how different the growth rates are in different parts of the euro area. well, the degree of difference now is something like we had in 1995—1996. in other words, it is a historical low. all countries nowadays are growing. by the way, some members questioned the effectiveness of our monetary policy for smes but, in fact, the lending conditions for smes have improved significantly across all sectors and countries. the gradual recovery in loan growth is continuing. the recovery started about four years ago and then really picked up, and it is continuing, though we are not seeing anything like we had before the crisis. so growth rates in lending are good, but nothing euphoric like we saw before the crisis. one point that was made was that we are focused on buying southern countries’ bonds. that is not true. we do not favour certain countries over others in the implementation of our programme. our purchases are guided by the ecb’s capital key, which takes into account gdp and population. but if one focuses on purchases at specific points in time, for example on 2017 only, this is bound to yield wrong interpretations. the overall stock of euro system holdings is the relevant metric for any assessment of the programme, and not the recent purchase flows. so, in fact, if you look at the stock, you will see that, as far as german bonds are concerned, we are above the capital key for that country. by and large, one should consider the design of the programme: it is flexible and the distribution of actual purchases on any given day often deviates from the ecb capital key. but just consider: this was in the original design of the programme when we had countries like greece, whose bonds we did not purchase. of course, then, we had to deviate from the capital key. some other observations concerned the side effects of our monetary policy. i just wish to reiterate that our measures are proving effective but, at the same time, we are aware of potential side effects and we have to differentiate between the various ways in which they affect economic actors. for example, for individual savers, an accommodative monetary policy means that they accrue fewer nominal returns on their savings. however, such a policy also supports economic expansion and this bolsters employment, income, returns on investment and tax revenues. it therefore benefits households in their capacity as workers, entrepreneurs, investors, borrowers and taxpayers. there is no one specific country that has benefited most from our monetary policy. everybody has benefited. public sectors in all countries saved billions on interest rate payments; private sectors across countries and sectors saved billions on interest rate payments to banks; and purchasers of houses could have access to mortgages with much lower interest rates than at any time in the past. this has not only boosted the construction industry but has also boosted investment for the purchase of houses. so we see benefits accruing right across society and not specifically located in one country. when the monetary policy is successful, both creditors and borrowers benefit from it. similarly, let me continue now on savers. there are several channels through which our policies affect pension and insurance schemes. beyond the effect on the liability side, it is important to see what happens on the asset side. our monetary policy has had a beneficial impact on this side of the equation, as the value of the investment portfolio has increased. but, having said that, i completely agree there is a need to put pension systems on a stable path because the survival of any single country’s pension system cannot be dependent only on the proper configuration of interest rates. it must be actuarially sensible. i have already addressed, in my introductory remarks, the issue of possible asset bubbles currently being formed in the euro area. for the time being, we have little indication that generalised financial imbalances are emerging. there are no signs of general asset-price misalignments in the euro area but some segments do need close monitoring and one of them is the prime commercial real-estate market, where we actually see stretched valuations. also, in some large cities and in some countries real-estate prices have increased at a faster pace than household incomes. this certainly requires monitoring. finally, yields in the euro area corporate bond markets, especially for some of the lower-rated issues, have started to look exceptionally low by historical standards, but what are we going to do? are we going to change monetary policy because of these side effects which are not, by the way, systemic? no, the answer is to enact macro-prudential policies which are the best tool for tackling these challenges – also given their country-specific and sector-specific remits. in late 2016, the european systemic risk board (esrb) issued a set of country-specific warnings on medium-term vulnerability in the eu residential real-estate sector. now a word about brexit. we are not party to these negotiations but we are certainly monitoring their evolution and, clearly, i agree that much depends on these negotiations and possible arrangements. of course we always prepare for any eventuality and, at the same time, we are assessing the direction, the probability and the potential impact of risk, but the bottom line is that either this transition is well managed and there will not be substantial risks, or it is not, and the risks will be there. we are certainly looking at that and we have to be prepared for that. let me also add that, as far as our role as supervisors is concerned, our good cooperation with the bank of england is important in coping with the potential risks, and especially the risks of any cliff-edge effects. certainly, transitional arrangements along the lines of the december european council guidelines could be useful to smooth out the brexit process but, as we all know, the materialisation of the transition period is still exposed to political uncertainty, and that will remain for some time to come. on financial supervision, i welcome the review of the european system of financial supervision, including changes to the european supervisory authorities. some of your comments touched upon the issue of transparency. here, let me reiterate that we are in complete agreement about the importance of ecb transparency vis-à-vis the european public. we have continuously assessed where we need to further strengthen our transparency framework, and we have demonstrated our commitment, improving our framework as necessary. just briefly, let me list a few of the actions we have taken. the accounts of governing council discussions are now published four weeks after each monetary policymaking meeting. there was none of that a few years ago. since 2015, the executive board members, as well as the chair of the supervisory board, publish their diaries covering professional meetings with external parties. none of that was in place until a few years ago. and in 2016 we decided to disclose the agreement on net financial assets (anfa). last year we also published the text of the emergency liquidity assistance agreement. we have announced transparency in relation to our purchase programme, especially transparency on the corporate sector purchase programme. some of you made reference to the european ombudsman’s recommendations on the interaction of members of the ecb decision-making bodies, including myself, with the group of 30 (g30). we have certainly taken note of the ombudsman’s letter and we will respond in time, but let us remember that the european ombudsman has already concluded that the ecb must conduct dialogue with market participants and that there is no evidence that the g30 meeting could have directly influenced, or have had an adverse impact on, the ecb’s supervisory tasks. the ombudsman has also confirmed that the ecb has a robust system of safeguards in place to manage its contacts with the financial sector. again on transparency, we publish on our website extensive documentation on all these interactions with markets. we disclose agendas and summaries of the discussions, so i can assure you that the ecb is, and remains, committed to reviewing, adjusting and updating our transparency framework. one or two speakers touched on bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies. let me first say that we are not observing a systemically relevant holding of digital currencies by supervised institutions – by banks, in other words. actually, the credit institutions established in the european union are showing a limited appetite for digital currencies like bitcoin, notwithstanding the high level of public interest. however, recent developments, such as the listing of bitcoin futures contracts by us exchanges, could lead european banks too to hold positions in bitcoin, and therefore we will certainly look at that. however, we should understand that bitcoin and other digital currencies are in the unregulated space and should be regarded as very risky assets. virtual currencies are subject to high volatility and their prices are entirely speculative. banks should measure the risk of any holdings of digital currencies in their portfolio accordingly. right now, digital currencies are not subject to a specific supervisory approach. work is under way in the single supervisory mechanism to identify potential prudential risks that these digital assets could pose to supervised institutions. there were some other specific points. we are going to consider the possibility of having a charlemagne commemorative coin. on monetary financing in hungary, we will assess the existence of monetary financing in our report. as you know, the ecb is accountable to the european parliament, but members of its executive board, myself included, have accepted invitations to discuss our monetary policy generally and broadly in national parliaments, so i would be glad to accept an invitation from the irish parliament if i were to receive it. i think i have gone through most of your questions. thank you.

vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, let me start by saying that what we see in venezuela is obviously, first and foremost, a political crisis, but it is also an economic, social and refugee crisis, with serious repercussions on neighbouring countries, starting with colombia and brazil. everything we are doing as the european union aims at a peaceful and democratic solution to all these different layers of the crisis, through credible and serious negotiations. as we speak, other efforts are ongoing to resume negotiations, and we can just hope that, this time, we will see some credibility and some concrete steps and openness in place. that has not been the case so far but it is never too late. when we last discussed venezuela in this plenary, last september, we indicated four main areas where steps needed to be taken: an agreed calendar and conditions for credible elections; the facilitation of an emergency access plan for external assistance; the liberation of political prisoners; and respect for democratically elected institutions, notably the national assembly. unfortunately, progress was not made on any of these points. throughout this period we have repeatedly engaged, all together as the european union and together with our member states, in a well-coordinated approach. in several meetings with our venezuelan interlocutors we have discussed the need to respect democratic principles, democratic institutions, human rights and fundamental freedoms. we have called for serious engagement and flexibility in the ongoing negotiations to achieve a political agreement as a matter of urgency. again, let me stress that talks are restarting, hopefully within hours. it was with a heavy heart that member states decided to adopt targeted restrictive measures, in the absence of concrete results and in view of the constant deterioration of the situation. it is the first time that we have imposed measures of this kind in a latin american context, and the decision was not taken lightly, as you can imagine. on 13 november, the council adopted together targeted, gradual and reversible restrictive measures. these comprised a ban on the export of arms and equipment for internal repression, and a framework decision for a travel ban and assets freeze. two months later, the council recognised the lack of progress in the national dialogue and the worrying deterioration of the political and social situation in the country. as a consequence, the council adopted a list of seven individuals subject to these measures. these targeted restrictive measures do not harm the people of venezuela, but are directed at seven individuals who are responsible for undermining democratic principles and the rule of law and for human rights violations. our measures are a signal to the authorities of venezuela, an invitation to engage seriously towards a negotiated solution to the crisis and to reverse the moves that have called into question venezuela’s constitutional order. we continue to monitor events on the ground and we stand ready to take appropriate measures in one way or another if the situation in the country evolves, with the constant aim of supporting democratic and negotiated solutions. the recent decision of the government of venezuela to declare the spanish ambassador persona non grata is wrong and unacceptable, first and foremost because closing diplomatic channels does not help at a time when it is more important than ever to keep them open and seek a solution. we expect the government of venezuela to show genuine engagement in the negotiations and openness to compromise. we also hope that the opposition can work in a united and constructive manner. this is what the country needs in order to address the current challenges. both parties should agree on a mutually acceptable date for the presidential elections. unilateral decisions will only create more polarisation and new obstacles to a peaceful solution. it is also essential to set up guarantees to ensure free, transparent and credible elections. no artificial conditions should be imposed to limit the participation of political parties. the supreme court has decided to block the participation of mesa de la unidad democrática in the elections, and clearly this goes against the goal of free, fair and inclusive elections. the people’s trust in elections can be regained only through a credible electoral process, with the lifting of bans on political opponents, with independent international observers and a balanced composition of the national electoral council. the future of venezuela should be determined by its people. this is what we are asking of the venezuelan authorities and all national political forces: the future of venezuela should be determined by its people. we do not take sides in venezuela’s domestic debate but we do ask for this debate to be democratic and inclusive, in line with the constitution of the country. we see that the people of venezuela are suffering, including the many european union citizens who are also venezuelan citizens. we have a stake in this. everything we do is to encourage and support the country to come out of this political, economic and social crisis. we are also concerned about the progressive deterioration of the social situation. the reports we are receiving from the united nations agencies are extremely worrying. more than one million people are currently food insecure and the percentage of children affected by global acute malnutrition has reached emergency levels. the lack of medicines is estimated at around 90% by the national chamber of pharmacists. diseases such as malaria and diphtheria that had disappeared are now spreading across the country. and there are no signs of recovery from the economic crisis. according to the united nations high commissioner for refugees (unhcr), more than 1.5 million venezuelans have already left the country. i want to reiterate that the repercussions in the region – on the fragile process in colombia, on brazil, on the regional organisations that are trying to move forward the regional integration process of latin america and the caribbean – are particularly worrying. the european civil protection and humanitarian aid operations department (dg echo) is present in bogotá and deploys regular missions to venezuela and bordering regions to evaluate the humanitarian situation, including the humanitarian conditions of the numerous venezuelans who are fleeing the country to neighbouring countries. we are exploring all possibilities to develop our support, together with member states and also with other donors and partner agencies. let me stress once again that we will adapt our policies to any change in the situation in venezuela, in one sense or the other. we need to see progress in the negotiations. i believe progress is still possible. it is a matter of political will. it is in the hands of the parties. as i mentioned, the government has a clear responsibility to show flexibility and to engage seriously in these negotiations, and we hope to see real, concrete, encouraging steps.

vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – let me first of all thank you for this debate. it is timely and it is important. it is important first of all because millions of people – men, women and children – depend on the united nations relief and works agency for education, healthcare and social services, humanitarian assistance and employment. so, supporting unwra is a humanitarian duty and it is also in our collective interest for peace and security in the middle east. i would like to mention a few reasons why it is essential to support unwra, its work and why the european union not only is supporting it but is going to continue to support it and argue for continued or increased support from other international partners. firstly, the work they do is crucial for the prospects of an agreement between israel and palestine. it is a key contribution that unwra is bringing to the prospect of relaunching a credible peace process, because a just, fair, agreed and realistic solution to the refugee question is one of the parameters of for peace negotiations, with the ultimate objective of achieving a two—state solution. the work that unwra does provides the political space towards achieving a peace deal and building a palestinian state. secondly, it is a matter of regional stability. this strikes me every time when international players don’t see the reality on the ground in the countries that have been hosting, for decades; a huge number of palestinian refugees. reducing the activities of unwra would cause instability and even security threats all around the region. this is true for the west bank and gaza, but this is also true for lebanon and jordan. they are themselves facing enormous challenges on other fronts and this is obvious to all of us i believe; there is no need for me to go into details about the huge pressure that both lebanon and jordan have been facing. investing in unwra is also investing in our collective regional security. thirdly, education. the european union has always invested and will always continue to invest in the education of people and children to avoid any lost generation. for palestinian kids, this means the possibility to keep hoping, to build their own future, and to believe in their own personal lives – which is no minor thing when you are a child; and it means also fighting radicalisation. so it’s also here an investment in our own security. fourthly, unwra is particularly important for the political process in gaza, where work is ongoing, efforts are ongoing for the return of the palestinian authority, and palestinian reconciliation is essential for the prospect of a viable state of palestine. so for all these reasons, we are – and we will continue to be – strong and reliable supporters of the work of unwra. together with our member states, we are doing all we can to avoid repercussions from the us decision to ensure that unwra can continue to operate and to ensure a continued engagement from all other international actors, but also from the united states. we have already increased our support in recent times. for 2018, the european union will assist unwra by accelerating our first scheduled payment for this year, and i also count on donors around the world with whom we are in contact, including in coordination with other players. here i would mention established partners for unwra, which already has important donors, but also all those that have so far been less engaged and who can step up their efforts in order to safeguard something that can be qualified as a global public good: the work that unwra does. peace between israel and palestine will clearly be built through negotiations, which requires a commitment from the two sides, but it must also be preserved every day on the ground and this is what unwra is doing with the palestinian refugees. investing in unwra is an interest we all share and the international community and the palestinian refugees and the countries in the region can count on the european union to continue to support its work.
member of the commission. – mr president, i also welcome this timely opportunity to join some of you today to discuss unrwa, which is currently facing unprecedented challenges. the european union is convinced that the two-state solution is the only possible answer if we want to achieve lasting peace in the middle east. we believe that any solution to the israeli—arab conflict will need to include an agreed just and fair solution to the refugee question. the palestinian refugee question has existed for almost 70 years. the united nations general assembly established and mandated unrwa to provide assistance and protection to registered palestinian refugees until a just and lasting solution is found to their plight. this is the work that unrwa continues to do, laying the groundwork for future development through its work in education and health, and contributing – as the high representative has just said – to security and stability in the region. the commission will disburse our scheduled payment for 2018, which is about eur 82 million, by the end of february – much earlier than originally planned. some of our member states have also announced plans to accelerate their contributions for this year and i can tell you that we will also do so in 2019 and 2020, at least, in order to reassure unrwa from our side. it is still too early to tell you how exactly unrwa will be affected since the scope and nature of the cuts in us funding are not entirely clear. what we do know is that the eu will not be able to compensate for substantial us cuts, given the pressure on available funds. we can and will actively assist unrwa in reaching out to non—traditional donors in order to help the agency to broaden its donor base and, given the magnitude of the problem, we also need to work with host governments on how they might consider providing certain services that unrwa cannot and maybe should not provide. unrwa needs reform. some of its financial problems are structural and predate the us decision. the eu has long been calling on unrwa to review its operational and financial planning approach in order to safeguard its basic and essential core services, intended to help the most marginalised refugees. we therefore commend unrwa’s commitment to a process of comprehensive financial reforms, including measures sustaining institutional change and increasing the cost-effectiveness of its programmes. but, in order to achieve improvements, we will work on this together with – and not against – the agency. there should be no doubt that the eu is and will remain a staunch and reliable supporter of unrwa, both politically and financially. the eu and its member states are by far the largest provider of assistance to palestinian refugees – they provide around eur 460 million a year. in june 2017, a joint declaration was signed between the eu and unrwa as a framework for our financial and political support for the agency as further proof of our continued commitment, not just this year, but also in the years to come.

mr president, i would like to congratulate the two rapporteurs, because i really think that a very interesting and very appropriate report has been produced. first, because it reduces the number of seats; second, because it compensates countries that were badly treated; and third, because no country loses. but i would like to refer to the more passionate debate on transnational lists by conveying my view that i sincerely believe that a european constituency, that the double vote of europeans is good. because i am a europeanist. i believe that it is better for europe, to make more europe, to make better europe and to improve european democracy. let me give you a simple historical reflection. the founding father, jean monnet, said that europe would be built step by step. and it has been. when the european union was created, there was no parliament, ladies and gentlemen. it was created later. the european parliament was a step in the process of european integration. members of the national parliaments came to this parliament. they were not elected by the citizens, but by the members of the national parliaments. the next step was, indeed, elections throughout europe. a day to elect the european parliament, to european sovereignty. this step we are taking today, ladies and gentlemen, is a step, as jean monnet would say, towards building europe. it's for a double vote. so that citizens connect with the european idea, and hopefully a spitzenkandidat leads each political family to elect the president of the commission. that is building europe. i think that the step we are taking is an extremely important political signal in favour of this idea which is being built up little by little. it's a long story, but it's a beautiful story. it is a wonderful story of building, on the nations, a space of peace and progress. and today we are taking a step forward with this political signal calling on the council to grant the possibility in the european electoral law that europeans vote in the country on two lists, the national and the european.
mr president, transnational lists are an important step in the process towards a single european constituency. having the opportunity to vote for a list with candidates from different member states helps to create in the imagination of citizens a sense of european general interest and a feeling of belonging. transnational lists can open the window to the creation of solidarity and a redistribution of wealth and can reinforce the idea of a european public sphere. all in all, we are debating something that can strengthen democracy. we have an opportunity to reinvigorate the european project and to rethink it, especially from a bottom-up perspective – for instance, by allowing member states to assign seats to regions having legislative powers. this is today the case in the åland islands and tomorrow it could be the case in others. it is a matter of political will. today, the european parliament has a chance to deliver a beneficial, transformative proposal.

in writing. on 11 november 2015, the european parliament (ep) adopted its proposal to amend the 1976 act concerning the election of the members of the european parliament by direct universal suffrage, which introduces a series of measures aimed at strengthening the european dimension of elections and ensuring greater electoral equality for citizens of the union. unfortunately, since then five council presidencies (luxembourg, the netherlands, slovakia, malta and now estonia) have worked on the parliament's proposal (made in accordance with article 223 (1) tfeu) but none has transmitted to the ep formal or informal results of the council's deliberations, highlighting the member states' unwillingness to harmonise the current rule dating from 1976. we therefore ask the council once again not to block further improvements to the rules for the election of meps and, given that the dossier must be completed by next spring at the latest, to submit a decision to the ep as soon as possible.
the rapporteur. madam president, in this report, in addition to the amendments, what is being discussed is whether the commission is a body with political responsibility, answerable to parliament and to the electors, a real government of europe, as this parliament wants, or just an administrative body that speaks in parliament but is answerable to the council, that is, a puppet of european governments. if you vote for this report, you will be voting for a european government; if you vote against it, you will be voting for a commission of the governments of the countries of europe. they're two very different models. president juncker warned us yesterday that there are voices within the council who want to eliminate the figure of the candidate for president of the commission. let me say that in my view that would be a step backwards for european democracy. i do not say a step backwards for the construction of europe, which is also, i say, a european election without a candidate for president of the commission is a less democratic election, almost a failed election. the figure of the candidate for president of the commission allows citizens to go to the polls knowing what each party's programme is and who each party's candidate is. the usual. because in european elections not only a parliament is elected, but also a european government, and it would be a democratic anomaly if citizens were unable to choose that government or if they did not even know who the candidates were to lead that government. this european union is still a democracy in the making and therefore vulnerable. the enemies of europe need only oppose european democracy. we cannot be friends of europe and at the same time be against european democracy. for national populists, it is easier to attack a european union with a democratic deficit than a european union that is built and sustained on the vote of citizens. national populists come to the european institutions to destroy them, they disguise themselves as democrats to attack democracy and they use the rule of law to destroy the rule of law. only true democracy can expose the false democrats. so our biggest problem is that more and more citizens are buying into the populist discourse because they feel that the community institutions are far from ordinary people; because they feel that the community institutions live in the universe of statistics and big numbers instead of in the real world of supermarket prices and childhood illnesses; because they feel that the european institutions are accountable to the council but not to the people. this growing disaffection can only be ended by increasing the possibilities for political participation: that citizens can choose with more european democracy, not less. when we say 'we need more europe' instead of 'we need more european democracy', what is meant is that we are looking for more european bureaucracy and not more european politics. if we do not build a democratic europe, if europe remains just another historic alliance between european nations, all the efforts made by european democrats after the second world war and after the dictatorships in eastern and southern europe will have been in vain. it is not a whim, nor is it even a democratic requirement, that citizens should know and be able to vote for the candidates for president of the commission; it is normal that the candidate's face should be known, and it would be strange to insist that a president of the european government should be elected without the citizens knowing his face, his nationality, his name or even his gender. that is why i propose in my report that the european parliament be prepared to reject any candidate for president of the commission proposed by the council who has not been previously nominated as the leading candidate in the european elections. this is not a conflict between the council and parliament. this is a conflict between power and democracy. and this cannot be the first parliament in history to choose between power and democracy.

mr president, we, the members of the socialist and democratic family in this house, truly care about the rule of law, separation of powers and the independence of the judiciary, and of course we understand the legitimate concerns every time there is a risk of breach of the rule of law in relation to a judicial reform in a member state. having said that, it is fair to point out that each and every act in this package of reforms has been in answer to previous rulings of the romanian constitutional court; that there has been a preventive exercise of constitutional review of those acts; and that the romanian government has shown readiness to comply with the rulings of the constitutional court. this reform aims to enhance the accountability of judges in a country which ranks first in terms of violations of article 6 of the european convention on human rights; it enhances the presumption of innocence with regard to its due observance by members of the public prosecution service; and, lastly, it is important to break the misuse or political abuse of the links between the judiciary and intelligence services. that is why many of us do not believe that this reform package poses a serious threat or represents a systemic breach of the rule of law in that member state which is romania. the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner katainen, president hoyer, in recent years there has been strong criticism of the european union for its inaction in the refugee crisis and, in fact, from this house we have called on the council and the commission many times to act urgently to put solutions on the table: short-term action, but also longer-term action, in order to be able to deal in a more structural way with the migration phenomenon and the situation of the countries around us which are taking in refugees in large numbers. and just as we criticize that inaction, i think it's also fair to acknowledge that the european plan for foreign investment, which was presented by the european commission in june 2016, addresses some of those needs that we have been pointing out. in july 2017, this plenary already gave the green light to one of the components of that plan, which was the european fund for sustainable development, and today we are debating here another of its components, which is the modification of the eib's external lending mandate, whose activities are guaranteed by the union budget. after eight months of tough negotiations with the maltese presidency first and then with the estonian presidency, we have managed to conclude an agreement which i believe substantially improves the current external lending mandate. i would like to start by recalling that all the countries of the union, and the commission too, signed up to the sustainable development goals and that all our actions must therefore be geared to achieving them. with the amendment of this regulation, we are going to improve the european union's action through the eib abroad, and especially in the countries of the southern and eastern neighbourhood, both quantitatively and qualitatively. we have improved quantitatively because we have increased investment capacity to eur 32.3 billion by 2020, with a very special effort in the mediterranean and balkan countries. as regards the qualitative improvement of our investments, we have worked on several aspects. the first, and probably the most important, is that we have added a new priority and cross-cutting objective so that all initiatives funded through this programme contribute to meeting the sustainable development goals and thus eradicate the causes for which people have to leave their homes. in this new objective we have not wanted to forget the countries around us which, in a clear demonstration of solidarity, are hosting millions of refugees and whose public services and infrastructure are completely overwhelmed. in addition, to meet the paris agreement and our commitment to helping developing countries, we have increased the percentage to be devoted to climate change-related the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, first of all i would like to thank the alternative rapporteurs for their cooperation on this dossier. i would also like to thank the secretariats of the envi committee and the epp group, as well as my assistant, for their cooperation, and also the commission services, who have always been ready to clarify any doubts about this report. the aim is to amend regulation (ec) no 110/2008 on spirit drinks which is currently in force. this regulation is a very good regulation and it is not about changing what works well, but it needed to be amended to bring it into line with the treaty on the functioning of the european union. existing legislation must be consistent with the new legal instruments introduced by the lisbon treaty and that is what this review is mainly about. at the same time, the alternative rapporteurs and i consider it essential that the prerogatives of parliament under the legislation in force be maintained. we have therefore tabled a number of amendments introducing delegated acts to protect the existing rights of parliament. in this connection, we have amended the proposal so that these delegated acts do not affect the essential elements of the regulation and, in addition, we propose to limit these powers in time so that they have a duration of five years with the possibility of being extended for an equivalent period. the commission proposes to harmonize the procedures for managing geographical indications in the spirit drinks sector with those already in force for foodstuffs in general and, to this end, introduces a major amendment to chapter iii governing geographical indications. this change was necessary, and parliament understands and shares this, since the various regimes applicable must be harmonized, but at the same time the specific issues of the spirit drinks sector must be taken into account. we have therefore tabled a number of amendments to this effect. another of the essential amendments to the proposal is the deletion of annex iii, which is in regulation (ec) no 110/2008, on geographical indications. the commission proposal introduces an electronic register similar to that provided for in the case of protected designations of origin and geographical indications for wines and foodstuffs. this electronic register is an innovative and easily accessible instrument. however, given the importance of the register, we propose that parliament be involved in future amendments to it by means of delegated acts. neither regulation (ec) no 110/2008 nor this proposal establishes a maximum sugar content for rounding flavourings. there are member states which have national legislation for certain categories and set a ceiling, and others which have none at all. parliament has considered it necessary to set a limit for each category, but always respecting the higher limit already existing in national legislation for each category. it is also important to point out, within the spirit drinks sector, the existence of traditional and centuries-old methods for their production and aging, and it is necessary and right to recognise and perpetuate them in legislation. in short, this is a fundamentally technical proposal and we must stick to it. i am aware, however, that the issues of health and consumer protection in relation to excessive alcohol consumption concern us all, but this is not the appropriate regulatory body in which we should deal with this problem. i am against including in this regulation those amendments which refer to the indication of the nutritional calorie content of spirit drinks on the labelling, but this does not mean that i think that alcoholic drinks should be exempted. what's going on is this is not the place to do it. the place is regulation (eu) no 1169/2011 on nutrition labelling.
mr president, i would like to join in congratulating the rapporteur, pilar ayuso, and the whole team of alternative rapporteurs, because i think there is a magnificent proposal left for the trilogue negotiating process. i think a great deal of updating has been done and all the local needs and varieties have been taken into account. i would particularly like to thank the work that has been done in incorporating the model applied to a well-known spirit drink, such as sherry brandy, a model in which, as regards the rounding of the final flavour of the product, natural sweet wine is usually used. this rounding is called 'solera y crianza' and is something very traditional in national legislation. this is reflected in the proposal 'i am glad of it', as are other varieties and traditional methods, and i welcome it. i would also like to refer to the amendments on nutritional profiles. i am not against it; i am against amendments: this is not the place. we must wait for the labelling regulation and make the appropriate contributions there.

in writing. the protection of the beekeeping sector should not be linked exclusively to honey production, as it involves the important aspect of pollination of crops and the conservation of biodiversity. about 80 percent of all cultivated plants need insects to be pollinated. yet, without warning, we are witnessing a dramatic reduction in insect populations on a global scale. we can see this effect in the beekeeping industry. although land use change is a major factor in the decline of insect populations, the use of pesticides such as neonicotinoids, which have been used worldwide since the 1980s, are the main cause of the global decline in bee populations. their effects persist in the environment long after use. although the use of these insecticides was restricted in the eu in 2013, their ban is necessary as the permitted applications are still an aggression on the natural environment that we cannot afford.

the rapporteur. madam president, the defeat of the islamic state in syria and iraq does not mean its end: in their hands is a huge amount of money that has been stored throughout their caliphate with the sale of oil, the capture or investments of legitimate businesses, revolutionary taxes, robberies, bank robberies, kidnappings, trafficking in antiquities, sale of weapons. it is estimated that some 400 million dollars are being laundered in syria and iraq, considering that the approximate volume of their economic movement, at the time of the caliphate, was about 80 million dollars a month. the aim of this recommendation is to collapse, to prevent these funds from being used, from being laundered, from being sold, because it is necessary for the intelligence services to work in a coordinated way to tackle the financing of terrorism. the commission, the member states and the european external action service are therefore being asked to take a comprehensive, holistic view, which will deepen the necessary cooperation between european intelligence services. the creation of a horizontal platform for european intelligence services where they can share data and research is a strategic necessity. it is not a question of creating a new institution but, realistically, of establishing a cooperation platform where a common database exists and where this data can be shared. and this platform that we are proposing has to be built on the basis of what already exists at europol, with the aim of proactive exchange of information on the financing of terrorist groups. member states are also encouraged to make greater efforts to equip themselves with qualified staff, computer engineers who can properly detect and investigate economically suspicious movements. we also call for the early implementation of the fifth anti-money laundering directive to improve the competence of national intelligence units and to enable them to access banking data, including within the scope of the directive, for their research, virtual currencies and prepaid cards, cards which, until now, were charged anonymously, and that must end. new technologies have a fundamental role and responsibility. virtual currencies, crowdfunding platforms are used by terrorists. new technologies are, by their very nature, transnational, as must be the response to terrorism, which is also transnational. we have international agreements on the exchange and traceability of financial information linked to terrorism, but, curiously enough, we do not do the same within the european union. this is the case with the single area for payments in euro, and we therefore propose that the commission should put forward measures which can complement the international system with a joint european response, all while strictly applying the data protection standards and respecting the fundamental rights which define us as rights-respecting in the european union. we also propose that in the european union, the traditional methods of transferring money, from hawala to chinese fei ch'ien and other traditional methods, should be regulated by means of a register of transactions, which is compulsory, as is the case with any of our fellow citizens, who, when they transfer money, do so in a controlled manner: equality before the law and non-discrimination. hawala is being used by the islamic state, by terrorist organizations to export their money from syria and from iraq, and that money is going to europe. similarly, in europe we must pay attention to religious, cultural and charitable associations - ostensible charitable associations - where there is reason to suspect that they have links with terrorism, to avoid a negligent or reckless use of the funds they receive, all this with very special attention to the fight against this new form of racism and xenophobia which is islamophobia. terrorism defined as jihadism is a blasphemy against the koran and the main victims of this terrorist activity are precisely the muslims. finally, in our external dimension, in the missions we send and finance from our common security and defence policy, within the assistance we provide for resilience building in states that are victims of terrorist crime, we must add the dimension of the fight against the financing of terrorism and, in particular, against the integration into the domestic economy of funds seized by terrorists, that is, money laundering through legal economic activities. in conclusion, i would like to thank the colleagues with whom i negotiated the text, and also commissioner king, with whom i had the opportunity to exchange views on the proposal for a recommendation. i have tried to make the recommendation realistic and possible and effective. and i am grateful that my efforts to strike the necessary and difficult balance between freedom and security have won the consensus of all political groups. thanks to all of them.

humanity as a whole and particularly relevant to the achievement of the millennium development goals, of which the fight against hunger, poverty and exclusion is a major one. and in that process, women, their empowerment and their position on an equal footing with men are decisive. and they are particularly so in rural areas, where women from all over the world are called upon to play a relevant role if their abilities and contributions are made visible and fully projected onto productive activities. in the developed world today, but especially in developing countries, women are particularly discriminated against in rural areas. un reports estimate that changing this situation would increase primary sector productivity by more than 30%, a progress that is essential to meet the population growth forecasts for the coming decades. this report therefore sets out basic conditions for ending discrimination and specific measures focusing on rural areas and on access to new technologies and the media, following the guidelines proposed by the united nations. the general conditions include stepping up action to combat violence against women, especially practices such as forced marriages and genital mutilation, and making progress in training, education and the provision of universal and free social services to promote equal opportunities for men and women. this is a goal which is now being weighed down by an obvious imbalance in the distribution of tasks linked to household logistics and the care of children and the elderly. to promote the professional performance of women in rural areas, we are committed to a statute for professional women in rural areas, such as the one already in force in the basque country. its basic pillars are access to ownership and ownership or joint ownership of holdings and to social security systems. the establishment of specific funding channels to promote new activities and products; specific training that incorporates digital and modern skills and gives another dimension to the role of women in the creation of new products and their marketing; the progressive incorporation of women into decision-making processes, both in the public and private sectors, including from institutions to producer organizations, cooperatives and production and processing companies; and a systematic and homogeneous collection of statistical data, which allows the evaluation of the results of policies in favour of full equality with this catalogue of measures. we are convinced that the consolidation of the status of professional women in rural areas, which promotes, recognizes and protects this equality, is an achievement not only of women but of humanity. and this is going to be especially visible if this real revolution for justice and equality accelerates in the developing world. madam president, with your generosity, i would like to add just one point: i regret that, among the highlights of this i would like to thank mrs jourová for her participation in this debate, and my colleague, mr izaskun bilbao, for her excellent work and cooperation and all the work we have done together on this report. i would also like to thank the various group alternate rapporteurs. the committee on women's rights and gender equality is submitting this recommendation to the council for the next session of the un commission on legal and social affairs for women, which will be held in new york shortly and in which a delegation from this parliament will be participating, including ourselves. the priority theme of this session is the empowerment of women and girls in rural areas, and this is where we as co-rapporteurs decided to focus our report. it is estimated that more than 75 per cent of the world's extreme poverty population lives in rural areas. ninety percent of the countries in the world have at least one law that limits women's economic equality. millions of girls in the rural world are deprived of the right to go to school every day because, without access to clean water or electricity, they are the ones primarily responsible for fetching water or fuel for their families. to do this, they often have to travel several kilometres, and are also exposed to sexual violence along the way. to break the cycle of poverty, it is essential to promote the empowerment of rural women and girls through access to education, health and productive resources. in our report, we therefore recommend that the council, at the next session of the un commission, promote policies aimed at eradicating poverty and ensuring an adequate standard of living for particularly vulnerable groups such as women and girls, and especially through the social protection system; programmes ensuring that women and their families have access to universal social protection systems that affect their future retirement status and thus contribute to reducing the multi-dimensional pension gap; the right and access to universal and quality health care, meeting the needs of rural women and girls, and in particular with regard to sexual and reproductive health and rights; universal access to adequate child and elderly care services in rural areas; and that rural women and girls have easy access to credit and support in their productive economic initiatives. and we also recommend that it guarantees rural women's property rights, in particular their right to farm ownership and inheritance of land, which is a very important tool for their economic empowerment and enables them to participate fully in and benefit from rural development; that it condemns all forms of violence against women and ensures that no victim in rural and isolated areas is deprived of equal access to assistance and protection; that it develops employment policies, services and programmes to address the precarious situations of those rural women who often work in the informal sector and who may face multiple forms of intersectional discrimination on the basis of sex, age, class, religion, ethnicity, disability or gender identity; that it provides gender-sensitive assistance and support; that it guarantees the fundamental human rights and interests of migrant women and ensures the integration of migrant women into their families and local communities; and that it promotes the integration of women workers into their families and communities. and i just want to add that at a critical moment, when there is actually a setback for the first time in decades in the rights of women and girls worldwide, we call on the european parliament to support this recommendation.

the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, thank you all for your contributions. i could end this debate by insisting on the measures we propose, by breaking down statistics. it could be a polite speech, correct, but i think cold. violence against women, discrimination, inequality, all deserve shock treatment. so i'm going to tell you about ifé, a woman who popped up on my personal blog one day in an entry i dedicated to condemning the violent murder of a woman like her. her name was ada, no axe, no luck and no magic wand... ifé is a sub-saharan woman. for three years in a row, he cried and despaired as he tried to survive in the first world, while saving to seek a better future in the third. for though her bright, smooth, black skin sometimes reflected neon, her every day was the red lamps that signaled her ordeal. it was the half-darkness. it was the dancing contract that allowed her to get a residency permit. it was the sinister choreography of domination, of abuse, of disrespect, of dehumanization. it was the bills he kept and it was the ones that the criminal took from him after every night of "services". jephthah wept much, but each tear reminded her that the alternative was to marry at twelve years of age a much older man chosen by her father, a stiff, rude one; to suffer a frightful mutilation to make her an object in the service of the lord of the house; to travel tens of kilometers daily hunched over the weight of fifteen liters of water; to breathe toxic smoke to transform what would here pass for waste into a single meal a day; to plow the earth with her nails; to give birth to a few children and see half of them die; to go hungry; to suffer, little by little, the loss of teeth, the brilliance of her eyes, the cracks in her skin; to shut down; to end up, at twenty-four, as a worn-out, worthless piece of furniture. a just, humane, values-based world still offers many rural women, like ifé, the terrible choice between bad and worse. this report is a cry of rebellion against that reality and an attempt to change it. getting it is everyone's responsibility.

member of the commission. – madam president, let me first thank parliament, the committee on women’s rights and gender equality (femm) and the committee on international trade (inta), and, of course, the co-rapporteurs ms malin björk and ms eleonora forenza, for the attention, the work and the time that they have invested in this report on gender equality in eu trade agreements. it makes a very valuable contribution to strengthening gender aspects in eu trade policy. the commission is committed to gender equality. eu trade policy already contributes to this goal through some of its instruments, for example, its sustainability impact assessments, the generalised system of preferences, the gsp+ and the trade and sustainable development chapters of the european union’s free trade agreements. however, we need to do more. to gather input from stakeholders, in june last year the commission and the international trade centre organised an international forum on women and trade, to which the honourable members mosca, rodríguez-piñero and forenza kindly contributed as speakers. the commission has already put some of the ideas that emerged from this event into practice, and i can assure you that we will continue to do so. the report identifies a lack of adequate data on trade and gender equality when it comes to determining the impact of trade policy instruments on women. in cooperation with other international organisations, for example the world trade organisation (wto), the international trade centre, united nations conference on trade and development (unctad), the oecd or the european institutes for gender equality, we are exploring how to better collect and use data on the impact of trade policy instruments on women. we are also looking to improve our analysis by using the most advanced methods, like the unctad toolbox on trade and gender. following a suggestion from this house, the commission and the international trade centre are also launching a collection of firm level data on women entrepreneurship and female employment in eu-exporting and importing firms. let me mention some further activities to contribute to the promotion of women’s economic empowerment: the european union’s recently reviewed aid for trade strategy introduces, for all its projects, the requirement of a systematic gender analysis. we are currently working with chile on gender-specific provisions in the context of modernisation of the existing eu-chile association agreement. these provisions will include commitments to effectively implement relevant international legal instruments on gender equality, such as the convention on the elimination of all forms of discrimination against women and a structured framework for cooperating and sharing best practices on women in international trade. the commission will keep the inta committee informed about the development of the eu proposals for these provisions on trade and gender. in the international arena, the eu actively supported the adoption of the joint declaration on trade and women’s economic empowerment on the occasion of the wto ministerial conference in buenos aires in december 2017. the declaration seeks to remove barriers to and foster women’s economic empowerment. we now need to move ahead with implementation. the commission is ready to sponsor several follow-up actions, such as organising workshops, collecting data on women’s participation in international trade, and applying a gender lens to our trade-related technical assistance. finally, the commission uses every opportunity to raise awareness of the importance of gender equality for economic growth and the opportunities that trade can provide, including through trade policy reviews in the wto. last but not least, the eu’s commitment towards gender equality and women’s empowerment has been expanded by the eu gender action plan too, placing gender at the heart of the european union’s actions, from international relations to commercial agreements, and holding all of us accountable for its achievements. i look forward to hearing your views.

on behalf of the alde group. mr president, commissioner, i would like to thank mr lundgren for his efforts to reach an agreement and the other alternative rapporteurs for the good work they have done. this directive will improve the training of professional drivers in professional transport and bring it closer to their needs today in a sector which is undergoing profound transformation thanks to the evolution of vehicles, roads and regulations. the incorporation of issues such as driving in extreme weather conditions, environmentally efficient driving or driving in particularly congested areas certainly adds to road safety. in addition, drivers' influence on the profitability of the service they provide is increased. finally, it will help to level the playing field in the internal market. these factors, combined, will improve the social and employment position of these professionals in the transport value chain. our main objective during the negotiations has therefore been to facilitate the processes of training and permanent recycling by means of technological tools or in-vehicle training processes. at the same time, we want to anticipate the needs of a sector which is already experiencing a real revolution in the new information and communication technologies and the emergence of new vehicles with clean engines and other features of autonomy and maintenance. finally, we regret that we have not succeeded in completely eliminating the exceptions which will remove from the scope of this directive those who carry out transport operations as part of their own business activity in the primary sector on journeys of less than 50 kilometres. most of these transports are carried out on secondary roads and these roads are generally in worse condition than the main roads, combined with the confidence that habit generates. more training would certainly increase road safety in these areas, which are the most accident-prone areas because of the intensity of traffic.
the rapporteur. madam president, madam commissioner, climate change is undeniable and a daily reality. and we're seeing an increase in extreme temperatures, forest fires, droughts, floods and storms, as well as the proliferation of invasive alien species and biodiversity loss, and on the other hand, competition for water and energy demand. the evidence of human responsibility for climate change is overwhelming and is already having devastating environmental effects and high socioeconomic costs, especially for the most vulnerable populations. climate change is also accentuating social disparities across our union. some social groups are more exposed than others because of poor health, low income, inadequate housing, lack of mobility or gender issues, among other factors. but the whole of the population is already suffering serious health problems due to pollution, with cancers, allergies, premature deaths, etc. a real social drama that also involves tremendous health costs. the money we don't spend on investing to correct the problem then multiplies in healthcare spending. the report i am presenting therefore deplores, first of all, the withdrawal of the united states from the paris agreement and presents alternatives and responses from the perspective of the role of cities and municipalities in the fight against climate change. the european union has a lot of work ahead of it and contributes - it must be said - to 9% of global emissions and its cities generate 75% of them. more than 70% of europeans and 73% of jobs are in urban areas. cities have a great responsibility for global warming and a great potential for solutions. as it cannot be otherwise, i really want to thank the efforts made by the other meps, the alternative rapporteurs, in reaching a majority consensus of all the political groups. it has been a lot of teamwork, involving several experts in the field, and we have collected an important social demand: to put the fight against climate change on the political agenda, once again and forcefully. the report can be a real political reference point on the role of european regions and cities in climate change. i also ask all the members of this house to vote in favour tomorrow and thus make an important step forward on the issue of global warming. it would be a real and definitive step forward in the fight against global warming. it should not be forgotten that the european parliament is the voice of the people and in this report it underlines the urgency and the extreme importance of combating global warming. the european commission must therefore take up and implement the proposals in this report, although sometimes i, as a spaniard, have to regret that it is precisely the commissioner for climate action and energy, mr arias cañete, who is known in my country for the measures against renewable energies that are being implemented in our country. you know it well: tax on the sun, etc. and, to make matters
