on behalf of the verts/ale group. – mr president, this parliament has to send a clear message to the commission and to the member states concerning the next multiannual financial framework (mff). if we want an ambitious eu, a union that is able to deal with key challenges of our times and to deliver real outcomes in terms of progress, sustainability, equality and fundamental freedoms, then we need to reverse the downward trend in the amount spent by the eu, a trend that has been aggravated by the current mff. if we need to fight against growing populism and euroscepticism, the worst thing we could do would be to adopt proposals from populists and from eurosceptics, because with a small budget the european union will be unable to deliver. thus it would be even more meaningless to those many people who already don’t see what the eu is here for. in other words, to demonstrate the added value of the eu, we need to invest more and more efficiently in policies where the eu can really make a difference. this has to be the first key message to the member states: don’t use brexit to make further cuts in our budget and diminish our ambitions. secondly, the next mff needs to focus more on delivering results in sustainability and in the fight against climate change. the eu must translate its commitment to the paris agreement into a real budgetary majority. that’s why our group stressed so much the importance of aligning the eu budget with the sustainable development goals and to significantly increase climate-related spending to reach at least the 30% target as soon as possible.
mr president, commissioner, today we are faced with one of the most important debates of the whole term of office, because we are talking, nothing more and nothing less, about what kind of europe we want to build in the next decade. and this is not just a budgetary debate, it is above all a political debate, because where we put the resources is where the real priorities of the union will be. we have signed many landmark agreements in this parliament: the paris agreement to combat climate change, the gothenburg agreements for a real social pillar; we have even signed the sustainable development goals. and it is now that we have to decide how we are going to finance them and, therefore, it is now that we are going to demonstrate the extent of our commitment. in recent months we have been hearing great philosophical phrases when we talk about the budget - mr omarjee said that too: some say it must be modernised and others say more must be done with less. this may look great in a headline, but this, budgetarily speaking, is not possible more with less, can't be done and the fact that we want to modernise a budget does not mean that we can cut it, quite the opposite. and this parliament has very clear ideas of what we want for the future financial framework and we could define it in three blocks. the first block: maintaining the financing of the traditional policies, i.e. agriculture and cohesion. we are asking our farmers and livestock farmers to produce in accordance with environmental criteria; to offer us quality products at affordable prices; to keep the population in the countryside and, above all, to encourage young people to enter the sector. and all of this cannot be done with less budget support. we also advocate a strong cohesion policy so that europe remains competitive, so that its regions reduce inequalities, so that it invests in innovation and, above all, so that this competitiveness does not come at the expense of wages and the social rights of workers. the second block is what we might call 'future' policies. here we not only want to maintain funding, but we want to increase erasmus grants, research programmes or investment programmes. and thirdly - and this is a very clear message - new needs require a new budget, and we do not want to pit one priority against another, as the commissioner said. i would like to end by highlighting two ideas which i hope the commission will listen to carefully. first proposal: the conditionality of the funds with respect to compliance with the rules, because we propose a system of sanctions for those countries which do not comply with the rules or their commitments, but we disconnect these sanctions from the cohesion funds completely. the union must help these regions and that is why we are proposing a just transition fund which will focus not only on the regions but also on the social challenges of this transition. and how do we finance all this? we have already said here: with new own resources; with taxes on sectors which no longer contribute to the public sector; with taxes on the financial sector; and with taxes on large companies which take advantage of the fact that there is no european regulation to avoid paying their taxes. i would like to conclude, mr president, by thanking all four rapporteurs for the excellent work they have done, for the negotiations and for the generosity with which they have negotiated, because that is how we can have a strong agreement, supported by the majority of the groups in this house.
mr. president, with a minute, i'll be direct and clear. we need a larger european budget, but one which does not undermine the fiscal capacity of the member states: they must complement each other. and we also have to have progressive models on capital income. we need more public resources, not less, to tackle the challenges that concern europeans, mainly unemployment, the environment, precariousness and poverty or tax fraud; the gains made in the fight against tax fraud would be an excellent source of revenue, along with new figures for eco-quotas or a tax on financial transactions. however, the priorities seem to be different. it seems to be rather the strengthening of europe's strength and its militarization, increasing or even doubling defence spending. we do not share these priorities set by the european commission. the priorities should be other: employment policy, support for small farmers, compliance with international asylum legislation, and the sociological transition of our economies and regions. and to do that, we need a stronger budget, but above all a fairer one.
madam president, commissioner, we are having a very important debate today which will shape the future of the european union, because we need to expand and improve the european union's own resources. and within that own resources package, these reports point to the need for the profits of the european central bank to contribute to the euro area budget, and to contribute to building that fiscal pillar throughout the euro area. it's a useful tool. it is an instrument which could bring in around 1 billion euros a year. it is a very important instrument, and it is not a tax instrument. there's no taxes behind this self-serve channel. and, moreover, there would be no need for a major reform of the treaties, as the house itself has said, the legal advice of this house itself. we need to value membership of the euro. we need to dignify the euro. parliament and the commission are united in this endeavour and the council must listen.

member of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, the comoros was included in the list of non-cooperating countries in the fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated (iuu) fishing on 11 july 2017, because it failed to comply with undertakings to combat iuu fishing. the decision to include the comoros on the list of non-cooperating countries was taken after a thorough analysis of the comoros’ stance on the fight against iuu fishing, and following its pre-identification in october 2015 and years of discussions with the comoros. the areas of concern haven’t been addressed by the comoros and the comoros haven’t fully implemented the measures agreed. the main shortcomings leading to this listing were related to, firstly, the flag-of-convenience policy pursued by the comorian authorities and lack of control over its foreign-based fleet register; secondly, evidence of illegal long-distance fishing activities by the comorian fleet; thirdly, the poor or non-existent monitoring and control capacities of the national authorities, and finally, the outdated comorian legal fisheries framework also played a part in the decision. according to our rules against iuu fishing, the commission must propose the denunciation of any bilateral fisheries agreement with such a country. therefore, the commission proposed a denunciation of the partnership agreement in the fisheries sector between the european community and the comoros. we share the issues raised by parliament in the draft motion for resolution and welcome your support. the commission remains fully open to working closely with the comorian authorities to guide them towards a better fisheries management framework, if they express the wish to do so. we are fully conscious of the difficult social situation in the comoros. taking effective measures against illegal fishing is essential to protecting the valuable national resources that can be a significant source of economic and social development in the comoros.
on behalf of the ppe group mr president, commissioner, the european union is one of the main actors in ocean governance and the fight against illegal fishing is one of its cornerstones. through its external action, it exports its sustainability standards and serves as an incentive for third countries to improve their fisheries management, which is beneficial both for the union and its consumers and for the sustainability of ecosystems and fisheries resources. the comoros has not taken any corrective action against the iuu vessels that are fishing in the comoros since the iuu vessels were flagged in 2015. therefore, i consider the 2017 decision to declare them as a non-cooperating country to be correct and i support the decision to terminate the fisheries agreement. i am aware that this decision will be detrimental to several member states, including my own, but we must send a clear and strong message, showing our firm commitment to the fight against illegal fishing and our rejection of any business that comes from it. however, this decision should not mean the end of cooperation relations with the comoros and it is important that this procedure be stopped in the event that its shortcomings are remedied by withdrawing the red card and allowing the return of the union fleet to the fishing grounds.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, commissioner, i would like to ask you to support a decision which we are taking for the first time in the history of fisheries agreements between the european union and third countries: the decision is to terminate the agreement we have with the comoros, which grants 70 fishing licences to vessels from spain, france and portugal in the waters of these islands. the agreement is part of the network of such agreements which enable our fleet to fish for tuna in the indian ocean. this action reflects the union's firm determination to maintain its global leadership in the fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, and that leadership is acquired by consistency between what we say and what we do, and it is on this that our credibility is based. the comoros is undergoing a 'red card' procedure which can identify it as a non-cooperating country in the fight against illegal fishing. this is because vessels flying this flag have been found to engage in illegal fishing practices. the authorities are putting very little energy and resources into monitoring and controlling fishing activity, and they are not updating their outdated fisheries legislation, which is in breach of their obligations under international law. for these reasons, we are proposing this decision for the first time. the european union has never before withdrawn from a fisheries agreement, and although the economic and social impact of this measure will not be great, we are clearly facing a failure, but a necessary failure, because to continue in this way is incompatible with the union's values. the european union is committed to sustainable fishing based on clear rules, but it must also show its strong commitment to fighting illegal fishing worldwide. today we are making this commitment a reality and we are doing so with two objectives: firstly, to help stimulate a different attitude in the sector and the fishing activities of the comoros; but, secondly, we are sending a message to other countries that may fall into the same temptations: if they want to continue working with the world's leading fishing power, they must assume their responsibilities, reform their fishing industry and adopt all the legal and material measures to eradicate this type of illegal fishing.
mr president, as other members have said, this is the first time that the european union has terminated a fisheries cooperation agreement on the grounds of illegal fishing. it's an important reason, what happens is that the situation of the country is a drama. i deeply regret that the comorian authorities have not taken corrective measures to solve the problems identified and that in these 30 years, in agreement with the european union, they have not been able to put in place a monitoring and surveillance system to control illegal fishing. the union of the comoros is a group of three islands in southeast africa, in the indian ocean, that stands out as one of the poorest countries in the world. i would also like to stress the importance of having effective measures to combat illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, one of the basic pillars of our fisheries policy. the union must ensure that these fishing activities, both at home and abroad, are based on the same principles and regulatory rules for the conservation and management of marine resources. i would like to stress what the european parliament stresses in its report: that the termination of the fisheries agreement must not, and must never, mean the end of cooperation with the comoros. we ask the european commission to continue the dialogue with these countries to ensure that cooperation with the fisheries sector can be revived as soon as possible and thus help to end the poverty of the people there.

member of the commission. – mr president, i am glad we are meeting today to finalise the adoption of two key files to achieve our 2030 climate target. bold regulations are essential elements of our legal framework for implementing the european union’s 2030 commitments under the paris agreement. they show our international partners that the european union is leading by example, because we turn our pledges into agreed action and we are on track on a long-term low emissions pathway. this week a step forward has been possible due to the constructive efforts of the negotiators from both institutions. in particular, i would like to wholeheartedly thank the rapporteurs mr gerbrandy and mr lins for their leadership on these challenging files and congratulate them on the result. we have been able to come to an ambitious and realistic agreement within three months. let me now highlight some specific elements of each of the two laws, starting with the effort sharing regulation, or climate action regulation. this regulation is a crucial instrument to accelerate the low—carbon transition in a number of key sectors of the economy, such as transport, buildings, agriculture and industry, not covered by the emissions trading system. it notably sets binding national targets covering well over half of the european union’s domestic greenhouse gas emissions in order to achieve a european union-wide reduction by 30% in 2030 compared to 2005. the trilogue agreement, which strikes a good balance between environmental integrity, fairness and efficiency, is the result of a thorough negotiation process that involved difficult compromises. the support and steering by the rapporteur mr gerbrandy, as well as the active engagement of the shadow rapporteurs ms ayuso, ms dalli, mr duncan and ms girling, ms konečná, mr eickhout, ms evi and mr jalkh, was crucial in this regard, and i particularly appreciate parliament’s crucial role in ensuring an ambitious outcome. parliament insisted on an early starting date for the emissions reduction trajectory. this saves more than 120 million tonnes of emissions over the period 2021-2030, hence it increases the additional effort by more than 10%. other examples where parliament left a good mark include the introduction of banking limits, the way the ets flexibility is accounted for with reference to the ets market stability reserve, stronger provisions on corrective action, a further substantiated review clause including reference to the manner in which all sectors of the economy contribute in the post-2030 framework and the lulucf flexibility with the inclusion of wetlands, and making their use conditional on annual member state reporting on their intended use. let me move to the lulucf regulation. the lulucf regulation sets for the first time a clear quantitative objective, together with a solid accounting framework, for emissions and removals from land use and forests. once again, this demonstrates to our international partners how the european union tries to lead by example. the contribution from land and forest in reaching the long-term climate mitigation objectives is critical because of the potential for anthropogenic removal of carbon from the atmosphere. forests alone currently cover more than 42% of the european union land surface. they have huge potential for climate change mitigation through regional sequestration and storage of co2. they also have the potential to substitute fossil—based energy materials. i am convinced that the lulucf agreement strikes a proper balance between conflicting interests, and as it was for effort-sharing, the trilogue agreement on this file involves some difficult compromises. the support and active engagement of the rapporteur mr lins, but also of the shadow rapporteurs mr brannen, mr turmes, mr flanagan, mr jávor and ms wiśniewska, was crucial in this regard. the european parliament has strongly contributed to the final shape of the legal text. the agreed provisions of the regulation clearly carry the european parliament’s signature, and i would like to offer some examples: mandatory accounting for emissions and the removal of wetlands towards the commitment of 2026, thus completing the european union’s scope for land accounting; the introduction of a safeguard to prevent decreasing the european union’s overall sink; obliging the commission to assess, at the review, the need for additional union policies and measures, and this includes exploring a post—2030 framework in view of the necessary strengthening of greenhouse gas emissions reductions and removals in the union. parliament’s hand can also be seen in a core article of the regulation on forest accounting. indeed, the rules and governance process for establishing forest reference levels were clarified, taking into account the main requests of parliament. first, the accounting rules were not locked in the harvest rates of the past and this should reassure forest-rich member states and the related industry. second, the forest reference level presented by member states through national plans will be adopted by delegated act. this will ensure the highest degree of involvement of parliament in setting these benchmarks. and thirdly, reflecting on the european parliament’s priorities, this regulation gives more prominence to long-lived harvested products. more wood products create positive incentives not only for the climate, but also for jobs and the economy. finally, keeping deadwood in forests will have environmental benefits such as for biodiversity. this shows the kind of balance that exemplifies the positive spirit of the negotiation. i invite you to support both motions and put europe on track to take its place as a champion of climate policy and to lay out our vision for the way this policy will implement the paris agreement over the next decade.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. mr president, climate change is a matter of global justice. fighting climate and empowering the world's poorest people are two sides of the same coin. and to do that, we need to generate negative emissions from land use and forests, and at the same time protect the right to food and land. with this view, i am glad that the trilogue has improved from the initial positions of the council and the european parliament, and i am also glad that the final report takes food security and food production into account. thanks to this, we will arrive at cop24 with a regulation that is a world first and can become a model for international negotiations. of course, let us not forget that we also had to take into account the rights to land tenure and indigenous peoples, because, again, the fight for climate and global justice go hand in hand.
on behalf of the ppe group mr president, the commission and this parliament are continuing to take steps towards compliance with the paris agreement and the fight against climate change. by 2030, emissions from transport, agriculture, buildings and waste management will be reduced by 30% compared to 2015. and this effort is going to be divided among the member states according to their per capita income. i think that is a good rule. this regulation will cover a number of measures to be implemented by the member states, such as improving forestry and agricultural management, replacing less efficient boilers in buildings, reducing waste disposal in landfills and promoting less polluting transport technologies. but member states have social, environmental, energy and industrial challenges, and so it is good that we have agreed to give countries different flexibilities in relation to meeting emissions targets. this will enable member states to target their reductions with the greatest technological advantages and lowest costs. i am also pleased that rules have been included which take account of the special situation of the countries most affected by the economic crisis. finally, i think it is very important that forestry removals can be counted in order to offset emissions. member states, however, need to develop computer systems that are robust and comparable. i would like to conclude by congratulating the commissioner on the efforts he has made during these months of negotiations, and also the council, and i would ask all the political groups to support the agreement in recognition of the great work done by the rapporteur of this house, mr gerbrandy, and because it is a good agreement. but above all, the collective political will to build a community in which we all recognize ourselves in our diversity has been diluted by more particular, more selfish, more extremist objectives: the only aim is to deepen a division of europe not seen since the end of the second world war. however, too often the debates we have in our house are far removed from what is perceived in the street. what do the media say about this europe which is moving away from the idea of integration of our founding fathers? the europeanist sentiment does not extend beyond the brussels bubble. we have long ago stopped seeking what unites us to defend what divides us. we've lost sight of our ivory towers. so in today's debate, i want to emphasise that the circular economy can and should be a circle to relaunch the european project of our founding fathers. i would like to draw the commission's attention to the fact that it should not miss the opportunity to turn this project into a new 'schuman declaration'. the transition to the circular economy is to choose the path of leadership in the world and to abandon the path of reaction. we must continue to exercise this leadership for the fight against climate change, as we committed to at cop21. a struggle which has the support of european society. these objectives are based on the reindustrialisation of europe with a low-emission industry. this is a feasible project that has a direct impact on the creation of quality and decently paid jobs. without jobs, any project will end up being an orphan of social support. only by creating new jobs can we bring about this change project; only with a cutting-edge, intelligent and sustainable economy will we offer a present and a future to our society. let us europeans make the circular economy our future in the 21st century, as the ecsc was the building block of the european union in the 20th century. we shall be adopting this first package of directives on waste, packaging, landfills and batteries and accumulators, drawn up by mrs bonafè, next wednesday. my report on environmental information is a small contribution to paving the way towards the circular economy so that we can make this transition to a new economy more agile and easier for our citizens, our economy and our common project. and mrs bonafè's reports, as well as the work of the alternative rapporteurs and all the people she has mentioned in her speech, are the crucial first stone of this new path that europe must take. our citizenship demands it of us. we say we are ready.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would like to thank, in this my second speech, all those who have worked on the dossier on environmental information, and especially andrés and kristi from the council, stefan and julia from this house, and andrew from the commission, without whom we would not have been able to get it through as quickly as we have. i would also like to thank the work of the alternative rapporteurs, whose collaboration has enriched and made the report more effective, and will help, as i said in my first speech, to pave the way for the implementation of the circular economy. when we began this mandate, president juncker made it a priority to create the conditions for job creation and the impetus for reindustrialisation after the dark years of the economic crisis that hit and continues to hit europe. in the moments before cop21 we all called for europe to take up the international leadership it had been losing in recent years and we committed ourselves to the fact that the progress of our economy had to go hand in hand with the environment. and next wednesday we must take this first step towards the european economy of the 21st century, a path we must take together with the european citizens, their industry and their social partners, to strengthen the ties that unite us in the european project of the coming decades; a real, feasible project in which each and every one of us can feel part every day of our lives.

companies and public institutions. in 2017, the commission also awarded the european digital skills award, presented to projects that encourage girls and women to take up digital skills and careers. entrepreneurship for women and lowering access barriers. the commission has funded web hubs, the first european community that connects business ecosystems and provides them with mentoring tools to support women entrepreneurs in the digital sector. every year, the eu prize for women innovators recognises outstanding women entrepreneurs and inspires others to follow in their footsteps. the pillar, with its work-life balance agenda. at the same time, i will try again over this year to unblock the situation in the council as regards the women on boards directive. another key priority is to end violence against women and girls. this is a particular challenge related to digitalisation – online violence and harassment against girls and women. we are working on several strands to prevent european commission is very pleased that the european parliament shares our vision about the place of women in media organisations as well as having in media a more diversified and realistic picture the rapporteur. madam president, the european union has been and must remain a global actor oriented towards peace, progress and solidarity. but peace cannot flourish amid poverty, injustice and insecurity. inequitable development - lack of opportunities - fuels conflict, destabilises regions and leads to disorderly population movements. climate change is threatening the very future of humanity and is increasing the frequency and intensity of many natural disasters. the summits in sendai, addis ababa, new york, paris and istanbul have underlined that we all live in one world, on a common planet, and that we will only improve and preserve it if we take on the shared responsibility of improving it between all and for all. this report calls for the european union to continue to take the lead in this solidarity responsibility. the lisbon treaty has established poverty reduction and eradication as the main objectives of the union's development cooperation policy, a policy aimed at promoting fundamental values such as respect for human rights, democracy, peace, solidarity and support for global public goods. in fact, the european union and its member states are the world's largest donors. they are so because of the financial weight of their contribution, but also because of their experience and leadership in the negotiations of the main international instruments. of the various financial instruments for the union's external action, the development committee is responsible for the review of three of them. the purpose of this report is to contribute to this review, initiated by the commission, of the european development fund, the development cooperation instrument and the humanitarian aid instrument. the report analyses the implementation of these instruments from january 2014 to june 2017 and 'although lacking important information, something that needs to be improved for the future' it gives a positive assessment of the implementation of these instruments, but also assesses them for the future and makes some recommendations until the end of their validity in 2020 and for the next multiannual financial framework. the evaluation has drawn on several of the commission's reports, a specific report prepared by the european parliamentary research service (specifically on humanitarian aid) and some other reports by non-governmental organisations and civil society actors. the challenges the european union has faced in recent years have not seriously undermined the effort of its actions, but above all they should not undermine them in the future, even with the foreseeable reducing impact of brexit, because there are other global actors who are willing to abandon their global responsibilities, something that the european union will have to take on at some point to replace them. that is going to be very necessary from the point of view of financial resources. we therefore call for a clear and committed timetable to achieve 0.7% of gdp. i would like to thank the alternative rapporteurs for their contribution to this report, because it is certainly not a contribution to correcting some of the points in the report but to re-incorporating whole paragraphs, different approaches, which have enriched that continent. the report stresses the need for at least 20% of the development cooperation instrument to continue to be allocated to the provision of basic social services and public goods. it called for the future budgeting of the european development fund, for greater involvement of civil society and local actors, for greater transparency, accountability and parliamentary scrutiny and for a review of the next multiannual financial framework. we are 12 years away from meeting the sustainable development goals: it seems like a long time, but it's just around the corner, and the effort has to be stepped up.
rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on budgets. – madam president, development policy instruments are of the utmost importance for showing the eu’s commitment to global justice and for the provision of public global goods. still, development aid needs long—term programing and predictability. the insufficient amount of eu resources devoted to external action and the need to react within the margins to unforeseen humanitarian emergencies are usually detrimental to meeting development aid goals in a more efficient way. furthermore, development money should only be used for development—related purposes, and not for other purposes such as covering internal refugee costs, externalising migration policies outside the eu’s border or paying the cost of returns and readmissions to countries of origin. last, but not least, the fight against climate change should play a more important role in development cooperation, and paris commitments should be fully reflected in instruments and programmes.
i would like to congratulate my colleague, mr enrique guerrero, on this report, although we are moderately optimistic about the report we are voting on tomorrow. optimistic, because parliament reaffirms that development aid is intended to eradicate poverty in a context of sustainable development and for nothing else; moderate, because we find it unacceptable that national interests in the field of migration management end up determining the european development agenda. we also denounce the fraudulent use of these items in the trust funds and we deeply regret the lack of coherence between development and trade policies, because business profit is continually prioritised over the objectives of sustainable development. the union's cooperation policy and instruments should follow comprehensively the 2030 agenda for sustainable development, the paris agreement on climate change and other relevant international agreements. our optimism, as i said, is moderate because we know that, although the position of this parliament is firm and clear, the ball is in the court of the states. we are asking that the voice of the european citizens represented here be respected, who are always much more supportive and fair than their governments and who have for years, for example, supported 0.7% of gdp for development aid.
the rapporteur. madam president, as the commissioner, mr nimica, has said, what we have to do now is to look to the future and win the future for development cooperation. it is clear that with these instruments we will live until 2020. but we have to look beyond that and we have to focus on the sustainable development goals at the 2030 frontier. it is true that we need more consistency. it is true that we need simplification, but this can be achieved without making development cooperation policy subordinate to short-term political strategies which may have a strategic interest. if this report is adopted by parliament tomorrow - as i hope - it will not be a report that will outline the future, but it will be a good basis for us to start discussing with the commission and the council the future of the multiannual financial perspective.

mr president, the new york declaration commits us to the adoption of a global compact on refugees in 2018 and a global pact for safe, regular and orderly migration, to be signed in morocco in december. forced migration is a human phenomenon, a reality as a consequence of armed conflict, terrorism or climate change. according to the unhcr, it is already known that, with data from 2015, about 65 million people were living in a situation of forced displacement. the emergency trust fund to address the root causes of migration in africa or the union's legislative package on migration and asylum are two key instruments to help manage this situation. the member states must commit themselves to the high representative and promote the agreements of the new york declaration. only together on a global scale can these challenges be addressed. we must assist, help and support the developing countries that are hosting refugees. coordination between humanitarian aid and development policies is essential to improve effectiveness, efficiency and assistance to refugees. cooperation between countries and regions is a must. we need the global approach as a global response, and that combines fundamentally three areas: the area of diplomacy, the area of security and the area of development cooperation.
mr president, we are witnessing a sharp increase in the phenomenon of mobility, not only for economic reasons but also because of political persecution, crises or conflicts. no region in the world is more or less immune to these population flows and therefore international coordination should be strengthened to better manage these flows while at the same time safeguarding the rights of migrants and refugees. dialogue between receiving, originating and transit countries is essential. the european parliament must play a leading role in the united nations in drawing up global agreements now that we are entering the so-called intergovernmental phase of negotiation: we can offer our experience and our views on this problem. i believe that a realistic analysis and debate of migration is necessary, taking into account its positive potential, but we cannot ignore the security concerns of the transit or home states, nor the limits to their capacity for economic and social integration. in recent years europeans have become well aware of the phenomena of migration and its tragic problems. we have experienced the so-called refugee crisis, which has affected the eastern mediterranean as well as the central mediterranean. even today, the mediterranean is still the scene of daily news about irregular migration attempts or flows. we need to continue to intensify dialogue and cooperation with countries of origin and transit. i would like to stress the importance of the valletta action plan and the agreements reached with some of the sahel countries. in short, we europeans must give priority to our relations with africa and tackle the deep roots of migration. underdevelopment, crises and conflicts explain many of these flows. and that's the end of it. i believe that we must also intensify - and i end with this - the fight against the mafias who traffic in the lives and dreams of so many human beings.
mr president, commissioner mogherini, it is rare in politics that the urgent and the important coincide, but this is the case, because if there is something urgent and important it is to change the european union's negative view of immigration, which is not a crisis, nor a threat, but a constant in history that is here to stay. and the european union has a duty to deal with it in an orderly and safe way with all the parties involved, and to do so in accordance with european law, which establishes not only the moral duty to provide help to those fleeing from despair, but also the legal obligation to do so in accordance with international law and european law in particular. this is the time to fulfill the objective of the united nations: a global compact, a global pact for immigration, that will order the matter and confront the enemies of that global commitment; outside the european union, the trump presidency, and within the european union, the xenophobic discourse of some countries, such as the orbán government. but it is time to do so also, in accordance with the common european asylum system and by finally imposing a legal and safe way for regular immigration into the european union: humanitarian visas.
vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, i listened carefully to this debate and i thank this house for its support for the difficult work we are trying to do in the un system on the global compacts on migration and refugees, in a global environment that, it is quite clear to all of us, is a challenging one and in particular on issues like this. we are well aware of our responsibilities in this respect, i would say on two different levels, both of them extremely important. one is the investment in the un system and in multilateral approaches, as such. we know very well that this is challenged from different sides in the world of today. and we know very well that the world looks at the european union to create, consolidate and strengthen alliances globally to work in a multilateral manner. this could be true for issues related to different things, from trade to human rights and crisis management, but also on migration and refugees. so we know that the un system counts on us. we know that the partners around the world count on us to make sure that the multilateral approach and the multilateral method are the ones followed when tackling a global issue. i would never – never – say ‘problem’, because we’re not talking about a problem, if not for those fleeing countries at war or facing forced movements. as for the specifics of our responsibilities, we know that we have a responsibility to uphold a certain approach to the migration issues and also on refugees. on refuges, this is clearly full respect of values and, in particular, full respect of international principles and regulations. and it is also a matter of the basic moral compass that for us as the european union is a must, and this entails full respect of human rights and the consideration that every single person that is a refugee or migrant is first and foremost a human being and, as such, has individual human rights that are impossible to be considered as subject to discussions or negotiations. we also know that we have a responsibility to build consensus globally on a certain way of managing migration. i say ‘managing migration’. i don’t say ‘stopping a problem’. i say managing migration, which is the partnership approach. the european union has not always been on this line. the european union has, in the past, several times either turned its eyes away from this issue, leaving the front-line member states alone. or some other times – i still sometimes see this temptation here and there – it has taken the security approach, as if it were a border management issue. migration movements are massive global phenomena that need to be managed together with partnerships that involve countries of origin, countries of transit, and countries of destination. some of these countries are at the same time the three and the international agencies of the united nations system. i will give you an example of how this partnership approach is bringing results, because this is the basis on which we are going to work. and we are already working in the un system to try to build a global alliance around this model. take the dramatic situation in the detention camps in libya. we have discussed this in this chamber several times. and several times i have told you we are working to close these camps. last december we established a joint task force between the european union, the african union, united nations with unhcr and the iom, and we set the target of emptying the detention camps and, as an intermediate target, to save 15 000 of the people that were in the detention camps in libya in the coming two months. we have managed to save more than 16 000 of them in less than two months and have assisted them in returning voluntarily to their own local communities and supported them with reintegration projects and economic start-up activities. and we are about to completely empty the detention centres in libya. the news was shocking and striking when we saw the images and the stories from the detention camps. i would also like us to tell the stories of those whom we managed to save as we empty the detention camps. because this helps us pass on the message inside europe and outside of europe, that this is not the policy we’ve chosen purely out of values and good feelings. this is also the policy that is bringing results. it’s cooperation and partnership, and not walls, that is bringing results in migration policies, and we are starting to see good results. we will continue to take this approach, hoping for a united position between the member states of the european union but let me tell you we will exercise our responsibilities and duties in the un context on migration and refugees. we will, i imagine, continue to discuss this issue in this chamber in the coming months as we go towards the summit and then the finalisation of this work towards the end of the year. i count on this parliament to follow this work very closely on a day-to-day basis to help us to build this way of working, both internally within the european union and outside it. i will not refer here to the issues related to dublin or to other decisions related to solidarity internally that still, i believe, should be tackled. but today in this building i speak of a global compact both on migration and on refugees based on the principles of human rights and respectful partnership across the globe.
vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, 10 days ago chemical weapons were used yet again in syria, on the outskirts of damascus this time. we have said very clearly time and again that, even when the war in syria disappears from the headlines, we always have to remember that the war in syria is not over yet and, in particular, that the use of chemical weapons is a pattern which we have seen developing from the regime side over the years. the entire international community, we believe, considers the regime’s use of chemical weapons entirely unacceptable, but for europeans, it most certainly is. our response as the european union was very clear, united, and immediate. the use of chemical weapons is unacceptable to us, and those responsible must be held accountable. accountability is also a key element when it comes to building a new future for syria, as i think president macron very rightly mentioned here this morning in the chamber. we, as the european union, have always worked in all the different contexts that we could, and we continue to do so, in order to re-establish an independent mechanism for investigating the use of chemical weapons in syria. today we are working to enable the organisation for the prohibition of chemical weapons to investigate and report on the most recent attack. you have all followed the targeted strikes carried out by france, the united states and the united kingdom on chemical facilities in syria with one objective: to prevent the regime from using chemical weapons again. you will also have seen the reactions, including the declaration i issued a few hours later on behalf of the 28 member states, and the council conclusions which we adopted yesterday and cover not only the issue of the use of chemical weapons, but also, more generally, our common position on the conflict in syria. the main point here is this: now more than ever, it is clear that the only sustainable, the only pragmatic, the only possible solution, to the war in syria is a political solution. after seven years, there is certainly no doubt: there is no military solution to the war. the only way to end this conflict is through the intra-syrian talks in geneva, between the syrian parties, under the leadership of the united nations. now more than ever, it is time to invest all our work, all our convening power, all our political capital, to push the syrian parties towards the negotiating table and finally start meaningful negotiations; not just talks for the sake of talks, but meaningful negotiations. this was the message that i delivered just the day before yesterday in saudi arabia, where i had the honour to open the annual summit of the arab league and where i also had the opportunity to meet the un special envoy, staffan de mistura, with whom i spoke at length about the current situation and how to relaunch the political process. i also had the chance there to discuss and share with all the leaders of the region not only our analysis, but also the need for a renewed regional effort in order to try to put an end to the war in syria through a political process. next week, exactly one week from now, all the relevant international and regional players will gather for the second brussels conference on the future of syria and the region, which i will have the honour and the responsibility to chair, together with the united nations. this brussels conference was planned long ago. we had a ministerial preparatory meeting as far back as september at the margins of the un general assembly. it will be even more relevant today in the current circumstances because it is the first huge international event that gathers different players that are, let’s say, on different sides in this war, and the eu-un co-chairmanship is obviously an excellent opportunity to try to build a path towards a political solution. we will make full use of the conference to do just that: to shift the focus now to diplomacy and peace-making. with no meaningful un-led political talks, it is only a matter of time before the next military escalation comes. the risk of splitting the country into zones of influence is increasing by the day. the geneva talks represent the only path that can lead towards a peaceful, united, independent and truly democratic syria, in all its diversity. at the brussels conference we will have over 80 delegations around the table, as i said, with very different positions among themselves. i see this as an opportunity to collectively and consistently commit to stopping the violence and supporting the geneva process. we want to bring together – it will not be easy, but nor will it be impossible – those who have leverage not just on the syrian parties, as we always mention – in part because on the syrian opposition we have the leverage ourselves and we have been working with them and we continue to work with them day by day –, but mainly those who have leverage on the syrian regime, which so far has not committed seriously to the political talks in geneva. it has not entered into the mechanism and the dynamic of negotiation. those who have leverage will work together towards new and meaningful intra-syrian talks under the auspices of the un. i am also proud of one thing that i believe this parliament will understand very well. we will host at the conference hundreds of delegates from syrian civil society groups – syrians – women and men, most of them coming from inside syria. i know that some may think that this is a marginal issue, that it is even something nice to say, something naive, that as war is going on it is a sort of distraction, but these are the real people on the ground who are experiencing the suffering of the war. they are also what i would call the everyday syrian heroes. they are incredibly precious for the country and its future because syria will not be taken out of the conflict or be reconstructed in the sense of building the country a democratic future if the international community, starting with the european union, does not invest in those syrians that want to build a democratic, peaceful and united country. the future of syria lies – and this is a minor detail that the international community tends to forget –and has to lie only in the hands of the syrian people and no one else. it is not a chessboard. it is a country with people and citizens, and we want to bring the voices, the faces, the hopes, the dreams, but also the ideas and the aspirations of the syrian people to the stage. that is democracy. that is the way we intend it. we believe it will have to be up to them to decide on the new institutions of the country, to make them inclusive, democratic, and, at the end of the day, make sure that every syrian man, woman and child, beyond ethnicity, faith and political or social background, everyone will have the right to feel protected, safe, welcome, and at home in the syria of the future. many people ask about preconditions – who has to step back or forwards, one step in or out. the real answer, which is borne of pragmatism, from our side, is this: we need a political process that guarantees that every single syrian inside the country, including those that are currently outside of the country, can feel at home in the syria of the future. that is it. that is what the political process in geneva should guarantee. what we can do as europe, as the international community, is to invest all our resources, to move from a context of never-ending escalation on the ground, which is repeating itself cyclically, to one of true political negotiations. it is not easy, otherwise it would probably have been successful long ago, it is not easy, but we will work on this in brussels next week, on renewing our humanitarian pledges, which are essential and vital, on the resilience of the syrian people, and on the only way to make our humanitarian work sustainable, which is to unlock the geneva talks. this is what we are working on every single day with the united nations, and this is what we will try to deliver in brussels next week.

on behalf of the vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, honourable members, let me thank the chair of the committee on foreign affairs, mr mcallister, and the rapporteur, ms schaake, for this important report and good collaboration over the past months. let me first share a few reflections on the mid-term review and the instruments covered by the report. i fully concur with the report’s findings that our instruments are generally fit for purpose, but have been stretched to their limits in the past years. in particular, the european neighbourhood instrument has been a pivotal tool to force reforms in our neighbourhood. at the same time, as the report notes, the challenges that we have faced in the neighbourhood have shown the need for greater financial resources and more flexibility. the instrument for pre-accession assistance is unique in addressing the objective of preparing candidate countries and potential candidates for eu membership. the next instrument for pre-accession should be clearly positioned in the context of the new western balkan strategy. the mid-term review concluded that our instrument contributing to stability and peace was relevant, effective, and efficient and had a unique added value, and we fully agree. the european instrument for democracy and human rights promotes some of our core values in a challenging global context. we have witnessed increased pressure on human rights defenders and closing spaces for civil society in many countries. we intend to enhance our support to human rights defenders even more in the coming years and continue our work on eu election observations. finally, the partnership instrument is a young instrument that has helped us invest in the european union’s soft power, where and when we needed it the most. in the next three years we want to focus it on some priorities, such as economic diplomacy, climate, health, peace and security, and digital issues including cybersecurity. let me come to the future architecture. i would like to reflect on the lessons from the mid-term review that guide our thinking for the proposal we will soon publish. first, the volume of external action funding needs to match our political ambitions. to deliver on our ambitions we need adequate financial resources. second, too often we have had to adapt our policies to our instruments. it is time that we adapt our instruments to our political priorities. this is why we have proposed merging our development and foreign policy instruments into one broad instrument covering neighbourhood as well as development and international cooperation. third, one broad instrument does not mean one single policy. it does not mean less funding for certain regions or themes. there will be clear funding dedicated to each policy area in order to reflect our political priorities. fourth, we need more flexibility and more responsiveness. our aim is also to set aside a significant share of unallocated funds. this will allow us to react to changing circumstances without diverting funds from other policies. we want – and we agree with the report on this – to make the eu budget more accountable, more transparent and understandable to the public. that includes, as announced yesterday, bringing the european development fund inside the budget, as this would significantly enhance parliamentary scrutiny. finally, it should be easier to work for the security of our citizens and partners. for this reason, the high representative has proposed setting up a european peace facility to finance missions and capacity building as an off-budget funding mechanism. let me conclude by saying that our debates on budgets should finally focus on our citizens’ priorities, instead of focusing simply on instruments. we would like our conversation to be driven by the great issues of our times, from migration to the situation in syria, from security to africa’s development.
on behalf of the ppe group madam president, as an alternative rapporteur for the ppe group i had the opportunity to coordinate my group's vision on a vital issue for the european union's foreign policy. i would like to thank and acknowledge the work done by my colleague marietje schaake, who has undoubtedly helped a great deal to get the text we are voting on tomorrow in this house. the effectiveness of the european union's external financing instruments is fundamental if we are to ensure that the european union has the necessary tools to implement its global, neighbourhood and enlargement policy. what we are discussing today is not just the mid-term review of these instruments, but also the recommendation for the new architecture from 2020 onwards: what needs to be changed or optimized in these instruments so that they can continue to do the important work they do in our foreign policy. i would like to emphasize three points. the current external relations budget is only 6% of the multiannual financial framework. however, with that amount the european union has achieved considerable successes in our external relations, from a successful agreement with turkey to stem migration flows to the minsk agreements to achieve stability and peace in ukraine. secondly, we must stress the importance of having specific instruments for specific aspects of our international agenda. the specific funding for our neighbourhood policy instruments must be secured. the european neighbourhood instrument is the most effective way to influence migration, security, economic development and better governance of our strategic partners who are geographically closer to us. i don't have time left.
on behalf of the verts/ale group. – madam president, i welcome ms schaake’s report, especially when it comes to reviewing the current external financing instruments, underlining the need to align them with the sustainable development goals and proposing some improvements. when it comes to making proposals on the post—2020 architecture, we are not so enthusiastic. we know – and we have just heard once again – that ms mogherini and the commission are working on a major overhaul of this architecture, merging the existing financing instruments, including the development cooperation instrument, the human rights and democracy instrument and the instrument contributing to stability and peace into a unified single instrument. until today, we have not heard – beyond the rather empty argument of simplification – of any good reason why all these important thematic tools of the union should disappear and be merged. on the contrary, the recent mid—term review conducted by the commission has just confirmed that these instruments are fit for purpose and, in the case of the instrument for stability and peace, ‘a key tool for the eu to underpin its diplomacy and tailor—made projects’. this mid—term review also stresses in its conclusions that this capacity ‘must be further strengthened in any future architecture’. we acknowledge that the new structure should be more rational and more flexible. we even acknowledge that there is room for merging some external-action and some development-cooperation instruments, but we stress the importance of maintaining separate instruments for enlargement, neighbourhood policy, development, human rights and democracy, civilian conflict prevention and civilian crisis response.

the rapporteur. madam president, we are debating in this house today the approval of the framework agreement between the european union and australia. the recommendation on the agreement and the report accompanying it received broad support in the committee on foreign affairs a few weeks ago. i expect the plenary to back it up tomorrow. but first i would like to thank the political group alternate rapporteurs for their cooperation. and i also thank the european external action service for its collaboration in the preparation of the report on this framework agreement. i will now highlight some aspects of the agreement and of relations between the european union and australia. the relationship is very solid, based on many historical links, common values and principles. there is, yes, a physical, geographical distance, but there is a great political and values proximity. australia is, so to speak, a natural ally of the european union in that vast asia-pacific space, which is very dynamic and increasingly important in today's world. in the 2017 foreign policy white paper, the australian government underlined the vital importance of relations with the european union. these relations have been growing in recent years, as is shown by this framework agreement, the leaders' forum and the first contacts already made with a view to negotiating a free trade agreement. in addition, we agree on many of the high-level dialogue mechanisms that take place in the asia-pacific. on the bilateral level, i stress the importance of launching negotiations on a free trade agreement. australia is a country that believes in free trade in the face of unfortunately rising protectionism. we have a growing trade and economic relationship in which the european union enjoys a large surplus. the other areas of dialogue and cooperation established by the agreement are numerous, for example: foreign and security policy, human rights, economy and trade, education, culture, research, innovation, energy, transport, justice and global challenges such as terrorism, climate change, weapons of mass destruction, global governance or development. australia is indeed a major regional player and also a very active member of global bodies addressing these global challenges. for example, he was recently on the security council, now on the united nations human rights council, and he is also a member of the g20 since its founding and has chaired it in 2014. australia is also represented in a number of regional and subregional organisations in asia-pacific. i would also like to stress its alignment with the european union's positions on sanctions against russia, north korea and syria. i would also mention its participation in operations against daesh and its numerous peacekeeping missions to the un. it is also present in the so-called combined maritime forces, in operations against piracy and terrorism in the western indian ocean. the framework agreement also provides for cooperation on other major global and regional challenges. i am referring, for example, to climate change, to migration and to the problem of development, all of which are dealt with in the resolution we are voting on tomorrow. finally, the positions of the european union and australia on the international scene and the challenges of our time are often the same. australia, like the european union, is also a player committed to global governance based on international law and multilateralism, which we also want to preserve. it also supports free trade, development aid and the fight against terrorism. the european union wants to be increasingly present in the asian regional forums; its positions are very similar to those of australia, and i therefore trust that australia will cooperate closely with the european union in these forums and make every effort to ensure that it fits in fully in all of them, including the so-called east asia summit. in this large and complex asia-pacific region, australia is a country very close to our values and interests; it is necessary to continue strengthening these relations and precisely for this purpose the framework agreement will be a very useful instrument. i hope that the support for the recommendation on the agreement and the accompanying report will remain very high.
on behalf of the vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, thank you for the opportunity for this debate on the eu—australia framework agreement. the agreement reflects our wish to give a modern framework to relations with one of the eu’s closest partners in the asia—pacific region. it will allow the promotion and expansion of our cooperation with australia across a broad range of areas of mutual interest. eu relations with australia are excellent and i sincerely believe that they will continue to evolve further. we are geographically very far apart but we work together on a daily basis on the global stage. our cooperation on foreign policy has been constant and intense. just to name a recent example, australia has shown great solidarity in condemning the salisbury attack and took concrete actions in response to it. we take part in the same military missions to preserve peace and security around the world and we particularly appreciate australia’s participation in our operation off the coast of the horn of africa. we also have good development cooperation, especially in the pacific, focusing on sustainable development, economic growth and gender equality. we are incredibly like—minded and, as a consequence, political dialogue with australia has been intensifying and an ever—increasing number of political contacts have taken place over the past years. in 2016, we launched the eu—australia leadership forum, a unique platform for european and australian political business, media and civil society leaders to meet and nurture the relationship with new ideas and proposals. in 2008, the eu and australia signed a partnership framework, which opened new avenues for cooperation. we also hold a regular security dialogue at senior official level. the signing of our framework agreement last summer by high representative mogherini and foreign minister bishop came as a natural evolution of our partnership. our framework agreement makes our relationship fit for the 21st century. the european union and australia share the same world view. we support democracy, the rule of law and human rights and we are active players in multilateral organisations such as the united nations and the world trade organization. we have also shared interests in tackling key global challenges, such as sustainable development, humanitarian aid and the fight against terrorism. we work together against climate change and to better manage migration. we both want international trade to be free and fair at the same time. eu—australia cooperation in the pacific is growing. we have many shared interests in sustainable energy, climate change and ocean governance. we are also looking into how to associate like—minded donors, like australia, in the post—cotonou process. to complete the advancing political relationship, we have decided to work towards launching negotiations for a free trade agreement. we have gone through a number of important stages of the preparatory process. the commission has carried out an impact assessment and held free trade agreement (fta) co—opening discussions with australia. the draft directives for negotiating the free trade agreement were published by the commission in september. the discussions in the council are ongoing. the european parliament has fed into these deliberations with a dedicated report adopted at the end of october. i trust that the council will adopt the negotiating directives soon, enabling the commission to launch the free trade agreement negotiations before the summer. the commission looks forward to continuing cooperation with the parliament in this matter.
