member of the commission. – madam president, i don’t need to repeat how important economically, politically and, in particular, symbolically schengen is. we all know. i would like to express my thanks to the members of the schengen working group for their continuous work and in particular the european parliament’s ‘mr schengen’, mr carlos coelho. thank you for your report and this very timely debate. it comes at the moment where we are reflecting a lot on the future of our common external border management but also on how to enhance our internal security and free movement in the schengen area. the thing is, we need to be pragmatic but without ever forsaking our values and fundamental principles. this is why one of our concerns is how to better make use of the existing tools at our disposal to fully implement the legislative measures we have recently adopted and to conclude pending legislation. but we also look to the future. how do we see the future as regards borders management but also as regards the free movement of european citizens in an area without border controls? my answer to this is clear and simple. we need to take joint responsibility for the management of our common external borders but also ensure mutual trust among member states and everything that is implied by this. during the last three years, as we all know, we have been working together intensively in order to safeguard schengen. during the last three years schengen has been confronted with the most important challenges since its conception. several member states have reintroduced temporary internal border controls to address irregular migration flows and secondary movements and also in reaction to the multiple terrorist attacks. but temporary internal border controls cannot and should not become permanent ones. that is why it is so important to preserve the right balance between ensuring mobility, on the one hand, whilst guaranteeing security on the other hand. it is important to use, but also to improve, all the tools we have at our disposal to ensure high standards of security. it is precisely to maintain this balance that the commission has proposed, among others, to amend the schengen borders code, which is also one of our priorities. member states retain the main responsibility when it comes to security. the temporary reintroduction of border controls is a legitimate measure available to member states confronted with a serious threat to internal security or public policy in exceptional cases. we should never forget this essential point: that internal border controls are, and should indeed remain, exceptional. our proposal does not intend to make controls at internal borders easier or permanent. on the contrary, we have proposed reinforcing the procedural safeguards. the reintroduction of border controls should only be a measure of last resort, with the council having the last word. and the views of the other member states affected by such decisions must be duly taken into account. alternative solutions, such as police checks and cross-border cooperation must always take priority. i would also like to stress the schengen borders code amendment, which aims to adapt the rules for the reintroduction of temporary internal border controls to the current needs to respond to evolving and persistent serious threats to public policy or internal security. in the meantime, the commission is in contact with the member states concerned on lifting internal border controls as soon as possible, allowing them to maintain the same level of security by using other tools, such as reinforced police checks and increased cross-border cooperation. we all agree that we should return to the full, normal functioning of the schengen area as soon as possible. i made this very clear in all my recent contacts with the countries that have done it. mobility inside our schengen area requires secure external borders. this is exactly why since 2015 we have made significant progress in our external borders management. a key element has been the establishment of the european border and coast guard agency, bringing together the national border guard authorities of the member state and the european borders and coast guard agency, which now operates along the european borders. as part of our proposal for the next multiannual financial framework which we put forward on 2 may 2018, we proposed to almost triple the expenditure for external borders management, migration and asylum, which could fund 10 000 border guards by 2027 for the european borders and coast guard agency. the eu budget for the management of external borders, migration and asylum would reach more than eur 34.9 billion overall, compared to eur 13 billion for the period 2014-2020. a new integrated border management fund will help to guarantee a high level of security in the european union by ensuring strong and effective border management, while safeguarding the free movement of persons. if adopted, it will reinforce financial and operational support given to member states in securing the european union’s common external borders. we equally need to know who is crossing our borders and be able to stop those who pose a threat whilst ensuring mobility for bona fide travellers. we have already made substantial progress. the development of the entry/exit system is starting. we have also reached a political agreement on the european travel information and authorisation system (etias). i would like to thank you for your work on this file too. we also have proposals on the table to strengthen existing systems, such as the schengen information system where negotiations are about to close, and the european criminal records information system in respect to third country nationals convicted in the european union by creating this centralised system on third-country nationals. again, we need to reach swift agreements on these files. we also aim to improve the exchange of information and to make our systems interoperable to help us counter terrorism and serious crime and secure our borders, with full respect for data protection. our proposal on interoperability will be a game-changer in this respect, and we need to complete the work on it by the end of this year. as you can see, we have many building blocks in place to strengthen our external borders, but we need to make yet further efforts to preserve schengen, to make it even stronger and more resilient. finally, let me repeat: the absence of internal border controls constitutes the very essence of schengen, but in a common area without border controls, security concerns are common too. this is why we must do everything to preserve the careful balance between free movement and mobility, on the one hand, and security on the other. this is also what our citizens expect from us, and we can only achieve this through a coordinated and united schengen framework, which brings me to my last point. schengen should include romania and bulgaria too, because a more inclusive schengen is a more secure schengen. we call on the council to finally decide on bulgaria and romania to join the schengen family and croatia too, once all criteria are met.

the rapporteur. mr president, i take this opportunity of the debate on victims to express my deepest condolences to the families of those killed today in liège. i want to say that we are not just talking about words here, i want to give you facts too, because this directive protects all victims and also the victims of terrorism. i would also like to thank the co-rapporteur, mrs mlinar, for her work, as well as all the alternative rapporteurs and the secretariat who have worked with us. since i came to this parliament i have seen the lack of victim laws and i have encouraged the commission to come forward with a directive on the support, rights and protection of victims of crime. today, seven years later, i am here again to discuss how we can improve that directive, because what we have now is not enough. the 2011 directive paved the way for a harmonisation of victims' rights, but not all member states have done their homework: some countries have not implemented it well. that is why we are making recommendations in this new report to the states to fulfil what we said in 2012. in addition, we introduced new guidelines to improve the lives of victims. some relevant issues are the role of victims during criminal proceedings, particularly witnesses, because they often suffer secondary victimisation. we have also stressed the importance of the istanbul convention in the fight against gender-based violence. for example, it is important to harmonize the crime of harassment because there are still many countries that do not have it. we also wanted to emphasize that, regardless of the state in which the crime was committed, the victim's rights are guaranteed. another important part of this report is the protection of children. in most cases, children are victims of gender-based violence and are the most vulnerable. one of the main failures we have seen in the implementation of this directive is that neither the professionals, nor the judges, nor the police have received sufficient training and education to explain to the victims that they had these rights. we have also included in the report the importance of awareness campaigns to inform victims and society about how to enjoy these rights. perhaps the most significant achievement of the directive, of which i was rapporteur in 2012, was what was called 'individual assessment' and, unfortunately, not all member states have been able to carry it out: an individual assessment is essential to know the specific needs that a victim has. the failure to implement article 22 has created many problems, for example, for victims of terrorism. so i worked to make sure that they were represented, because in the 2012 directive they were not - there was only a small reference. the latest attacks in europe - paris, brussels, nice, berlin, barcelona, liège - have caused a great many victims. the commission notes that the 2012 guidelines do not provide for any specific rules on the application of the principle of equal treatment for men and women. in the various hearings we have held in this parliament they have complained about how they have been treated, and in this report we have highlighted the needs that these victims of terrorism have told us during these months. we should guarantee them not only their economic rights, but also their right to memory, justice and dignity. the report also calls on the member states to establish legal mechanisms to criminalise the glorification of an act of terrorism if this humiliates the victims, because it can cause second victimization. and finally, mr president, i would like to end by calling for a regulation or directive for victims of terrorism.

mr. president, mr. prime minister, first of all, thank you for coming before us today. as this is a debate on the future, i would like to refer mainly to young people and i welcome, first of all, their commitment to the erasmus programme, which you have experienced yourself. i am also pleased that the multiannual financial framework which president juncker presented to us at the beginning of the month provides for a significant increase in funding for this programme. but i also believe that young people need to be better informed in schools about the background, the objectives and the functioning of the union's institutions. you can't value what you don't know. and that is why i am very pleased that on 22 may the council adopted the commission's recommendation on the promotion of common values, inclusive education and the european dimension in education. this european subject, so to speak, seems to me very appropriate and i very much welcome this initiative by commissioner navracsics. secondly, i would like to point out a serious problem which is now affecting the whole of europe: the low birth rate, ageing and, consequently, a future with fewer young people. we are facing a demographic winter, which is already here in some regions, and i would have liked the demographic question to have been given a little more weight in the multiannual financial framework when allocating funds between the regions. i would like you, mr prime minister, to share with us some thoughts on these issues of young people and demographic decline.
mr president, since the fight against climate change is a major challenge facing the world as a whole, but also the european union, i believe that the leadership that luxembourg is exercising in the council of ministers to promote an energy transition towards clean energy is very positive and can be strengthened by the addition of claude turmes to the council of ministers. i encourage you to continue in this direction to achieve greater penetration of renewables in the next directive. but it is true that, having heard of the multiannual financial framework and, yesterday, the proposals for the cohesion fund, and since demographic decline is one of the major challenges facing the european union, i cannot understand how the depopulation criterion is not part of the criteria for redistributing resources and thus putting the spotlight on an important challenge. i would certainly ask you, mr prime minister, to take this criterion into account and to make the objective of depopulation a priority objective in the council of ministers of the european union.
mr president, mr prime minister, i share your view that unanimity is essential for an effective foreign policy. you have said that the policy of peace in europe is a weak policy based on unanimity. i ask you whether you do not think that this unanimity is an insurmountable obstacle to fair taxation in the european union, to sustainable taxation with the internal market. do you not think that unanimity must be overcome in order to achieve mechanisms in the field of taxation which will make it possible to overcome the existing disloyalty between the states in the field of taxation, in the field of tax harmonization? you say we must wait for the world to move forward on this matter. but then we will never make progress, because the very construction of the welfare state is the consequence of some countries starting as vanguards, as we did with social security, the progress towards justice. we have fair social security today because a hundred years ago we made that very breakthrough.
mr president, mr bettel, you have heard in this debate on the future of europe words of appreciation for luxembourg, a founding country of the european union from which great figures in its construction have come. a small country, one of the smallest, but i have not heard a word about the ravages of inequality, not precisely between big and small - caused by the crisis - but between rich and poor, between creditors and debtors. and it is essential, in the face of inequality, that when you talk about taxation, you do not talk about lowering taxes, but about ensuring that luxembourg is not the depository of the illicitly acquired fortunes of the corrupt in the middle of europe; and when you talk about resources for the european union, you express your willingness to contribute more as a rich country to the construction of a better europe than this, because that will be the key to being able to combat the malaise and populism that have redefined the political landscape of the most impoverished by the crisis in italy, greece, spain; because, without tackling this problem, there will be no future for europe.
mr president, the general tone of the european commission in dealing with unemployment or industrial problems, such as the world overproduction of steel and aluminium, has been to do nothing. in spain, in 2009 the directorate general of labour approved an employment regulation file of arcelormittal for twelve thousand employees which has been extended until the end of 2018. and all this, despite the global profits of this multinational: 3 670 million euros in 2017. the position of the european union should be to defend the working people and not the profits of the multinationals. we should protect ourselves from imports in order to have the capacity to build an alternative and sustainable production model. however, for the commerce commissioner, there is no harm in good that does not come. you are taking advantage of the situation to renegotiate with the united states government neoliberal policies, a new zombie ttip. and without any transparency. and without any negotiating mandate from the council. because all they want to defend are the interests of the german car industry and the multinationals.
mr president, this report is very important because we must know where fish comes from. in my country, galicia, canned fish is very important in the representation of the volume of production. as far as labelling is concerned, it is very important that the species, the zone, the method of production and also the fishing technique are shown. unfair competition cannot be allowed to continue, but i also call parliament's attention to working conditions. the report says that the european union clearly has little credibility in terms of labour standards for fishermen in other countries, as it does not take on its international responsibilities within its own borders. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on this report, which is also very important for my country.
mr. president, residency-for-investment schemes are a real scandal, because we have no control over where the money comes from. basically, it is a policy that what it does is that people who want to come to the european union to earn their honest bread we do not let them in, and people who bring money that we do not know where from we give them residence permits. in addition, i have to say that in spain, where since 2013 we have given up to thirty thousand visas, we are leading this issue with two identified very serious problems. the first is the impact on the housing market. money has been allowed to enter the housing market, favoring developers, but with a very, very negative impact on housing prices for the majority of the citizens. and then, on the issue of the origin of money, in the spanish case, the first country of origin of money is china. and in china, it's illegal to take more than $50,000 out of the country. how is it possible that chinese investors come to spain later to invest, in exchange for residence, five hundred thousand, one million euros? it is a real scandal and that is why we are asking the commission to please act and to draw up a european legal framework to tackle this issue.
mr president, as is well known, there are states which offer 'golden visas' in exchange for an economic investment of between 250 000 and 10 million euros. third-country nationals thus obtain a residence permit which, depending on the member state granting it, grants freedom of movement, tax advantages, access to the single market or citizenship. but they've been investigated by the oecd. they have been for possible abuse for the purpose of tax evasion. these investigations have detailed how 'golden visas' are used to weaken the fight against corruption in the european union and its neighbouring countries. the phenomenon has increased in the last six years, driven mainly by millionaires from china, russia, libya, iran or venezuela eager to find a safe place for their money and a passport that saves them the paperwork in case they have to leave their home countries in a hurry. 'golden visas' issued in exchange for a particular investment have been linked in many cases to money laundering, corruption and organised crime. and therefore to the financing of all kinds of illegal activities, such as drug trafficking and terrorism. i am therefore, along with other members, saying: 'european citizenship, european legislation'. i am the rapporteur for council regulation (ec) no 539/2001 on the issue of visas. in this connection, commissioner, i propose that you launch a legislative initiative amending that regulation in due course and making it compulsory for all member states to comply with it.
mr president, golden visas, residence and citizenship look like issues which belong to the national legislation of the member states. but they are not – and they never have been since the lisbon treaty entered into force – because they fall under a common european visa policy and european legislation. golden visas have a negative impact on the status of eu residence and citizenship. they have a negative impact on the common fight against corruption, money laundering and fiscal unfairness. european residence or citizenship should not be bought in a black market or sold out by member states’ governments. finally, they have a negative impact on equal rights, equality before the law, because they benefit the rich, and they are an offence against most fundamental eu values. my conclusion is clear, crystal clear. a new european visa code and a common european strategy are needed in order to fight against not only corruption but also tax evasion, fraud, fiscal fairness and fairness for all.
in writing. with the crisis some eu member states saw the possibility of improving their income by granting citizenship and residency to applicants who bring money into the country by buying real estate or investing in a company. this has repercussions on the rest of the union, especially in the case of citizenship, as holders of the citizenship of a member state automatically acquire citizenship of the union and several of its rights and privileges, and can therefore become a form of parasitism on the common assets of the union. at least half of the member states allow the granting of 'golden visas'. the ep has expressed concern that beneficiaries of these programmes do not have to meet the same conditions as other applicants. their grant may prove unfair because they offer opportunities to the rich that are denied to people without money. they provide opportunities for corruption and crime, as second passports are useful to criminals, tax evaders and money launderers, who may need new identities and places to escape to.

on behalf of the ppe group mr president, first of all, i would like to say that this is a very important report, because in recent years the european union has had to face several catastrophes in the form of fires, floods, storms, earthquakes or migration crises. these emergencies have shown that the resources available in the european union are not sufficient when a disaster reaches very large dimensions or affects several states, and the example we have is the forest fires in the warm dry seasons. the european union needs cooperation mechanisms adapted to this reality and to the new circumstances that conflict or climate change may bring. we therefore support the creation of a european reserve in addition to the resources of the member states, but without replacing them and provided that it is coordinated by the european union. it should also be borne in mind that some member states affected by the crisis may not be in a position to contribute the funds previously committed to the european union mechanism. prevention by the member states and monitoring by the commission should also be strengthened. the existence of this mechanism should not allow member states to relax their guard, either in the means or in prevention. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mrs gardini, on the very effective and balanced work she has done on this report which we are going to vote on tomorrow. and finally, i would like to applaud the budget increase proposed by the commission, which is consistent with an increase in the capacity of the civil protection mechanism.

mr president, i congratulate the commission and also the rapporteur, mrs gardini, and the alternate rapporteurs on this work. a job that helps to create the european union, to make more europe. responding and protecting citizens from solidarity and coordination in the face of disasters is one of the great initiatives we are discussing here today. climate change is one of the biggest challenges we face in the immediate future and we could say we are already fighting it, but we need to know in advance and be able to prevent the consequences. every year we have examples of disasters; last year, doñana, portugal - with even human lives lost. so we have to work from this unity and coordination to prevent it. these disasters have also highlighted the need to work from a higher efficiency and effectiveness. the member states alone are not able or incapable of combating them in the necessary way. i therefore welcome this initiative and would like to stress two points in particular. i am aware that the climate change observatory has not been launched and i think that would be an important initiative, but other initiatives are being put forward that can help us move forward and which i hope will have the necessary support tomorrow. we need a risk map that allows us to differentiate which areas face specific risks and thus be able to prevent them better, whether they are seismic risks or lack of water resources, etc. in short, we can anticipate the circumstances of each of the regions, and also adapt and coordinate this with other mechanisms such as the solidarity fund. we must make this fund more responsive to needs and more equitable, better adapted to the per capita wealth of the area, but most importantly also including the value of the environment. the environment when it suffers also has to be repaired and therefore this fund has to incorporate the economic value that the environment also has.
mr president, there is undeniable evidence that in recent decades natural disasters have increased in frequency and intensity, taking many lives and destroying many infrastructures and ways of life. but we're also seeing the recurrence of these natural disasters, and that means we have the capacity to learn and to prevent and to try to respond in advance to what's predictably going to happen to us. this has been the fundamental lesson of the sendai framework and the cancun global platform, which we have to apply within the european union. i think it is a good proposal to increase the capacity and resources of the european union for action, because while maintaining subsidiarity we must increase solidarity. we must have a european response to disasters affecting european citizens.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank the european parliament for raising the issue of registered partnerships in connection with the commission’s proposal for a recast brussels iia regulation. this proposal facilitates the resolution of cross-border legal issues in family matters and provides protection to children. our proposal focuses on the shortcomings regarding parental responsibility matters. parliament has also flagged these up in the past. they now require our urgent action. as parliament has noted, we did not propose changes to the provision on matrimonial matters by addressing, for example, the possibility for couples to choose a court for divorce, or extending the regulation’s scope to same-sex couples or registered partnerships. the results of the public consultation undertaken by the commission did not provide sufficient evidence to justify making urgent changes in the area of matrimonial matters. our assessment was that it is not the right time to change these rules. the key objective of the brussels iia revision is to propose significant improvements for children facing difficult situations. these need to be addressed urgently. i am happy that parliament and the commission have a common goal. in cross-border cases we want to prevent children from ending up as hostages of long legal disputes. we also want to facilitate cross-border legal proceedings for families by various means, including by reducing the length and cost of procedures. very importantly, both parliament and the commission want to provide the same level of protection to all children. i would like to stress that, in our proposal, we have ensured that the improved protection of children applies to all children, irrespective of the civil status of their parents: that is, regardless of whether or not they are married or in a registered partnership. a prompt agreement on this proposal, requiring unanimity in the council, is within reach. the commission is committed to engaging closely in the negotiations with a view to finding a good outcome for the benefit of children.

about understanding that gender is fundamental and a key driver in all sectors when it comes to sustainable development. all our staff must also be more sensitive to this across the board. we also need adequate funding. the recent midterm review of the external financing instruments has been, as you suggest, a great opportunity to measure the scope of gender-sensitive initiatives in our development cooperation. following this analysis, eur 50 million has been reallocated to provide additional funding to this key priority in the period 2018-2020. our overall financial support to gender equality is increasing. from the data already available for the 2017 report, around 65% of eu official development assistance (oda) has been committed in gender-sensitive ways. this covers all sectors, from education and health, to agriculture, transport, justice and employment. this is a visible increase from 2016 when the percentage was 58% of eu oda. with regard to data collection and targets, it is now mandatory to measure the impact on gender equality of all eu-funded actions. a big effort has also been made to align the monitoring framework with the 2030 agenda. the 2016 gender action plan report provided us with a solid basis for measuring quantitative progress made. the ensuing 2017 report will allow us to go even deeper in the analyses, also from a qualitative perspective. overall, gender analyses are increasingly informing our new initiatives. awareness raising and training of commission staff have also been promoted. finally, let me recall that last september, together with the united nations, we launched an unprecedented spotlight initiative to eliminate violence against women and girls. the initiative focuses on particular forms of violence against women and girls that are prevalent in specific world regions: femicide in latin america, trafficking and economic exploitation in asia, sexual and gender-based violence, including harmful practices, in sub-saharan africa, domestic violence in the pacific and the caribbean. despite the large amount the eu has dedicated to this initiative – eur 500 million – it will not be sufficient to tackle all forms of violence. so we have invited other donors to join forces with us. with regards to the women, peace and security field, let me just underline that it is highly important when working in conflict prevention and peace building processes to integrate effectively a gender perspective in all operations and missions from the inception phase. this year we have been making an effort to harmonise reporting requirements and leverage as much as possible the coordinating mechanism at the country level. i hope you will agree that we still have a lot of work ahead of us to the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, young people represent about 17% of the union's population. one in three is at risk of falling into poverty or social exclusion. more than 11% of those the growing frustration of young europeans and that this was translating into a rejection of the institutions, which we are already seeing in several countries. too many university graduates are unable to find employment or are stuck in one precarious job after another with no clear future. the austerity measures adopted in the context of the crisis have had a negative impact on citizens in general, but especially on the youngest, who have been the most affected by the cuts in education, culture and social services. europe cannot afford to have its young people disconnected and socially excluded. nor, of course, waste his talent. we cannot ignore the potential and creativity of 90 million young europeans. we cannot afford to have a generation so prepared not to take an active part in social and political life. it is essential that young people feel heard and are engaged in strengthening the european project. it is essential that they have spaces for participation. this is one of the main demands of the european youth and therefore also in my report. in it i wanted to highlight the european cooperation in the field of youth, the implementation of structured dialogue to ensure the participation of young people, the open method of coordination and, of course, some of the policy proposals and initiatives such as the 'investing in european youth' initiative, the new european solidarity corps and the youth employment initiative. however, much remains to be done. and, for example, we need clearer links between the implementation of youth policy and all european programmes; an improved framework for transparency and monitoring of youth policies; central coordination involving all relevant actors in the different sectors; a strategy with better communication and participation tools and, of course, greater financial support from all programmes. and to achieve this, we have set out four key recommendations in this report. the first is to give young people a voice, to facilitate their participation in decision-making and policy development, so that their needs and ambitions are reflected and we also take into account the diversity of european youth; we must explore alternative forms of participation both individually and collectively. the second recommendation is to reduce inequalities, ensure sustainable inclusion in the labour market and ensure a dignified and independent life for young people; further work must be done to ensure that job opportunities are of quality and commensurate with their training. the third recommendation is that we need to pay attention to all the key areas to ensure a sustainable future, from modernizing education to paying special attention to the mental health of young people. and finally, of course, a financial commitment; we cannot increase participation in programmes such as erasmus or strengthen the european youth guarantee if we do not provide the necessary funds; we cannot finance some programmes if we have to cut others; and of course we cannot accept a cut in the european social fund, which is key to the acquisition of new skills for the unemployed and, above all, in the fight against social exclusion. commissioner, this bleak future i spoke of at the beginning is not inevitable. we all have a responsibility here to make a difference. i hope that the new european youth strategy will help to build a better future for them. if we accept that our youth must be one of our priorities, let us put all the means at our disposal so that this generation does not live worse than the previous ones. it's just a matter of will.

member of the commission. – madam president, for more than 10 years now, the union’s ecodesign policy has proven to be an effective instrument for improving the environmental performance of energy-related products. one of the success factors of this policy framework is the way we go about establishing the requirements; through a robust and transparent process, with the close involvement of all stakeholders along the way. this has resulted in broad support for ecodesign and energy labelling from member states, businesses, consumer organisations and environmental ngos. the commission is very pleased to see that also in this house there is strong support for a continued, and strengthened, implementation of this policy. let me outline briefly what the commission is already doing to improve its implementation. firstly, as regards the decision-making process we are aware that the development of measures takes time. this time is needed to ensure a robust technical analysis and have a transparent process where stakeholders have many opportunities to comment on our work. moreover, given the sensitivity of this policy in some quarters, the college has decided to strengthen political oversight. this includes, amongst others, political level scrutiny at different stages of the process and the adoption of measures in packages to underline the added value of this policy in terms of monetary and energy savings. as regards market surveillance, member states clearly need to do more to ensure compliance of products with ecodesign and energy labelling requirements. the commission is assisting national authorities with this task, in particular by funding joint surveillance projects and facilitating exchange of information. the product registration database that we are establishing for energy labelling will also help in this respect. another important way to strengthen ecodesign implementation is in its contribution to the objectives of the circular economy. in fact, our current ecodesign regulations already tackle reparability, durability and end-of-life aspects of certain products in support of circular economy objectives. but more can be done and your own-initiative report indicates many areas where improvements could be made. the commission is keen to explore various possibilities, and in fact the current ecodesign working plan 2016-2019 makes a strong commitment to contribute to the objectives of the circular economy. issues such as durability, reparability and recyclability will be examined in a more systematic way when proposing new regulations and when reviewing the existing ones. for example, we are investigating whether a reparability score for domestic appliances could be included in energy labels in the future. the core idea is to provide incentives to make products last longer and be easier to upgrade, repair and recycle. this is not an easy discussion: for example, while a more energy efficient product directly leads to money saved for consumers, a product that is easier to disassemble does not necessarily have such direct benefits. also, if there are circular economy requirements, it needs to be possible to check them. it is one thing to check how a product performs. it is quite another thing to check how it was produced, for example using recycled materials. the commission is however convinced that these challenges can be overcome and that, together, we can enhance our existing policy framework to drive our markets towards more sustainable products and a truly low-emission, energy efficient and circular economy.
on behalf of the ppe group madam president, commissioner, ecodesign is a key step in continuing to move towards the new european model of a circular and low-emission economy. better regulation of the design and manufacturing phase of products is essential. this will make it easier to reuse products, to disassemble them, to repair them and to combat planned obsolescence. in this way we will avoid damage to the environment and reduce manufacturing costs. the importance of ecodesign has led the vast majority of parliament's groups to agree on the measures to be taken. we have been aware that, in order to move towards a new way of producing and consuming, it is essential to regulate all stages of the life cycle of a product. this report deals with the directive adopted under this title in 2009. however, almost ten years after its approval, we cannot be completely satisfied with its implementation. we must learn from our mistakes and come up with more firm and concrete solutions, which in turn will be a powerful tool against climate change. we are therefore convinced that the report presented today represents a step forward and progress towards the circular economy model, the model which will allow us to pollute less and create more and better jobs in europe. i would like to thank the rapporteur for her work and for the willingness of the other rapporteurs to work together.

member of the commission. – madam president, thank you so much for your remarks and for you suggestions. i completely agree with you about zero tolerance and, of course – above all – prevention. the recent cases of sexual misconduct reminded us firstly, that we need to continue to work towards a zero-tolerance culture against sexual exploitation and abuse. there is absolutely no room for relaxed efforts and lenient behaviour towards allegations of any kind of misconduct. secondly, we need to live up to our ethical and legal responsibilities as a leading donor of humanitarian and development assistance across the world. we need to support all our partners in their efforts to prevent, to identify at an early stage, and to respond to cases of sexual misconduct. we also need more transparency and more accountability across the board. we need to safeguard our work. our role is unique; saving lives and empowering people is a fair and upright duty. so our work is too important to be compromised. this is my very strict message to all our partners. i shall now answer some specific issues, and i would like to start with oxfam. we have collectively suspended the conclusion of any new contracts – these amount to a total of more than eur 90 million – until we are satisfied with the new mechanisms put in place to prevent, report and respond to sexual abuse. with regard to our support to antónio guterres’s efforts, as the european union we fully apply the un standards of behaviour in its common security and defence policy missions, and this year the council adopted revised standards of behaviour. of course, as antónio guterres has said many times, again, no zero tolerance for sexual abuse allegations. and as regards our monitoring of the use of our funding: first, we assess the financial, operational and administrative capacities of the ngos that apply to receive funding. secondly, we carry out regular on-site visits during the implementation of the project on the ground. third, audits of management and control systems are performed during the implementation of the action, and this includes visits to the project sites, implementing partners and beneficiaries. and fourth, there are audits of legality and regularity of the operations once the projects are finished. by way of example, in the humanitarian field (in my field), last year 50 projects with a value of almost eur 500 million were audited during their implementation and no issues relating to sexual misconduct were detected during these audits. so no doubt we have to continue in order to fight against any sexual abuse, but there is also the other side of the coin, and this is why i mention our audits through 50 partners on the ground.
in writing. the european socialists consider it essential to bear in mind that in any humanitarian emergency there is a serious risk of abuse and/or sexual exploitation of people in extremely vulnerable situations. we are therefore gravely concerned that the culture of silence, intimidation and abuse will continue as soon as the media focus on this issue is removed. the european union should reconsider funding of non-governmental organizations such as oxfam after reports emerged that some of their employees had paid for years for sex with disaster victims while on humanitarian missions. special mention should be made of the united nations, which has turned a deaf ear to allegations of abuses against syrian women by some of its staff and organizations such as the international rescue committee for at least three years. it is necessary to raise awareness of this problem and to ensure the protection of women and girls in order to prevent sexual exploitation in situations of war or in the context of humanitarian disasters of any kind. it is not possible to continue to ignore systematic abuse and to tolerate victims fearing precisely those organisations which are supposed to guarantee their well-being and ultimately their survival.

in writing. transport is responsible for a quarter of eu ghg emissions. since 2013, despite warnings from the scientific community, emissions from this sector have been growing steadily, threatening the achievement of the goals of the paris agreement on climate change. as it is not subject to emissions trading, it is the states that have to develop transport policies to reduce emissions, but little or nothing can be done with economies heavily conditioned by the automobile industry, on which up to 10% of gdp depends. the sector continues to produce polluting vehicles, with a more than amortized model, and no changes are envisaged even in the face of a high real demand for electric vehicles, to the extent that german delivery companies have had to manufacture their own vans. without penalties in europe for misrepresenting emissions and with governments and the commission fearful of job losses or relocation, even the least ambitious targets are falling short. the new measures adopted to reduce emissions from combustion engines will be of no use without a genuine commitment to the electrification of freight transport in all its aspects.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, the development paradigm we have chosen to maintain our identity as a union, to maintain our global leadership and our social model, is based on sustainable, smart and inclusive growth. these three characteristics are manufactured with knowledge and values. they therefore need the support of a flexible education system, which is constantly changing and focused on providing people with the training they will need to enter adult life in the best conditions. i think it should be emphasized that all the improvements in education that we demand from the institutional, from the public, will only work if we take on what is our responsibility as citizens, as parents. we cannot assume that we are complying, and not doing so delegitimizes us to demand anything from teachers, from teachers and from the system in which they work. we need an education in equality. no stereotypes, you know? we need digital literacy, mastery of visual language, the ability to develop critical and creative thinking and the habit of working in teams, combining skills, abilities and knowledge. we need to teach diversity as a source of value that must be respected. and of course, to promote pluralism and solidarity. because this is the basis of inclusive growth which is the basis of stability and social justice. the challenge of achieving these objectives requires investing, first, in the professionals in the sector, reviewing the tools we offer them to train and adapt to change. and to offer them technology not as an end but as a tool in the service of a profession, of an intelligence that can never be artificial. organize the whole system with equal opportunity in mind. i therefore fully support extending the principle on which the european higher education area is based to the other levels of education. that is the basis of the european educational area to which this report refers: facilitating mobility, mutual recognition. to encourage exchanges of people, teachers and students, and of good practice. i believe that this process would make it possible to move towards a concept that we need: the european talent.
in writing. the challenges facing the union cannot be met without an education system better adapted to a global, changing and competitive environment. when we talk about 'modernizing' education, however, we are not just talking about making better use of new technological and digital opportunities. it is also about updating educational methods according to the best scientific evidence. we know that schools are not just 'assembly lines' of educational outcomes, but that people, their skills and preferences, matter. the education system is not working with crude, docile materials, but with diverse human brains, shaped by millennia of biological evolution and exposed to different social and cultural influences. identifying both the talent and the learning difficulties of students early is crucial to reconciling equality and excellence. in this respect, individual differences in the abilities of european pupils should be studied and taken into account. education must be at the heart of the european political agenda. quality education is fundamental to the development of a strong and united europe, with active citizenship participating in the construction of the european project.
the rapporteur. madam president, i would like to thank my colleagues, first of all, from the committee on fisheries, for all their contributions to this report. ladies and gentlemen, aquaculture in the european union provides sustainable, high-quality products to the consumer, and our european sector is one to be proud of. however, although aquaculture has been growing steadily worldwide for half a century, its potential has not yet been fully realised in the european union. the growth of the sector sometimes faces several problems. among them are the lack of available sea space for their activities or administrative obstacles, particularly those arising from licensing procedures, or the competition that exists on the world market, combined with insufficient information to the consumer about aquaculture products from third countries, as regards their quality, environmental footprint, social conditions, fish welfare, or the bad image that citizens sometimes have of aquaculture, and so on and so forth. it is true that good initiatives and intentions abound. the european commission published a communication in 2009 focused on building a sustainable future for aquaculture. in 2013, it published a report on the strategic guidelines for the sustainable development of aquaculture in the european union. the new common fisheries policy also aims, among other things, to give new impetus to aquaculture in the european union, allocating funding of eur 1.2 billion for its dissemination for the period 2014-2020. however, implementation did not meet the sector's expectations, and the initial enthusiasm soon turned to disappointment and defeatism. what do we need to do, then? the strategies proposed by the european commission are still very relevant today. we must simplify administrative procedures, ensuring the sustainable development and growth of aquaculture through spatial coordination planning, enhancing the competences of aquaculture in the european union or promoting a level playing field for operators in the european union and exploiting their competitive advantages. and all of this remains a challenge that must be met. a large group of scientific advisers has recently issued, at the request of commissioner vella, a report entitled 'food from the oceans: how can we get more food and biomass from the oceans without depriving future generations of their benefits?' your recommendations, ladies and gentlemen, are very relevant, and i share them all fully. we need to integrate a paradigm - as they say - of responsible ocean food culture into the overall policy agendas at the level of european and global systems. and also, as the report says, the development of mariculture in europe must be taken to a higher and more strategic level, through a comprehensive and coordinated political strategy. in summary, the problems have been identified, the diagnosis is good and the solutions proposed so far are very relevant. what is needed is political momentum in a context of mutual respect for each other's roles between the institutions of the european union and the local and regional administrations of the member states. the necessary subsidiarity for the management of aquaculture in the european union must be combined with reinforced action at the level of the european union, setting objectives at the level of the european union, while opting for regionalised objectives adapted to the particularities of each branch of aquaculture at local and regional level. i'm finished, your honours. we should not forget that the european parliament has been a co-legislator since 2009 and that any future policy will have to be jointly developed by the council and the european parliament. and i'm particularly proud of these accomplishments. i would like to conclude by saying that there are imminent opportunities and appointments which we must not miss if we are to give the european union's saltwater and freshwater aquaculture the place it deserves. and we must also seize the opportunity that this report gives us.

vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, first of all, let me thank you all for having expressed quite clearly a sort of convergence and a certain unity behind the work we are doing to try to preserve the nuclear deal with iran. it is the same unity that i have seen in the commission, the same unity that i have seen in the european council, in the foreign affairs council, and the same unity that i have seen uniting the european union within our union, but also with our international partners all around the world. let me stress this point because we have a responsibility as europeans at this time. the world is looking at us to try and preserve this achievement – no achievement is perfect, but it’s an achievement – and it’s also looking at us to find ways themselves – our international partners – to contribute to preserving these agreements. i have heard a certain confusion on the extreme right of the chamber. you know i never enter into these discussions, but i think i have to clarify a couple of things. one is the nature of the joint comprehensive plan of action (jcpoa) because fake news can produce fake news and can itself become fake news. let me be very clear on this: the nuclear deal with iran is not a treaty. it has never been a treaty. it is a multilateral agreement that was negotiated for 12 years under the mandate of the un security council, which mandated the high representative of the european union to facilitate the negotiations between iran, on one side, and germany, france, the uk, the us, china and russia, on the other side, to reach an agreement that then became a un security council resolution annex. so the legal framework that legitimates the jcpoa is not in the nature of being a bilateral or multilateral treaty. this is why it has not been ratified by parliament, but it is an annex to the un security council resolution. there is a un security council resolution that unanimously endorsed and approved the text of the jcpoa and if you want to see it – sorry, the colleague has disappeared, as fake news disappears from time to time – the signed version of the jcpoa is in my office. you’re free to come and see it. it exists. it’s 102-3 pages long – it takes some time to read it and probably a lot of time to understand it – but it exists and it’s available on the website for everybody to consult it. indeed it has a legal basis, being a un security council resolution document. as such, technically speaking, the unilateral move of the united states administration is the unilateral decision to stop complying with the un security council resolution the united states itself voted. that is just to clarify what the jcpoa is. the second element of confusion i see especially – well, only – on the extreme right part of the chamber is this – and i understand the political dilemma that some political forces might have at this stage, namely following the trump agenda of destroying multilateralism and going only to bilateral agreements or affirming european autonomy. in french i would say ‘c’est où votre souverainisme?’, because for me protecting and preserving european interests – security interests, economic decisions – at this stage is a matter of priority. i’m surprised that some forces that have always argued for sovereignty and autonomy are now tempted to follow not brussels but washington. i think this is a mistake. this is a mistake that goes beyond the nuclear deal with iran, but i leave this for political reflection in some parts of europe. what is at stake today? first of all, what is a stake is the risk that iran decides to restart its process to achieve a nuclear weapon. this is what we are talking about. the agreement is not perfect. i don’t know about you, but i don’t know anything in diplomacy – not even in life – that is perfect. no agreement, no deal is perfect, but this agreement is working. this agreement’s purpose was – and still is – to prevent iran from developing a nuclear weapon and it is preventing iran from developing a nuclear weapon. that’s it. the risk is that, were this agreement not in place tomorrow, what would be the immediate consequence? nuclear proliferation? iran developing a nuclear programme that is not peaceful? the region going into a spiral of nuclear proliferation? and we know the region. we know the conflictuality of the region and some of you were perfectly right: the risk of slipping into a major scale conflict is real. it’s perfectly possible. there are two other issues at stake: the credibility of multilateralism and of international agreements – i would say of un security council resolutions. the arguments that whatever is signed can be destroyed unilaterally after a few years is a dangerous one. i often gave this example in washington. if a private company signs an agreement, when the ceo changes the agreement stays in place. if we introduce the element of uncertainty of agreements signed, the entire world collapses and the credibility of any negotiation – of any negotiation – collapses, and the international system also goes in that direction. so what is at stake is – and our responsibility is big in this – to try to maintain the credibility of diplomacy and multilateralism and, at the end of the day, bilateral agreements as well, because if you can unilaterally withdraw from a multilateral agreement, why shouldn’t you do the same on a bilateral agreement if at a certain moment you change your mind? third, what is at stake is the autonomy of the european union. this goes beyond the nuclear agreement with iran. this would lead us to a different kind of debate, one that we will surely have at some point, but it is essential that the european union, together with our international partners, is able to take decisions based on merit, based on our interests and our values, and based on what we think and decide is good for us and for the rest of the region and the world, that, by the way, was a joint analysis and a joint decision not only with our american friends, but also with the rest of international community. otherwise, the un security council resolution would not have been unanimously adopted. we didn’t move from where we were, and our analysis of what is in our interest and the global interest stays the same, especially after 11 reports that the deal has worked and that iran is compliant. i believe that we need to be able to affirm that the european union positions are determined in europe. having said that, the risk of not managing to save this agreement is real and i think we should not underestimate that we are running a risk. even if we do all we can – and we are doing all we can – to preserve this agreement, there is a risk that this derails. i think we have the power and the instruments, together with our member states and together with the other international partners we have, to prevent this agreement from being completely disrupted. but there is a risk that this work does not succeed. i think this is the worst case scenario because this would undermine security – nothing to do with stability – and would undermine the nuclear non—proliferation regime and the credibility of the west and of multilateralism and diplomacy. this is why i believe that, even if it’s difficult – and i see all the limitations – we have the responsibility to try to achieve this result. even if it’s difficult, we must we must do all we can together to preserve this agreement, and this is exactly what we are doing because, again, the scenario of not having the agreement in place would be a disaster for europe, for the security of the middle east, for the proliferation of nuclear weapons, and i believe also for the united states of america. (applause)

madam president, in a debate on human rights in the world it is also important that we talk about what is happening in europe. because here austerity policies have affected the basic rights of the population, such as education, health, social security or housing. moreover, we are witnessing how punitive populism is used as an excuse for terrorism and immigration to generate hate speech. in this way, the far right has gotten its anti-immigration, anti-refugee and islamophobic rhetoric adopted in many countries by the main parties and, above all and most worryingly, by governments like hungary's or now also italy's. we also have european countries which continue to apply legislation which allows detentions without charge or trial and, under the pretext of security, normalize repression and the restriction of the right to demonstrate or freedom of expression. we are facing an authoritarian invasion of our democracies, of which valtonyc or alsasua are clear examples. let us not be hypocrites, let us not demand from third countries what we do not fulfil in our own. let us strive to respect human rights and freedom of expression in europe.

member of the commission,on behalf of the vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, honourable members, thank you on behalf of the commission and the high representative. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr paet, for today’s report and the light he is shining on this very important subject. in recent years, as he said, the cyber—threat landscape has changed dramatically, underlining the need for a strategic approach to cyber—threats and challenges. that includes the need to look at the defence dimension. the best way we have to face such a rapidly evolving series of challenges is to join forces and to mobilise all the resources we have. to protect our cyberspace we need better capabilities, more research, more training and exercises on how to respond to eventual attacks, and in the last few months and years i’m glad to say we have joined forces across the institutions – the european commission and member states, the external action service and the european defence agency – all in close coordination with our partners at nato. the report we are discussing today provides an excellent strategic vision and puts forward a series of very realistic recommendations. the report will help further reinforce our ongoing efforts to support member states’ capability development for cyber—defence and deterrence. cyber—defence of csdp missions and operations, cyber—defence education and training, international norms applicable to cyberspace, civil military cooperation, public—private partnerships and eu nato cyber—cooperation. we are working to build the eu’s resilience to cyber—attacks, provide for better defence capabilities and to build a credible cyber—deterrence. indeed, these were the key elements of the commission’s cyber package brought forward in september last year. in taking this work forward, we need to remember that most cyber—infrastructure is in civilian hands, so an important part of strengthening our cyber—resilience – making ourselves harder to attack – involves strengthening civil cooperation, which is why we proposed transforming enisa into an eu cybersecurity agency and developing an eu—wide certification framework for cybersecurity. we also need to send a clear message to those who wish to cause us harm, and in this regard we welcome the reference in the report to europol’s role in coordinating the law enforcement response to cyber—threats. i’d also like to draw your attention to the recent commission proposals for facilitating access to e—evidence. but we also identified the need to further invest in the development of dual use cyber—technologies and cyber—skills. earlier this year, the european defence agency, led by the high representative, set up an eu cyber—defence, education and training exercise evaluation platform. it will help advance training and educational opportunities within the member states to cover the full range of cyber—defence training. this initiative will also bring together civilian and military training needs. the eas and the european defence agency have in fact been engaged with member states for some years now to develop capabilities for cyber—defence. in march this year, they conducted a survey of the member states on their cyber—defence requirements in order to update the eu cyber—defence policy framework. that survey showed that some member states are already very advanced in terms of structures and doctrine and that all of our member states have at least minimum cyber—protection capabilities in place and are building their national cyber—defence systems. we’ve identified several areas where the eu could support these efforts further, such as investment in research and technology, providing training and education opportunities and facilitating civil—military cooperation. the funding through the european defence fund should be focused on delivering these capability priorities. some member states, as has been mentioned, have also agreed to invest together in cybersecurity through the new permanent structured cooperation on defence. member states have set up to cyber—related pesco projects. one of them focuses on the sharing of cyber—threat intelligence through a network platform with the objective to strengthen national cyber—defence capabilities, the second aims to set up cyber rapid response teams to respond together to cyber—attacks. in order to strengthen cyber—deterrence, we continue to step up eu response to malicious cyber—activities and incursive cyber—operations in the framework for a joint eu diplomatic response to malicious cyber—activities. this sets out several eu measures to prevent and respond to cyber—attacks by state and non—state actors. mr paet’s report also highlights the role of international law and cyber norms in cyberspace. in this respect, we work closely with member states to develop a strategic framework for conflict prevention and cyber—stability, promoting adherence to existing international law and implementation of cyber—norms and confidence—building measures are, and will remain, a centrepiece of our efforts. finally, we are working to deepen eu—nato cooperation on cyber—defence, including against hybrid threats. you were talking about eu—nato cooperation earlier today. we will continue to foster interoperability through coherent cyber—defence requirements and standards, to strengthen cooperation on training exercises, to harmonise training requirements and to mainstream cyber aspects into crisis management. the report also makes some recommendations on institutional reinforcement, such as developing cyber aspects further in a white book for security and defence, to invest more in cyber—defence in the next mff, to strengthen the eu intelligence and situation centre and set up a new cyber—defence council. i want to assure the rapporteur that we will consider all of these ideas very closely. further investment in cyber—defence has already been highlighted in the current discussions on the next mff. in conclusion, we’ve made considerable progress in the past few years on this range of issues connected to cyber—defence. we will continue to work to strengthen member states’ capabilities and reinforce civ—mil synergies. we will continue to strengthen deterrence by bolstering our resilience and stepping up diplomatic responses to cyber—attacks. thank you again for focusing on this issue and i look forward to our discussion.

i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. madam president, the new communication technologies have shown their dark side, by using hackers who are able to penetrate the systems of competitors, companies or institutions to spy on or sabotage them. it has also revealed the vulnerability of users of communication and social networks to powerful intelligence companies or those who turn our data into business. as recent examples, there are cases of facebook or intelligence agencies like the nsa stealing and accumulating zero-day vulnerabilities, keeping them secret. this report does not protect vulnerable citizens, network users, from powerful corporations or intelligence agencies that steal our data for their control or their businesses. the gue/ngl group will vote against this report because it supports a single market for cybersecurity, promoting synergies between civil and military markets; because it urges member states to use the framework provided for by the permanent structured cooperation or the european defence fund; because it supports eu-nato cooperation for cyber defence; because it supports security policies and restrictions on the rights and freedoms of citizens of the member states of the european union, or because it advocates, for cyber defence, the use of some instruments of the multiannual financial framework.
madam president, while the competence for cyber defence lies with the member states, there needs to be cooperation and coordination between them all. progress through the european defence agency and the new permanent structured cooperation (pesco) should be acknowledged. however, cooperation between the partners is still far from being organised. the european structures, from europol's ec3 to the it emergency response team to the still weak enisa, lack a robust cooperation system and are in need of major improvements. the european union and nato cooperation is fundamental. shared efforts and knowledge are needed to be able to neutralize 4 000 attacks per day in 2016. a substantial enhancement of cyber defence capabilities would have an impact on the union's autonomy, which is central to the global security strategy 2016. it would also reduce the dependence on our international partners, such as the united states.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, it is not the first time the council has been asked to intervene in this house on the situation in poland. this shows again that the protection and promotion of rule of law – including its core element, the independence of the judiciary – is a constant endeavour. it requires unwavering attention and efforts across different policy areas. common values, such as human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and human rights, are the cornerstone of the european union. each member state must therefore respect, protect and promote them. the bulgarian presidency, and indeed all of us, agree that the protection of the rule of law, democracy and fundamental rights in our union cannot be taken for granted. the commission triggered, on 20 december 2017, the procedure foreseen by article 7(1) of the treaty on european union. this procedure is designed to assess if there is a clear risk of serious breach by poland of the values referred to in article 2 of the treaty. the council is regularly updated on the outcome of the dialogue between poland and the european commission. the dialogue is ongoing, and the final assessment has not yet been presented. the issue is on the agenda of the upcoming general affairs council meeting on 26 june. at this stage, i cannot prejudge and draw conclusions as regards the next step. the presidency has acted, and will continue to act, as an honest broker considering all circumstances and positions. let me conclude by saying that the issues raised in the debate go to the heart of our commitment to this union. we therefore trust that all sides will act responsibly and constructively to reach an outcome that leaves no doubt about our core values.
