the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner moscovici, at this late hour of the night and probably until after midnight, this parliament is finally debating legislative acts. european legislation. firstly, a regulation a directly binding rule on cash control at borders, which is part of the set of initiatives adopted by the european commission to respond to the counter-terrorism security emergency that took place, especially throughout 2016, after the terrible terrorist attacks that swept and devastated europe in 2015. it is indeed a regulation on which mrs delvaux and i have worked together as rapporteur for the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, and i am grateful for all the cooperation throughout this period and also for the willingness to meet with the council, which has not exactly been available for any legislative commitment with the european parliament during this term. but here it has been possible, as in the directive on combating money laundering by means of european criminal law, which we shall discuss immediately afterwards. this initiative aims to strengthen europe's response capacity in the area of money laundering, illicit capital flows and asset freezing and confiscation. it does so through a regulation which is part of the fight against transnational economic fraud, money laundering and, in particular, the financing of terrorism. the purpose is to provide a legal basis (article 114 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, in conjunction with article 33) for the strengthening of customs cooperation between member states and the commission in the field of cash control. with a legislative background, 2005, a regulation that established at the time the control of metal "cash" up to an amount of 10 000 euros, but with clear defects that we are now correcting. firstly, there is an incomplete coverage of crossborder cash movements. it is a question of completing a full declaration and of ensuring that criminals who send money in cash or use employment methods know that these funds will be better and more effectively controlled from now on. secondly, the difficulties in the exchange of information between member states' authorities, because until now there was an obligation to make available to a financial intelligence unit of a state nature, but from now on there will be an active obligation - not just the making available - to transmit that information. thirdly, to take account of the fact that the competent authorities were unable to temporarily withhold cash that reached the threshold. fourthly, the definition of cash, which includes not only the amount of liquid money but also other highly liquid commodities such as gold; information can therefore also be transmitted at the border entry. and fifthly, to respond to the great disparity in the penalties applied by the member states, the heterogeneity in the levels of enforcement. in this report we have tried to take account of all these elements and, in addition, we have tried to ensure that the cash declaration is completed regardless of whether travellers bring the money in person or send it by any other means of transport, which is called unaccompanied cash, with a disclosure declaration. member states' authorities should exchange all information where there are indications that this cash is related to any criminal activity that may adversely affect the financial interests of the european union and should transmit this information to the european commission. customs administrations have a leading role in this front line. we have not succeeded in establishing a european financial intelligence unit, but we have succeeded in establishing a strong review clause which gives the commission the task of responding to this request from the european parliament for the establishment of a european financial intelligence unit. and finally, the efforts of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs have also aimed at ensuring that this european legislation, which is directly binding on the member states and which can be invoked by citizens in court, respects european data protection law, because we have a general data protection regulation which must be consistent and which must inspire, as the european data protection supervisor has indicated, all european legislation. we are putting it in connection with the european criminal law case against money laundering which we shall discuss immediately afterwards. we are making progress and i can only welcome the exercise of parliamentary cooperation and the willingness to reach an understanding with the council on this point - at least on this point.

i think, mr president, that the rapporteur for the ppe on this directive made it clear when he said that the adoption of this directive was a great step forward for the cultural industry. they tried to sell us that it was to protect creators, but no: it was to protect the industry, to protect it precisely against the right to information and against a free internet. at podemos we know that creators' rights are not sufficiently protected, and that is why we support creators' right to fair remuneration. but that doesn't have to go against the freedom of the internet. we consider freedom of expression and information to be a fundamental value of any democratic state. we therefore believe that the platforms cannot become arbiters of freedom of expression, as this directive that has been adopted today says. we will only have a critical society with a free and uncensored internet, where knowledge can be shared and the rights of creators and creators respected. today we took a step backwards in internet freedom.

on behalf of the green group, madam president, it is very important that we have this debate and, of course, that we move forward to the demographic challenges when we talk about the pension system. but the big problem with the public pension system is not the ageing of the population: it is precarious employment and it is the attacks on workers' rights that have caused contributions to fall very sharply and at the moment, indeed, some public pension systems are in difficulty. and of course it is a generational issue, but it is a generational issue because the precariousness of young people today puts at risk the pensions of today and tomorrow in many of our member states. that is the fundamental problem. what can the commission do? what he does not have to do is to send specific recommendations to countries like spain, criticizing very small and very low increases in pensions when there have been successive reforms in 2011 and 2013 to cut them even further. so strengthening pillar i and tackling precariousness in the labour market in particular in order to have good social security contributions is what the european union must do to have decent pensions now and in the future.
madam president, commissioner, you are creating a social alarm. redistribute wealth and ensure a decent pension is to contribute to not being socially excluded at the end of working life. make no mistake, it's not a demographic problem, it's not a problem of increasing the number of pensioners. the only thing that is endangering public pensions is a problem of focusing financial interest and economic policy in favour of austerity. there is a catch in the system because, first of all, the commission is helping to raise social awareness. then he enforces austerity policies so that governments, many of his own rank, carry out labor reforms and pension reforms. this social alarm is leading many people to the streets, as was the case with the coordinator for the defence of the public pension system in the spanish state of galicia, my country, who is working on this issue. finally, i would like to mention another problem: the average european effort to maintain the pension system is higher, for example, than the spanish average, which is the lowest in europe. in galicia in particular, much more, and in particular, in non-contributory pensions, especially.
madam president, pensions are not a gift: they are the result of years of contributions, they are workers' wages. when you talk about pensions, you propose extending working years and private schemes, like the pan-european pension product, which we totally reject. if public pension systems are at risk, it is because of their policy of reform and the limits on public pension spending, which stem from their unjust spending rule. it is important to remember that pensions are linked to employment, to good wages, to stability and to rights. that is why we must put an end to the precariousness, the temporariness, the zero-hour contracts suffered by young people. and we also have to close the gender pay gap. the reforms you have encouraged in the fields of employment and pensions must of course be reversed. so if you radically change your policies and your neoliberal agenda, you will see how you find positive solutions for the social majority and, above all, you will see how the workers will thank you and the far right will not continue to grow.
madam president, commissioner, i want to express my commitment to public, universal and dignified social security systems, which are expressions of intergenerational solidarity. the union's demographic decline is therefore threatening its viability. this is such a serious and obvious problem that it requires a smarter and more open immigration and integration policy for people who must be, for all intents and purposes, new europeans. precarious employment is the second greatest threat to social security. with temporary contracts and low wages, even if the number of people employed increases, the contributions will not be enough. the revision of the retirement age may be necessary, but the dignification of the conditions of employment is even more so. finally, it is urgent that social security systems be consistent with the mobility of workers that must operate in the union. and that requires taking seriously the establishment of minimum standards of coverage and efficient procedures for linking the systems of the different member states.
madam president, the objective of pension systems should be nothing other than to guarantee our elderly people adequate income levels, ensuring the overall economic sustainability of the system. clearly, employment is the best guarantee of achieving this. however, demographic change requires us to propose reforms to achieve this, reforms which should not be focused on a general tax increase, as this would have negative effects in the medium and long term on economic growth and job creation and would therefore have a negative impact on social security systems. we must move gradually towards a mixed system which ensures that current and future pensioners receive what they have contributed in their working lives and does not jeopardise the future rights of our young people. that is, combining a distribution pillar with a capitalisation pillar, in which what is received is linked to what is contributed and which can be complemented by private pension plans. this complementarity does not mean that the public sector is no longer needed, since its role is fundamental, above all, to meet the basic needs of those who have paid less or who have been unable to pay for various reasons. it is also important to underline the role of public systems in supporting widows, orphans and the disabled, and in supporting the elderly who need it most, in order to ensure a minimum income that avoids situations of risk of poverty or social exclusion. it means adapting to the present reality, looking to the future and being as fair as possible to our citizens.
madam president, a part of the european citizenry looks at retirement with fear and anxiety. they wonder whether they will be entitled to a benefit, whether this benefit will be miserable and whether they will be able to survive on it, or whether they will have enough strength to work all the years that today give access to pensions - by the way, more and more. and to respond to this anxiety and this fear the only answer can be the security, the guarantees and the protection of our public pension system: a well-endowed, well-guaranteed system that ensures that benefits are increasing at the same level as the cost of living and that ensures all our pensioners a life of dignity. and to reject outright any mechanism for privatising our pension systems, which have proved unfair and ineffective. but not just this. what we also need to do is to ensure a robust state, quality jobs and to combat inequality; also the gender gap. because these three issues - employment, state capacity and inequality - impact the sustainability and equity of our pension system.
madam president, from the white paper on pensions to the pan-european private pension product, all the commission's measures have been aimed at dismantling the public pension system. i do not want to say that pensions are not sustainable, but rather that pensions are essential to sustain life. today in spain, precisely where there have been two reforms to dismantle pensions - one in 2011 by the socialist party, and another in 2013 by the popular party - unfortunately 300 000 families live on the pensions of their grandparents, because while they have applied cuts, the welfare state has been dismantled, and working conditions, wages and employment have been devalued, it has been the pensioners who have borne the burden of the crisis on their backs. there are solutions: raising wages, fighting the wage gap, promoting stable employment, improving sources of finance, eliminating contribution ceilings for the highest wages. it's a matter of will and purpose. who are we with? are we with the financial institutions that want to make a business out of pensions or are we with the families that need them and deserve them?
madam president, a decent pension cannot depend on the individual savings capacity of each person. a decent pension must be guaranteed by public institutions. that is why i am calling on the commission, parliament and also the council to withdraw the pan-european product for individual pensions, and instead to get the three institutions to work on a new regulation that guarantees dignified public pensions and pension systems and measures so that the transition from working life to retirement does not mean entering poverty; that public budgets guarantee public pensions; the end of the gender gap in pensions, and also of people working in agriculture and at sea and the self-employed in general; to end - as i say - the inequality that will mean maintaining pensions through the pan-european products for private pensions.
in writing. it is our task to ensure that european citizens can look to the future with the peace of mind that the pension system they are in for will be sound, well-funded and will guarantee them decent pensions. pension funds in the global economy, in a 0% interest rate scenario, have a difficult task to secure future pensions, as their investments will be less and less profitable. who and how the rules of the game are set in the global economy will have a crucial impact on the future of pensions. privatization is not the answer to the sustainability of the pension system. private pension funds are risky financial products that are based on speculation. a robust, well-organised and well-managed public social security system is much safer and more economically efficient. the privatisation of pension systems not only fails to protect pensioners from the insolvency of the system, but increases the deficit of the states by diverting funds from the public to private pension funds.
madam president, commissioner jourová, this european parliament is never more parliamentary than when it legislates and certainly never more politically relevant than when it legislates on fundamental rights, because that is one of the assets of the lisbon treaty, which recognises the right to privacy in article 16 and its fundamental character in article 8 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. we took it very seriously in the previous parliament when we introduced the data protection regulation, which is a huge step forward, and the directive on law enforcement, police and judicial agencies, on the investigation of crimes and the clearance of their accounts. but it is also doing so now when it updates regulation (ec) no 45/2001 with a new one aimed at data processing in the european institutions. we celebrate it. we can only regret that there is no uniform treatment, that there are still a number of agencies which are not covered (eurojust or europol). but we have emphasised the strength of the european data protection supervisor to ensure very effective sanctions for breaches of this new right in force.
mr president, the scientific community agrees that the consumption of plastics is seriously endangering the environment, and you will have seen that in the summer. we may already have more plastic than tourists on our beaches. but it's more -- and now i'm serious -- if we don't do anything, according to the united nations, by 2050, there will be more plastic than fish in the sea. can you imagine that? i think it would be really terrible. it must be admitted that the commission's proposals on this matter are in the right direction, but we are late and therefore cannot be inadequate, as i fear we are. what is at stake here is a radical change in the way we produce and therefore also consume, putting at the centre, first, the drastic reduction of plastics, reuse and, ultimately, recycling. i mean, it's not just about creating - and i say "just" new materials or advertising campaigns for recycling only, but it's about telling markets, companies, that images like this of fruit wrapped in plastic, which you will recognize, no longer have meaning or place. and to do that, plastic producers and lobbyists must be left out of future decision-making.
madam president, i would like to congratulate mr demesmaeker on this report on european plastic policy, because we are facing an opportunity which must not be wasted. the citizens of the union are becoming increasingly aware of the environmental effects of this material, which is encouraging the necessary change in habits to move forward in a necessary revolution. a change that requires us, for starters, to recycle much more than the 30% of disposable plastic we now collect for that purpose. this same environmental awareness is driving technological initiatives that will focus plastic packaging design on circularity rather than recycling. a movement that will drive innovation and create sustainable wealth and jobs. we also have advanced waste legislation, and we know that designing one that will regulate the secondary raw materials market, implementing quality standards and stimulating change with tax measures, is the next step. i therefore encourage european innovation programmes to join this movement, giving special attention to initiatives and enterprises in this sector of the circular economy.
madam president, every year, over eight million tons of plastic is dumped into our seas and oceans. to give you an idea, this has already created an island in the pacific the size of spain, italy and france combined. most of those plastics were single-use, but their degradation, which can take up to 1,000 years, is flooding our seas with microplastics that then end up in our food or on our plates. the single-use plastics we use may be cheap, but what you don't see -- and that's the problem -- is the price we pay, our health and the environment. that is why the european greens insist so much on prevention and on the price of producing plastics reflecting their real direct and indirect costs. ridiculous images that we've all seen, like these individually wrapped fruits in plastic, have to stop now.
madam president, congratulations to the rapporteur who knows very well the importance of the sea for many peoples, including my own. plastic waste in the sea is a big problem. eighty percent of the garbage in the sea is plastic, microplastic, so abundant that it's already part of our ecosystem. microplastics absorb other pollutants like pesticides and heavy materials that cause health problems. the marine sector, which is ecologically conscious, is very concerned and wants to fish instead of plastic bags or bottles. we need an ambitious policy, not a timid one, but a radical and urgent one, because the model is no longer appropriate. the model of production and consumption no longer works. and the circular economy is an opportunity, before the garbage invades us by land and sea.
madam president, it is gratifying to hear the unanimity of this house, of all the colleagues from different political groups, on how to address the need we have to address the elimination of plastic in the everyday use of our lives. plastic has, without a doubt, uses that are interesting and that have made our lives easier, but we have to be aware that this utility that it has given us in society is now a big problem. we've overused plastics in too many applications. so we must take action and i congratulate the commission on that because the strategy, the directive we are already discussing, is on the right track. let's take advantage of the time before the end of the legislature to take action on this reduction of plastics, on this education in habits and information to consumers and on innovation and new opportunities for economic sectors.
madam president, protecting the environment is essential to guaranteeing the future. but in the meantime, plastics are choking the sea. more than 80% of marine litter is plastic. the european union produces no more and no less than 25 - almost 26 - million tonnes a year. this is a lot, a lot of waste on our part and very little recycling: less than 30%. this is a great challenge that cannot be delayed. it needs concrete legislative initiatives from the commission, initiatives that stimulate the economy towards a transition of businesses towards the circular economy, a sustainable economy. we need prevention measures, education of the population. we need to involve the municipalities if we want this strategy to succeed. and we need a specific measure to start cleaning up the plastic in the seas, which is already a reality.

i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, according to the european environment agency, transport accounts for one third of europe's final energy consumption. so talking about an agenda for the future of mobility in europe is - or should be - without any doubt, talking about sustainable and smart mobility, less polluting, safer, more accessible and also more affordable. promoting sustainable mobility in road transport involves reducing co2 emissions, and a clear commitment to electric vehicles, with clean batteries and the use of renewable energy, where efforts are just beginning. and yet - let us not be mistaken - it clearly involves a commitment to public transport, to reducing the use of individual road transport, where, however, demand continues to increase. we have seen how the fourth railway package was passed in this parliament, which is a liberalisation and in a way an attack on the train, which is the most sustainable and safest means of transport we have. i think this is something we should review and make a priority. to speak of sustainable mobility is also to take into account the social impact of transport at the different territorial levels, the need to structure the rural territory, to engineer new forms of collective transport. and we are not talking about the false sharing economy, we are talking about forms of public transport, so that transport serves to nourish the territorial sphere and not to depopulate it. and of course, urban areas are the places where co2 emissions are most concentrated and it is necessary and urgent to bet on greener, more sustainable, more human mobility, promoting the bicycle, promoting putting the pedestrian in the center of cities and designing cities in such a way that the use of public transport is encouraged to connect with other territories. it is certainly something that should not be done only by the year 2050, but it is urgent and it must be done now.
i would like to support the spirit of this report on mobility, mr president, and to advocate that local authorities be involved from the outset in the necessary public-private partnership process which must stimulate innovation and maintain european technological leadership in the world transport market and especially in the integration of its different modes. cities are the medium in which the most complex mobility problems have to be solved. the positive impact that better mobility will have on them, with more humane and sustainable development, is already one of the key factors in good governance and sustainable development. in implementing strategic actions to address major challenges, cities are key to hosting and driving practical experiences based on research and development. they are effective levers for changing people's habits; they allow for rapid testing, evaluation and sharing of results. therefore, experiments such as those that are about to be launched in the capital of the basque country, which will turn the city of vitoria-gasteiz into a mobility laboratory, are the way forward. a path which i hope will find support and encouragement in the european union.

member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank the honourable members for this fruitful debate. i listened very carefully to your proposals and suggestions, especially in relation to trade. when we are discussing our trade agreements with third countries, we are very much involved in debates about the use of pesticides which are banned in the eu. it is and will always be on our agenda. ms mcguinness rightly mentioned a less ideological approach in our debates. i was in carcassonne a few weeks ago and had a meeting with organic farmers who were producing organic wine, and we have debates, which are not easy, about copper. sometimes, too, i see how some are vocal about a ban on glyphosate, for example, knowing that a scientific assessment was done transparently. this is excluding the monsanto papers, which are always mentioned. it is not about the monsanto papers: it is about the possibility of really assessing the situation from an evidence-based point of view, from the precautionary principle, and about having arguments in our hands. look, ban glyphosate and copper, and what about organic farming? what can we do? ms mcguinness has very rightly raised questions. we need to understand the complexity of the issues and to see how we can achieve proper enforcement, implementation, control and integrated management. all this should, of course, be done in a proper manner. about the use of derogations: yes, we sent letters to those member states because we asked the european food safety authority (efsa) to assess once again all the issues related to the use of such derogations in the area of neonicotinoids. we assess the situation and then we inform governments once again, especially those who use them without evidence. we are doing our job. we are not scapegoating, which is always bad, bad, bad. no! for me, as a medical doctor, there is no doubt that health is a priority, but if i am using medicines in animal health or plant health, or using medicines in treating people, i know what this means. we need to have a very balanced approach. i am, of course, ready to work together with you. we all share the same belief in achieving the goals regarding health, the environment and food safety. we need to work together to maintain and reinforce the european union’s very stringent regulatory system for pesticides. enforcement and implementation are the key. i assure you that we are committed to working towards greater transparency, increased trust and more a sustainable system of food production. once again, thank you for your engagement and for your own—initiative report. we will be very sensitive to the report and we will see how it can be included in the whole picture, bearing in mind the possibility of having different assessments, and we will then propose to parliament the further steps to be taken.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place today. written declarations (rule 162) of the rules of procedure
in writing. since the entry into force of the 2009 plant protection products directive, a large number of dangerous substances have been removed from the market and others with new effects, in principle less harmful to humans but in some cases proven to be lethal to bees, and other pollinators, such as neonicotinoids, are still incomprehensibly authorised in cereals. other issues that should be addressed in the new biocidal strategy, as determined by the directive itself, are the exclusion of substances with the capacity to produce endocrine disrupting effects in humans and non-target organisms. this reluctance to apply this exclusion criterion has allowed the extension of the use of glyphosate, whose effects as an endocrine regulator are demonstrated by different organisations, as is its potentially carcinogenic effect. in addition, the 'environmentally toxic' exclusion criterion should be developed in detail, which, as has been shown in the case of neonicotinoids, does not seem to count, since, although extremely harmful to the environment, the use of these materials is legal. the commission should establish a clear definition of endocrine disruptor and a detailed description of the environmental toxicities of plant protection products.

the rapporteur. madam president, i should like to begin by thanking the various rapporteurs from the various groups for the constructive attitude which has made possible a text with 62 commitments, which has been virtually agreed. the commission proposal was a timely one. i said that when i presented it, but it needed to be aligned with the challenges that health technologies, access to health and sustainability of health systems really present. i think that the agreement we reached in the committee on the environment, public health and food safety is a good agreement because of how balanced it is, because it is patient-centred and because, in turn, it is respectful of the member states which, through the health systems, have to provide the right to access to health, a fundamental right. i should also like to begin by saying that this is not the first time that harmonization has been carried out in this sector at community level. it was already done in 1965 on safety, in 1995 the ema started work and in 2001 the foundations were laid for the regulation of medicines at european level. and i think the results have been positive. but today the challenges are different: today we have the challenge of improving quality; research needs have to be better aligned with medical needs, and prices, the high prices also have to be regulated. these and other concerns were already expressed by the council in june 2016 and by the european parliament. i am also aware that medicines and health technology are covered by european consumer goods legislation, but this must respect and guarantee at all times, in the final analysis, the fundamental right to access to health and, in short, access to health technology. i believe that this proposal, especially with the amendments and the proposal made by parliament, will improve quality, improve and align medical needs with research and, moreover, contribute to the sustainability of health systems; in short, improve the access of european citizens to medicines and new health products. in particular, and to illustrate this need, i would just like to give you a fact, and that is that in the last ten years, despite an increase of up to ten times the price of cancer drugs, only 14 or 15 percent of them have been shown to increase five-year survival. the fact is that the marketing authorization requires or assesses safety and efficacy, but it is not its task to assess effectiveness or comparative efficacy. there was already an attempt in 2004 to establish the therapeutic added value of medicinal products through regulation (ec) no 726/2004, but no agreement was possible. the reality today is that member states are conducting this evaluation process prior to the pricing and reimbursement process, which creates not only duplication but, more importantly, the loss of the opportunity to improve the available clinical evidence, to direct research priorities to the medical needs of patients, to improve the quality of research and ultimately access to it. i therefore believe that this proposal is timely and can be positive. the commission presented it to us justified on the basis of article 114 tfeu 'internal market to eliminate duplication'. i believe that this is neither the only nor the most important objective to be achieved, but that article 168 (4) tfeu allows us to take these decisions on the basis of the need to ensure the quality, safety and efficacy of medicinal products. the mandatory nature of this evaluation by the member states requires the necessary confidence that i believe the text gives, a confidence based on a high-quality scientific methodology that compares on the basis of the best available evidence, that is transparent, independent and public, and that is carried out by the coordination groups, by the experts at national level. at the same time, it should not prevent the member states themselves from adapting these assessments to the specificities of their national context. i would also like to mention a very important aspect, namely the agreement reached on medical devices. i am aware of the difficulties and differences that existed, but we have reached an agreement which i believe is positive, in an emerging sector that needs that necessary increase in evidence. the involvement of all stakeholders - patients, consumers, professionals - is also guaranteed and heard. at the same time, it opens the door to voluntary cooperation in new areas, such as precision medicine, discouraging those technologies... (the president withdrew the floor to the speaker) )
the rapporteur. mr president, the eurobarometer shows that health is one of the most important values for european citizens, and this regulation can help to do that, because they are asking us to do more. it is therefore a regulation which can have a high european added value. i am aware that the commission would have liked us to have gone even a little further, but i think that an important work we have done in this parliament has been to bring positions closer together to make this regulation possible, because we do indeed think it is necessary. as regards medical products, i understand that some groups would like to go further - as did my first proposal - but i think that the starting point and the meeting point have been good. i think there is a pending implementation of important legislation on this and time must be given, and i think that the scope that has been maintained can be an interesting first step. as regards patient involvement, i think it is especially guaranteed: all stakeholders will be involved not only in the network, but in the process, with the different contributions. and finally, qualified majority. i understand mr liese's position and i really share the view of certain member states where there is such experience - or long experience - in the evaluation of medicinal products, and which comes especially from those large countries. but it's not a standard method of approving these reports when it comes to scientific procedures, and there's no precedent in other agencies. i understand that, but, well. in short, thank you for all the contributions: they have all been positive. and i think that what we have to do now is to continue to work towards that necessary consensus with the council so that this regulation, which, as i say, is necessary for the patients of the european union, can finally be brought into being.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, honourable members, thank you for this opportunity to exchange views on the issue of the eu’s input into a possible international, legally—binding instrument on transnational corporations and other business enterprises with respect to human rights. i shall endeavour to give you briefly the broad eu view from the council’s perspective, and afterwards the commission will be in a position to elaborate on the topics concerned. i would first of all like to stress that advancing on business and human rights is an important priority of the eu’s human rights agenda, as set out in the eu action plan on human rights and democracy for the period 2015—2019, adopted by the council on 20 july 2015. it should be noted that the recurrent element which is underpinning all our actions identified in the action plan is the united nations guiding principles of 2011 as the first, and so far only authoritative global framework to address the impact of business on human rights. in its 2016 conclusions on business and human rights, the council recalled the global consensus reached on the un guiding principles adopted in 2011 and stressed that any possible further steps regarding the international legal framework for business and human rights at un level must be inclusive, firmly rooted in the un guiding principles, and address all types of companies, not only transnational. these three principles have always constituted our barometers for engagement in the intergovernmental working group process. president, honourable members, i can reassure you that the council, in particular through its working party on human rights, continues working on the business and human rights file, including on developing our common position on the process regarding a possible legally binding instrument. the eu is, at the same time, progressing on other tracks, notably the working group on business and human rights and the annual forum on business and human rights, specifically on efforts to achieve a coherent approach throughout the eu on access to remedy for victims of business-related human rights violations. the eu continues to offer its support to the accountability and remedy project led by the office of the high commissioner on human rights, recognising that the initiative may provide best practices that can be implemented at eu and member state level, including on improved cooperation between states in cross-border cases. i’m looking forward to the debate and to hearing the commission’s input.
member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to try to inform you of all aspects of this very challenging issue and to be constructive after the remarks on the council side. the european union is fully engaged in the ongoing discussions on business and human rights. we are not only exploring possible future initiatives, we are also intensively working both internally and with partners to implement the un guiding principles on business and human rights. already, 14 eu member states have adopted a national action plan on business and human rights. our policy is based on a mix of voluntary and regulatory measures that provide for tangible protection against human rights abuses. the eu is therefore not opposed, as a matter of principle, to discussing a potential legally binding instrument, and this is why we have engaged in the process led by ecuador. nonetheless, we insist that the scope of the discussion should include all companies, not only transnationals or multinationals, as many human rights violations are committed by domestic companies. the draft text submitted by ecuador last july contains important elements, including on access to remedy by victims of corporate abuse. yet its scope is still too restrictive. another prerequisite for the european union is that the negotiations are based on the existing un guiding principles. what is also clear at this moment is that the process is not yet fully ripe for negotiations. for the moment, the human rights council is still divided on this issue. we nevertheless engaged in discussions in geneva in the hope that process issues would be solved and a meaningful discussion possible. what is, in our view, essential is a process that would be chaired in an impartial manner and that would be inclusive, transparent and predictable. we also ask that rules and established practice in intergovernmental working groups are respected. we hope that we can count on the european parliament to also signal the need for a better process. as the european union, we have engaged in in—depth discussions with member states, industry and ngos on these very complex issues. we have done extensive work on the principles for eu engagement and on the possible format and points of substance of a possible legally binding instrument, and we stand ready to debrief the european parliament at any stage of this process. we believe the added value of any possible legally binding instrument should be to ensure a level playing field for companies globally. therefore, it is essential for a proposal to reach sufficient traction amongst un member states. it is also important to ensure policy coherence and avoid the duplication of efforts. we are reflecting on which format of a legally binding instrument would stand better chances to achieve this level playing field. these discussions are also a good opportunity to encourage others to upgrade their standards. the european union can offer its experience on corporate due diligence in the field of human rights, including transparency requirements and public procurement rules. we need better prevention of abuses, and better access to remedy for victims when abuses occur. the european union has measures in place to ensure judicial and non-judicial access to remedy for victims, including access to justice and acknowledgement of victims’ rights, with a focus on provisions to clarify issues of jurisdiction, and to make international judicial cooperation and mutual legal assistance more effective. in addition, on access to remedy, the commission is conducting a study aimed at collecting information on existing judicial and non-judicial mechanisms in the eu member states concerning access to remedy for victims of business-related abuses. the results are expected by the end of next year, 2019. to conclude, the european union is committed to continuing a discussion with a view to finding feasible and sustainable solutions to the existing protection gaps, on a basis that ensures a true level playing field for all.

mr president, there is no denying that globalisation and its extension have had positive effects. for example, they have lifted hundreds of millions of people out of poverty. but it is also true that they have had many negative effects, including giving excessive power to transnational companies. some have behaved responsibly, but many others, especially the larger ones, have not. they have frequently ignored labour rights, in some cases violated human rights, altered or destroyed the environment or exploited the weakness of the workforce, in some cases child labour. to frame the actions of these companies, a binding treaty has been negotiated at the united nations, which affects all companies, obliges them to act responsibly and also allows victims access to reparation. the problem we have is that the european union is not a negotiating party within the united nations and that the member states have, in many cases, not supported this process. some of those who have supported it have not yet put national strategies into action. we need to get more involved as the european union, and we propose that the commission, the european external action service and the various committees involved in this parliament work together to strengthen the position of the european union in the forthcoming negotiations on 15 october in geneva. this matter deserves our support. it is about defending the weak when they are subjected to the power of the strong.
mr president, thank you, commissioner, for being here. the defence of human rights requires more than good words, it requires effectiveness. and when we talk about transnational companies with centres in developing countries, we find that the instruments we have have not been fully and really effective. we need to equip ourselves with legally binding tools. this has been established by the united nations since 2014. as the home of many transnational companies, the european union should have led the way in creating these binding mechanisms. but the union still does not have a mandate to participate in the negotiating process, even though this house has approved it. this inaction, this disinterestedness is not acceptable from any point of view, and i know that to some people this still sounds like interventionism, that it seems to them illiberal for politics to interfere in the sphere of private business. but it is just the opposite: what is liberal is to defend human rights all over the world and it is not acceptable for our companies to do abroad what is forbidden here, what would seem intolerable to us here. economic globalisation will be a beneficial process if it is accompanied by a globalisation of rights and duties.
mr president, commissioner, there is a limit to the prosperity of companies: human dignity. respect for human rights is a fundamental value and principle of the european union. the right to life and physical integrity, access to land, decent work are fundamental elements that cannot be left to voluntarism. there are too many legal loopholes that allow companies that violate these principles to go unpunished. and worse, there are too many victims, most of them women. they lose everything. that they can't access the justice or reparations they deserve. we cannot - experience shows us - continue like this. the european union must lead this process. and that is why i am asking, i am demanding that the european union has an urgent mandate to negotiate a binding international treaty on business and human rights. let's stop looking the other way. let's look at the victims. they need us. the european union must lead this process.
mr president, commissioner, this oral question has been put by the parliament's committees on international trade, development and foreign affairs, but it could also have been put perfectly well by the committee on freedom, justice and home affairs because it concerns a backbone of the european union's external and global action - the commitment to fundamental rights - and it is a requirement of the commission's responsibility to obtain from the council a negotiating mandate from the european union to fill the gap in international regulations with which multinationals exploit defenseless people - particularly vulnerable children and women - in their commercial actions, whether in uzbekistan, bangladesh - as this european parliament has made clear - or anywhere else in the world. the message is therefore clear: commission, european union, fundamental rights, human rights everywhere, also applicable to the social responsibility of multinational companies.
member of the commission, on behalf of the vice—president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, this plenary is taking place a few days after the high representative co-chaired a ministerial meeting in new york on the un agency for palestinian refugees. at the meeting, which i also attended, the european union reaffirmed once more its political and financial support. unrwa is essential to peace in the holy land. it is serving millions of palestine refugees and preserving the very possibility of a palestinian state. the ministerial meeting was an opportunity to underline the importance of guaranteeing full financial support to unrwa, and we managed to mobilise very significant resources that reduce the funding gap enormously. this means that palestine will continue to be assisted by the un agency. the commission proposed additional support to unrwa of eur 40 million. the eu and its member states collectively provide almost half of unrwa’s budget. we have all invested over eur 1 billion in funding over the last three years. we are, and we will continue to be, strong, reliable, and critical supporters of the agency. supporting unrwa is, above all, a humanitarian responsibility, but it is also in our collective interest for the sake of peace in the middle east. first, millions of people, many of them extremely young, rely on unrwa for essential services such as education, health services and food assistance. this is true in the west bank and gaza, but also in countries such as jordan, lebanon and syria that host a large number of palestinian refugees. thanks to these funds, half a million children can go to school every day, millions of patients receive health care, and thousands of people have access to jobs. second, unrwa’s activities are particularly important for the people in gaza who face a complex political and humanitarian situation. at last week’s ad hoc liaison committee meeting on palestine in new york, we recalled that our priority must be to avoid another escalation and to restore a political horizon for the people of gaza, but this will never be possible if we don’t also address the humanitarian situation right now and remain committed to assisting the most vulnerable people in gaza. finally, without unrwa it would be even more difficult to reach a negotiated two-state solution. a just, fair, agreed and realistic solution for palestine refugees is a final status issue that only the two parties can resolve through negotiations, with the support of the international community. today, the agency is reforming itself to be more effective, efficient and to have a perspective for the future. unrwa has expanded its donor base and taken internal management measures to increase efficiency and reduce costs. next year will be an even tougher year for unrwa. in this context, we need to stress once more the crucial importance for unrwa to intensify its efforts to put in place cost saving measures and reforms, including refocusing unrwa’s activities on core services for the most vulnerable refugees. we are engaging with unrwa to explore synergies with other potential service providers to safeguard key services to palestinian refugees. precisely because we believe that unrwa is essential, we want it to be more effective and efficient than it is today. we will do our utmost to ensure that unrwa and its staff continue to operate until a just, fair, agreed and realistic solution to the plight of palestinian refugees is finally reached. without unrwa and without the two—state perspective, there would just be chaos and violence for both the israeli and the palestinian people. we need a multilateral framework to support negotiations, we need a collective engagement to push for political progress and we need the region and the entire international community to continue to play their role. the european union will double down on efforts to work with our partners – the us and other regional and international partners – towards our common goal of a negotiated two—state solution.

on behalf of the alde group. mr president, thank you, mrs jourová, for coming here today, because we are talking about the free movement of persons, which has been one of the main historical flags of the european union. however, this freedom is perverted when a european citizen moves to another country of the union and loses his right to vote in his country of origin. this is the case in several member states - including the united kingdom - which withdraw the right to vote from citizens when they change their residence. what would have happened to brexit if the million britons living in other eu countries had been able to vote in that referendum? and there is also the case of countries like spain, which do not withdraw the right to vote, but create procedures so complex that it is practically impossible to exercise it. it's called a "pleaded vow". it is profoundly anti-european that there are borders for fundamental rights, that when a european changes his residence within the union he becomes a second-class citizen. it's in our hands to prevent it.

first vice-president of the commission. – mr president, we last discussed the state of the rule of law in romania in february, and today is a useful opportunity to take stock of the developments which have taken place in the months since. i’ll try to be as concise as i can. we are all aware that the initiatives taken by the romanian authorities since 2017 concerning the reform of the justice laws, the criminal procedure and criminal codes and the processes regarding the judiciary have led to concerns from a wide range of stakeholders, both inside and outside romania and the eu. many romanians are worried that the proposed changes to these laws may undermine the longstanding efforts in the fight against corruption and the independence of the judiciary. these are concerns that the commission very much shares. as guardian of the treaties, when it comes to the application of eu law and respect for the eu’s fundamental values, the commission intervenes on the basis of accurate and thorough legal analysis. it focuses on concrete national measures and engages in a dialogue with the authorities. in these matters, the commission is politically colour-blind and clinical in our approach. that is the case for romania just as much as for any other member state. with your permission, i will set out the main developments in romania. first, regarding the justice laws: the three justice laws, dating back to 2004, define the status of magistrates and organise the judicial system and the superior council of magistracy. at the end of last year, the laws were amended by the romanian parliament. these amendments have been challenged several times before the constitutional court. these laws have attracted criticism from institutions inside romania and from outside. the council of europe anti—corruption watchdog, greco, adopted a very critical report in march. the venice commission’s preliminary opinion, issued in july, was equally critical, raising serious concerns about the independence of the judiciary, its efficiency and its quality. it made a series of recommendations. the final opinion is expected to be adopted later this month. i know this house will pay as close attention to that opinion as we will at the commission, but unfortunately the fact is that the romanian parliament has so far not shown signs of responding to the opinions and recommendations. secondly, as concerns the overhaul of the criminal codes and the code of criminal procedures, in may the romanian parliament launched a procedure to amend the criminal code and the code of criminal procedures. they were passed in the months of june and july. the romanian law enforcement authorities, as well as other member states, expressed their concerns. the amendments have been challenged before the constitutional court, and judgments are expected in mid-october. the venice commission is preparing another opinion on these amended codes, which is also expected to be adopted later in october. these laws are crucial for the capacity of prosecutors to investigate, and judges to sentence, high-level corruption, as well as for the ability of the judicial system to pursue crime effectively. the climate needed for reform has deteriorated due to the secret protocols between the prosecution and the intelligence services. i call on the romanian authorities to conduct full and impartial investigations into this issue. romanians deserve a law enforcement order with all authorities properly supervised and full judicial independence. the reforms of the judicial laws and of the criminal codes are interlinked, and they must be prevented from having a negative impact on the independence of the judiciary and its effectiveness in combating corruption. that is why the commission has discussed this issue regularly with the romanian government at the highest level and has made its concerns public. we have examined the texts passed by the romanian parliament to fully assess their impact. we are seeking further clarification on how specific elements of these laws should be interpreted. thirdly, as concerns a procedure to dismiss the chief anti-corruption prosecutor and the evaluation of the general prosecutor, i would like to recall that the track record of the anti-corruption prosecution, the so-called dna, was a central reason for the more positive assessment of romania that the commission made back in our cooperation and verification mechanism (cvm) report in january 2017. (applause) moreover, robust and independent procedures for the dismissal and appointment of top prosecutors have always been a key element in our recommendations. the commission has also recommended that the romanian authorities seek the help of the venice commission in this matter. this remains one of the outstanding recommendations under the cooperation and verification mechanism. we are following the latest developments in romania with concern. the independence of romania’s judicial system and its capacity to fight corruption effectively are essential cornerstones of a strong romania in the european union. we have seen substantial progress in the past, but things are now moving backwards in a way that would be damaging for the place that romania has built as an eu member state in recent years. the commission has repeatedly called on the romanian authorities to rethink their course of action, and to build a broad consensus on the way forward, and i want to reiterate that call today. i would stress once again that the commission is always ready to cooperate with and support the romanian authorities in this process. i trust this dialogue will continue, and we will be meticulous and precise in all the elements of the proposals that we would like to discuss with the romanian authorities. the latest developments are a source of growing concern for the commission. if adopted without changes, the combined effect of the amended justice laws and the criminal codes would affect the capacity of the justice system, including the prosecution service, to effectively fight against corruption and other crimes. this means backtracking from the situation that led the commission to make a positive assessment in our report of january 2017. we will report on the situation in our next cvm report next month. you can see what our cvm progress report stated in january 2017 and what it did in the last report in november 2017. the situation has deteriorated. rest assured that all developments will be thoroughly assessed and reflected in our upcoming report. president juncker and i issued a joint statement in january this year, setting out our concerns on the direction of travel. we stated clearly at that point that the irreversibility of the progress achieved so far under the cvm is an essential precondition to phase out the mechanism. without that, we cannot phase out the mechanism. so, while we will continue pursuing our objective of a sustainably positive situation in a dialogue with the romanian authorities, i wish also to be clear today that the commission will draw the appropriate conclusions if the amendments to the justice law, criminal codes and laws on conflict of interest and corruption are promulgated without taking account of the concerns. concretely, this means following up our recommendations from the january 2017 cvm report, and the recommendations expressed by the venice commission and greco. as the guardian of the treaties, we will not hesitate to take action, where necessary, to ensure compatibility with the treaties. indeed, the commission will use all the means at its disposal, be it under cvm or otherwise. the commission urges romania to put the reform process back on track immediately. this means going forwards, not backwards, and abstaining from any steps which reverse the progress accomplished over the past years. i honestly think there is still an opportunity to turn things around. the laws are not yet promulgated, and therefore it is not yet too late for the romanian institutions to act to turn the situation around. as always, we stand ready to help, but the responsibility and the power to deliver change lie firmly with the romanian institutions. i call again on them to take the right steps now. (applause)

and citizens' rights are respected, and those who violate them will be punished. it is legitimate to ask: in what way has mcv protected romanian citizens from the serious violation of their rights? in the mcv reports there was a lot of talk about institutions, about the appointment of magistrates, about the fight against corruption. that's all very well, but i haven't seen anything about human rights violations, about secret protocols between intelligence services and judicial institutions. under these protocols, millions of romanians were placed under surveillance by the secret services in the name of fighting corruption. there are court decisions that show how evidence was falsified, how transcripts of intercepts were altered to create guilt, or how witnesses were blackmailed into giving false testimony. nothing about these things in the mcv reports. this does not mean - or rather it means - that this mechanism has failed in its purpose for which it was created and i am officially asking you to tell us who wrote the cvm reports, who provided the data and who omitted, through negligence or bad faith, these inconceivable realities in the european union. if we are honest, we have to start with these serious abuses, because they are taking place on the territory of the european union. the venice commission said that in the soviet system, the public prosecutor's office was a powerful means of controlling the judiciary. in the last four years, over three thousand magistrates have been investigated by dna. in practice, half of the romanian magistrates had years of files through which they were probably influenced to give settled solutions outside the courtroom. it's not just me saying it. the romanian associations of magistrates say this with great concern. on the basis of such falsified files, a judge of the constitutional court, a vice-president of the superior council of magistracy, four judges of the high court, several judges of higher courts, a general prosecutor, a head of the superior public prosecutor's office were removed from office. eventually, they were all acquitted or the cases were closed, but they were removed. the new justice laws restore the independence of judges. no political decision-maker interferes anymore in the appointment and dismissal of judges. the independence is total, not restricted in any way, and i assure you that we are in good faith and will take into account the recommendations of the venice commission. there is, however, a good side to this meeting. today i have informed you all, officially, about the abuses in romania. from now on, you can no longer ignore these things, you can no longer talk about justice in romania without talking about these abuses, unless you make a political game that has nothing to do with justice. ask yourself why you've been kept from these things. why didn't they tell you anything, if it was all legitimate and legal? ask yourself these questions before you raise a stone against romania. about the august 10th rally, i'll say just a few words. i see that the romanian gendarmerie is being accused of intervening in an unauthorized rally against violent protesters who tried to occupy the government building. we did not see the same attitude towards last week's event in brussels or towards other rallies in france, spain, germany, the uk, when the police intervened with exactly the same means and procedures as those used in romania. i cannot accept in any way that the romanian gendarmerie is accused of actions and procedures practiced everywhere in europe. finally, i ask you this: do not forbid romania what is allowed in other states of the union and do not allow things to happen in romania that are unacceptable in other member states. we want to be your partners, but we want to be your equal partners. no one will ever be able to turn romania off its european course. thank you. thank you.

in writing. the properties of plastic have made significant improvements in food quality, transport, medicine and construction possible, but at the same time they are creating one of the main problems facing humanity alongside climate change. the lack of waste management policies for separate treatment and the lack of co-responsibility of packers has brought us to the current point where almost half a ton of plastic waste ends up in the oceans every second, and the amount is increasing at an alarming rate. under the pretext of making affordable products available to consumers, no one pays for the environmental costs that this waste generates and will continue to generate for centuries, in the form of microplastics. the problem is even greater when we talk about single-use plastics, designed to be used and thrown away, creating unsustainable consumption habits that must be curbed, especially when biodegradable alternatives are available. european industry has an opportunity to be a benchmark and a leader in the move away from single-use plastics. this directive is the first of many steps the eu must take to achieve a true circular economy.

the country. even though an ocean geographically divides us, we europeans cannot stand on the sidelines of this crisis. it concerns us simply because of the number of eu nationals who are also venezuelans, not to mention the social, cultural and economic ties that exist between europe and venezuela. our response so far has been both humanitarian and political. on the humanitarian side, we are currently mobilising eur 35 million in assistance to venezuelans both within and outside the country. we are investing in health assistance, food and water sanitation. we are working to support the socio—economic inclusion of venezuelans and to help the local economies of host communities in neighbouring countries. half of this eur 35 million package is already being implemented in near-record time and the remainder will be made operational by early next year. we are also exploring the possibility of further increasing the commission’s financial support beyond this already very significant contribution. we have welcomed the appointment of eduardo stein as a unhcr-iom joint special representative for venezuelan refugees and migrants, and, with the foreign ministers of the 28 member states, we had the opportunity to discuss the venezuelan migration crisis last monday in luxembourg during the foreign affairs council, expressing our support to both mr grandi and mr vitorino for this work, which we want to be joint work. on that occasion we had both mr grandi and mr vitorino with us. we didn’t focus purely on issues relating to migration and europe, and i believe that to be right. we stand ready to support any further coordinated action, both at regional and international level, to address this humanitarian crisis more effectively. but the only possible solution is political. last week – again with the foreign affairs council, with the foreign ministers – we discussed what more the european union can do to prevent a further deterioration in the situation or help change the course of these negative developments. ministers from all 28 member states have confirmed that, first of all, any sustainable political solution to the venezuelan crisis has to be democratic and peaceful, and those are the two pillars that are guiding our action. external intervention or any use of force would simply be unacceptable to us and would make things much worse. our immediate request to the government of venezuela is that it takes unilateral confidence-building measures to ease tensions, first and foremost by restoring the full constitutional powers of the national assembly and respecting the immunity of its members, releasing all political prisoners and taking concrete steps to restore political pluralism and guarantee respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. we expect, in particular, a full, independent and impartial investigation into the circumstances of councillor albán’s death. it is the duty of the state to ensure the safety and physical integrity of all people in its custody. finally, we ask the government to allow free, credible and transparent elections with full respect for the constitution. on all these points, we have not changed our minds. you have heard them and have said as much yourselves several times. the requests from our side remain on the table and we don’t intend to change our minds on these starting points: the people of venezuela are simply asking for democracy, and this crisis will end only with a political process heading in that direction. this is very clear to us europeans. in response to the human rights violations in venezuela and the ongoing attack on democratic institutions, we decided a year ago to impose targeted restrictive measures on a number of individuals who are responsible for the current situation. this is the first time that we are imposing these kinds of measures in latin america and, as you can imagine, we didn’t take the decision lightly. we took it not only because of the deteriorating situation, but also as a message for the authorities in venezuela, with which we are keeping a channel of dialogue open, to commit themselves seriously to a negotiated political solution to the current crisis. today, the situation has not improved at all. on the contrary. so we are sticking to our decision, and the restrictive measures will stay for as long as human rights are violated and democratic principles are disregarded. we do not intend to soften our position while there is no substantive progress on the ground. at the foreign affairs council last week, we started a discussion with the ministers on what else we, as the european union and as member states, can do, in addition to these positions and the decision to continue the sanctions, to end the downward spiral and help start some kind of political process, as the absence of a political process might in itself lead to a further deterioration in the situation. so we will explore, first of all together with latin american countries, the possibility of establishing a contact group with relevant and interested countries, not only from the region, and international players. we don’t think that, at this point in time, mediation or a dialogue would have any chance of succeeding. i want to be very clear on that point. it’s not a question of buying time. no way. the conditions for either a dialogue or for mediation are not there, but an international initiative – a european initiative together with others – could, with plenty of question marks, help build the conditions that would eventually make it possible to relaunch a political process. for the moment, this is just a possibility that we are exploring. i don’t want to raise expectations. we are simply worried about the lack of a political process and, personally, i don’t want to be in a position, six months or a year from now, of looking back and asking whether we could have done more on the political side to prevent the situation from deteriorating even further. so again, without raising expectations or launching an initiative today, the idea is simply to explore whether it might be possible to put something in place that could help create the conditions for something to happen in the future. i believe that we should try any peaceful option to end the current stalemate and prevent a violent escalation because, if the situation does not improve – and we do not see the situation improving – an escalation of violence cannot be ruled out, and that would mean even greater suffering for the people of venezuela. this is an option that we have to avert and prevent. we don’t want to impose any outside outsourced solution. that is never the european approach. we believe in democracy, we believe in ownership, we believe in cooperation and we believe in respect. we believe that the future of venezuela – and also the present of venezuela – must be written by its people and no one else, without any external intervention. but we will do everything we can to help the venezuelan people take the future and the present of the country back into their hands. i am looking forward to listening to your views.

the next item is the debate on the second report by mr marco valli, on behalf of the committee on budgetary control, on discharge in respect of the implementation of the general budget of the european union for the financial year 2016, section ii european council and council (com (2017) 0365 - c8-0249/2017 - 2017/2138 (dec)) (a8-0300/2018).
president-in-office of the council. – mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur and assure him that with regard to his words about feeling disappointed, i was told that they are all watching our debate on tv so there are more people watching than are here in the room. let’s come to the subject of the debate. this issue has been controversial between parliament and the council for a long time. let me first say something about the specific exercise of discharge for the 2016 budget and then comment on the state of play in general. in relation to the implementation of the 2016 budget, you know of course that the court of auditors, in its annual report, and i quote: ‘did not identify any issue concerning the council’. this will, most probably, not affect your vote this week, which is expected to be the same as in previous years, but it is worth underlining. i would now like to share with you my assessment of where we are on this issue in more general terms. since 2011, the council has proposed a memorandum of understanding to parliament in order to better organise the cooperation between our two institutions during the discharge procedure. for several years this initiative was not followed up by any concrete discussion between our two institutions. finally, over the last 11 months, some new efforts have been made on both sides. the idea is to reach an understanding which allows a pragmatic cooperation, while preserving the position of principle of both institutions. the council has contributed to these efforts by revising its 2011 position and sent a new proposal to parliament in may 2018. following further contacts and exchanges, the competent preparatory bodies of the council are currently examining the situation. i can assure you that the austrian presidency of the council is ready to do its utmost to find a solution if there is sufficient political will on both sides to bridge the gap.
on behalf of the ppe group mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would simply like to thank the rapporteur, mr valli, for the work he has done in preparing this report, which reproduces an old and longstanding polemic we have been having with the union's council of ministers. the rapporteur has reminded us very well of the powers that the treaties confer on the european parliament in terms of discharge, and since 2009 this parliament has been systematically refusing to approve the annual accounts, which is also what will happen for 2016. it is not a question of equivalence or reciprocity, madam president-in-office of the council, it is a question of respect for the powers conferred by the treaties, and in this sense the european parliament cannot accept equivalence or reciprocity in the sphere of their respective powers. we welcome the willingness to find an understanding which respects the powers of both institutions. in the meantime, the rapporteur's report points out some areas where improvements are needed. the council has not presented separate accounts for the european council and the council of the union. staff costs have to be separated by category, by sex, by function, by grade and by professional competence. and it is also clear that we must welcome the efforts made to consolidate the european union's transparency record, which also affects the union's council of ministers. so, mr president, it is clear that this situation should be overcome, but it should be overcome - as the council representative has said - on the basis of a mobilization of political will which can in some way represent respect for the rules, respect for the institutions, respect for the treaties and the rules derived from them, such as the financial regulation of the union.

madam president, i would like to bring some quiet and peaceful words after the previous disgraceful dispute. i will concentrate on northern ireland, because thatʼs an important point, and summarise the situation. the goal of including a protocol or not in ireland in the withdrawal agreement is to protect the good friday agreement by avoiding a hard border and by ensuring that there will be no diminution of rights for the citizens in the north. this protocol will be used as a backstop to protect the good friday agreement in case the future relationship does not solve the issue. we propose the participation of northern ireland in the single market and the customs union for goods through regulatory alignment. but this solution cannot be extended to the whole of the uk, as westminster would like, precisely because the uk’s government majority in westminster – of which the democratic unionist party is a key element – does not accept any differential solution for northern ireland, since this would create a border in the irish sea. the commission remains open to discussing other proposals to secure a backstop solution for northern ireland in the withdrawal agreement, but at the moment the uk has not presented any alternatives. unfortunately, we didnʼt achieve any agreement at the political level. in any case, we support the position of the commission on the need to include the backstop in the withdrawal agreement; on the proposal itself; on the fact that we are open to discussing other proposals if the uk comes up with something reasonable. the last council meeting was not able to take steps forward on this extremely sensitive issue, which needs a prompt and clear solution.
