cult. - (fr) mr president, this regulation is a new proposal, since there was no legislation on this subject, only the export regulation, which concerns only european goods. and i think it is especially relevant because this year, 2018, is the european year of cultural heritage. in the committee on culture and education we had two objectives: on the one hand, to prevent terrorism, organised crime and money laundering from being financed by the illegal purchase and sale of cultural goods from third countries; and on the other, to ensure the preservation of the cultural heritage of these countries. we also had to combine these fundamental objectives so that the european art market would not be harmed by too strict regulation, which would complicate the legal and usual market for european dealers, auction houses and museums. it has not been an easy task, as there were many conflicting interests, but i think we have managed to agree on a balanced text, and we are therefore pleased that the objectives i indicated earlier have been met.
the rapporteur. mr president, i am also pleased with the report on the regulation on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of medicated feedingstuffs and with the result achieved with my colleagues mrs grossetête and mr tănăsescu. i think in the end the result is quite positive. four years after the european commission launched a package of proposals to update the legislative framework for veterinary medicines, stricter rules have been proposed to make progress in the fight against antimicrobial resistance and to improve the availability and correct use of veterinary medicines in the european union. the proposal on medicated feedingstuffs is part of this legislative package. these feeds - 'medicated feeds' - are a route of administration of veterinary medicinal products, an effective tool for the treatment of animals in collectivities. as has already been said, the proposal on feedingstuffs is linked to the new legislation on medicinal products, to the three regulations. the proposal aims to update the 1990 directive, which is obsolete in many of its provisions, and to advance the internal market in medicated feedingstuffs by means of legislative harmonization which will now be established by means of regulations. the new text regulates the production, marketing and transport of medicated feedingstuffs and the correct administration to both animals intended for human consumption and pets. i would remind everyone that in addition to the specific provisions contained in this text, medicated feedingstuffs are also subject to other general legislation on hygiene and labelling of feedingstuffs, rules on the marketing and use of feedingstuffs and additives in animal feed. the agreement at first reading brings the feed regulation into line with the agreement on veterinary medicines reached by mrs grossetête. we have put a lot of emphasis on coordination, making our decisions in the trilogue dependent on the decisions and progress of the veterinary medicines trilogues as the main instrument. all matters relating to the authorization and requirements of the veterinary medicinal product to be applied to feed are regulated in the general text on veterinary medicinal products. we have paid particular attention to the coherence of the provisions designed to increase measures against antimicrobial resistance. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of antibiotics as growth promoters, which has been banned for many years. some important provisions: the preventive use of medicated feed with antibiotics is prohibited. prophylaxis is banned in the european union. metaphylaxis is reduced to cases of high risk to animal and/or human health under close surveillance, and explicit reference is made to the international dimension in the fight against antimicrobial resistance as set out in article 118 of the medicines regulation. in the context of international cooperation, and in line with the actions and policies of the world health organisation and the world organisation for animal health, progress in reducing the use of medicated feed containing antibiotics should be taken into account at global level for animals and products of animal origin from third countries exported to the european union. cross-contamination in the manufacturing process has also been a very important issue, and the efsa proposal will be submitted within four years. finally, thanks to the general coordination with the other two rapporteurs, we have achieved results which i believe are more than optimal. i believe we have achieved an ambitious regulation which will give consumers more certainty about livestock products in the european union and help us to achieve a victory in our fight against antimicrobial resistance.
mr president, as has already been said, there are many benefits to this regulation, but i would also like to highlight what i consider to be the most important: the fact that it has been able to include among its priorities one of the greatest challenges facing human health today, namely the fight against antimicrobial resistance. there are 25,000 deaths a year from not having the right antibiotic. and by 2050, if this continues, it will be higher than the number of cancer deaths. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the animal welfare system is properly managed. it has allowed for a restricted use list to be made of those antibiotics for human use; it has restricted the use of prophylaxis to exceptional and justified circumstances, or metaphylaxis, never to the detriment of hygiene or cleanliness; it has made veterinary prescription a must; it has, of course, banned the use for fattening or online sale, and it has made data collection possible. in short, as i said, a comprehensive vision, a very difficult job, but one that i think has been worthwhile. my congratulations to each of the speakers who have made this possible. i also join the call on the commission to legislate now and adopt a strong initiative so that we can combat this problem from the point of view of human health and human use.

the rapporteur. madam president, today we can say that europe is responding to the challenge of climate change. the agreement reached in june on the directive on the promotion of the use of energy from renewable sources is a great agreement. for a number of reasons: firstly, because we are going to double the current rate of renewable energy and go beyond that, i have no doubt, in the review of 2023; because we are increasing legal certainty and simplifying administrative procedures, which are crucial to guaranteeing investments; or because we are increasing the share of renewables in highly polluting sectors such as heating, cooling or transport. but there is one unique element in this directive which i would like to stress. europe is often accused of being aloof, out of step and not listening to its citizens, and today we can proudly say that europe has not only listened to them but has put them at the heart of energy policy. we have done so by enshrining for the first time the right to self-consumption, that is to say, the right to produce, the right to consume, the right to store and the right to sell the surplus energy produced. we have done so by committing to extend the benefits of renewables to the most vulnerable citizens, contributing to the fight against energy poverty. and we have done this by pushing for just energy transition measures so that those territories where the weight of coal was very important can have a just transition process, that they understand that no one leaves them to their fate. the commitment to renewables is a commitment to innovation, it is a commitment to economic activity, it is a commitment to quality employment in a sector where europe has the basis to regain world leadership, and it is a commitment to our own energy sources to become more energy independent. yes, one of the pillars of the energy union is precisely to strengthen our energy independence. that is why we have opened the way with this directive. moreover, this agreement we have reached, together with the efficiency agreement, will allow us to be much more ambitious, commissioner, in the decarbonisation targets that the european union had set for itself of 40% by 2030. we can go further, we can review it and we can reach 45%. europe must be ambitious and therefore raise its commitments at the next climate summit by giving a sign of leadership and above all by giving a sign of commitment to the world, especially now that the united states has left the paris agreement. and if these achievements have been possible, it has been because of the climate of mutual trust, teamwork and commitment of the whole negotiating team of parliament and also the commitment of the commission and, very singularly, of the alternative rapporteurs - kelly, federley, tamburrano, henkel, paloma and turmes - and also of the colleagues in the committee on the environment, led by mr bas. the motto of the european union is 'united in diversity'. our views were different, but we were able to move forward together to achieve our goals. that has certainly been our strength and the key to our success.
member of the commission. – madam president, it is a real pleasure to be here today to discuss three files which are central for the clean energy for all europeans package. i would like to take this opportunity in plenary to thank you all for the role that the european parliament delegation played in june in securing a political agreement. my special thanks go to the four rapporteurs: josé blanco lópez, miroslav poche, michèle rivasi and claude turmes, and also jakop dalunde. i would of course also like to thank president jerzy buzek and adina-ioana vălean, and all the shadow rapporteurs involved. without them we would not have got such an ambitious package. at the beginning of next month the cop 24 meets in katowice, where we are aiming for a successful outcome to agree on the detailed rules for the implementation of the paris agreement. the european union needs to assert its leadership and, by giving the files under the clean energy package its strong support, this parliament can play an important role in making this happen. closing these files strengthens the european union position as one of the most active leaders in the energy transition process and helps raise our collective ambition. these are perhaps the three most important dossiers in terms of delivering tangible benefits because of the targets contained in these new rules. they will set a stable and predictable legal framework for the way forward and enable us to make this major transformation for the economy and society – the clean energy transition. let me now say a few words about the three different dossiers, starting with energy efficiency. the key element in the agreement is that it sets a new headline energy efficiency target for the european union for 2030 of at least 32.5%, with an upward revision clause by 2023. thanks to the european parliament, we now have an ambitious outcome for 2030. the changes will also extend the current annual energy-saving obligation beyond 2020. this is a measure that has been a key driver in the progress made in recent years. taken together, these targets are vital as they will attract private investment and support the emergence of new market actors. this will also help drive research and innovation towards finding new solutions. ‘energy efficiency first’ is a key principle of our energy policy. it is an area where ambition pays off in terms of benefits for reinforced security of supply, improved competitiveness of our industries, gdp growth, and increased employment. the agreed text includes a number of tangible benefits for consumers, such as possible savings on their energy bills, improved living conditions and improved air quality. furthermore, consumer rights on billing and individual metering will be strengthened. the new rules will make household bills more transparent to ensure that they are more understandable. last but not least, energy efficiency measures also represent an important instrument for alleviating energy poverty. let me turn now to the renewable energy directive. here again the position of the parliament delegation was instrumental in securing a higher target for 2030. the text foresees a new binding renewable energy target for the european union for 2030 of at least 32%. it also includes a review clause by 2023 for an upward revision of the european union-level target. this is considerably higher than the 27% target originally outlined two years ago. in broader terms, the revised directive further ‘europeanises’ our approach to renewable energy, creating conditions for a cost—efficient deployment of renewables across the european union. it introduces the principle of non—retroactivity for support provided, improves the design of support schemes for renewables to make it more market-oriented, and it streamlines the administrative procedures. for consumers, it establishes a clear and stable regulatory framework on self—consumption – for the first time in european union legislation – which i believe will encourage more and more households to become actively involved in the clean energy transition as consumers. on the design and support schemes and the scope of tendering, the commission would like to reiterate, though, that while fully supporting the objectives of the directive, the commission considers that they could be achieved without the respective wording of article 4. this declaration has been transmitted to the european parliament and will be annexed to the minutes. that brings me to the third and final file, the new governance regulation. while the revisions of the two directives will provide further impetus for investment in renewables and energy efficiency – the two major elements contributing to reducing greenhouse gas emissions – the governance regulation establishes the process, ensuring member states achieve this in a coherent and the most efficient way possible across all dimensions of the energy union. it complements the european union ets directive, the efforts sharing and lulucf regulations, and provides genuine european added value. the new regulation requires each member state to prepare an integrated national energy and climate plan for a 10-year period, starting with 2021 to 2030. this unique tool will allow assessing progress in achieving the energy union and our targets as it will, for the first time, encompass all relevant policies and measures of member states and the results of regional cooperation. the commission may then make recommendations on the plans aimed at ensuring, in case of deviations, that the european union meets the 2030 energy and climate targets in the most coherent, collaborative and cost—effective way. the european parliament and the council will address, on an annual basis, progress achieved in the energy union in all dimensions of energy and climate policy. i must underline that the rules fully respect member states’ choices in determining their own energy mix. but it brings a fair and robust mechanism to facilitate the collective attainment of the binding european union renewables target, the european union energy efficiency target and the 15% interconnection target, while also considering research, innovation and competitiveness. for the sake of completeness, let me recall two declarations made by the commission during the negotiations: our commitment to analyse methane emissions, while at the same time preserving our right of initiative; and on the importance of a clear division of competences within the future two committees assisting the commission in the implementation of the regulation, which we would have preferred to be in one single committee. these declarations are transmitted to the european parliament and will be annexed to the minutes. the adoption of these three dossiers will mean that we will have finalised half of the clean energy for all europeans package and set our main energy-related targets for 2030. the fact that the targets agreed are higher than those originally proposed by the commission means that we can probably achieve even steeper emission reductions by 2030. our latest modelling suggests that meeting these targets will de facto enable a reduction of emissions of roughly 45% across the european union by 2030, going beyond the 40% paris agreement commitment. this will allow the european union to show true leadership with real action in next month’s cop 24 talks in katowice. we are making progress on the other clean energy dossiers – regarding electricity market design, including risk preparedness – and i am optimistic that, with the same ambition and constructive approach from all sides that we have shown on these files, we can conclude these before the end of the year under the austrian council presidency. taken together with other parts of the package, i am convinced that these changes will have a positive impact on our quality of life and ultimately lead to cheaper household energy bills. similarly, negotiations on the low—carbon mobility package are advancing and we hope to conclude the files under this parliament. you will also be aware that the commission concept for the next multiannual financial framework will put climate—related spending at the heart of our budget. as well as raising the ambition for climate, including clean energy transition mainstreaming across all european union programmes from 20% to at least 25% from 2021 onwards, we are looking to boost the level of spending in all the main budget areas, notably research and structural investment. one of the main legacies of this commission and this parliament will be that we have put climate change and clean energy transition at the heart of our agenda. this is what we need to explain to our citizens, especially in the run—up to the next european elections, where you can be proud of the important progress achieved together. i look forward to the debate. statements the rapporteur. madam president, mr ansip, ladies and gentlemen, we are voting today on the new european regulation on electronic communications. the last one was in 2009 and since then, there have been extraordinary technological changes, changes that have affected business models, user interests, and the experiences of consumers themselves, and that have completely transformed the landscape of electronic communications. we have to start by saying that connectivity has always been the precondition, the necessary condition for the extraordinary advances that have been known to mankind, especially in the 20th century, through the hand of technology. i am sure that the situation of our economy and the development of our society would be very, very different. today we are in a similar situation, where connectivity is a necessary and urgent condition for the european union to be able to harness the potential of the most advanced digital technologies, such as the internet of things, big data, artificial intelligence, robotics, quantum computing and a long list of others. these are technologies that are breaking through, that are breaking through in an extraordinary way, at a very, very high speed and are waiting to have the connectivity they need to be able to develop fully and thus unleash their full potential of new opportunities for the economy and society. think about the development possibilities that 5g can offer us for the future - for the very near future - such as, for example, performing long-distance surgical interventions; high-risk work that can be done from a safe place; or for the farmers themselves, for the agricultural sector, which, by obtaining real-time data, can greatly improve agricultural holdings. for all these reasons, the new regulatory framework, in addition to the digital market, reinforces and places connectivity as the backbone of this regulation of the electronic communications market. it includes a series of measures to this end, measures which will attract investment, make investment more attractive, such as co-investment models, better and more harmonized management of radio spectrum, improving the duration of licences with a minimum duration of, for example, twenty years. the code also obliges all member states to release and allow the use of the known 5g bands before the end of 2020 and, in protecting consumers, establishes and improves emergency services, giving more opportunities for localization in case of disaster, in addition to introducing a very significant reduction in pan-european calls, intra-european calls, which, after the disappearance of roaming costs, is very good news also for citizens. in short, the european electronic communications code is intended to play a key role in the digitalisation of europe and does so by putting connectivity at its heart.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, europe is playing its future competitiveness on its digital agenda. with this reform, we are laying the foundations for boosting investment in high-speed networks and the deployment of 5g, which are crucial to making new services such as autonomous mobility or the new era of the internet of things possible. this means new opportunities to boost innovation, economic activity and quality employment. but thanks to parliament - i would like to congratulate pilar del castillo and the rapporteurs - we have also introduced limits on the price of calls between member states, which is good for all citizens. that is how europe advances, by breaking down barriers to communication.
vice-president of the commission – madam president, thank you to everyone who has made it possible for this package to become a reality. it will make a huge difference to people and business, to our society and economy. the european commission is pleased that the european parliament and the council share many of the same objectives that will take us towards a gigabit society. together we managed to agree on a balanced text that benefits and protects all europeans and paves the way towards very high—capacity networks, including 5g. although we have created a structure and environment for the next decade of european telecoms, our work is not yet done. in fact, it has just started. for the commission, our focus will now be to make sure that the code is properly implemented, and we will also monitor this. eu member states have two years to transpose and implement the rules. not only must they do this on time, they must also do it correctly and efficiently. we will assist member states in transposing the new rules into national law.
the rapporteur. madam president, i would like to start by thanking the other parliamentary group alternate rapporteurs: miapetra kumpula-natri, evžen tošenovský, kaja kallas, dita charanzová and julia reda for their excellent cooperation. the cooperation with the commission has been excellent and this must be emphasized. and i would also like to mention jerzy buzek, who has masterfully, masterfully, as he always does, chaired all the trilogues we have had with the council. the debate we have had today on the european electronic communications code is a great example of concrete solutions to concrete problems which can only be tackled within the framework of the european union, which we must tackle together. in this case, solutions to a connection, to a connectivity that is absolutely necessary if we want citizens and all economic sectors to have opportunities in this age of digitization. i am sure that the commission will be able to take account of this. and i insist: the european union's added value in tackling the great challenges of digitisation is essential; only together can we do it. and this regulation is a magnificent example that we can present as a great achievement to the european citizens, to the voters who, in a few months, will again take part in european elections.
madam president, commissioner, i too welcome this proposal, which is being put forward for the first time, because heavy vehicles account for 6% of emissions, they are increasing and ambitious targets for reducing emissions in the european union also need to be set. this regulation is an important complement to all that has been done on fuzzy sectors, such as the e4-share or the light vehicle standards. but to send a clear signal to industry, as you have very well said, commissioner, we need reduction targets which are both ambitious and achievable by manufacturers. we need a clear definition of what low-emission vehicles are. we need the necessary adjustments to account for emissions avoided by certain combustion of renewables and we need a system of reasonable fines. the fact is that we have reached a vote in this house without the rapporteur having succeeded in reaching agreement between the parliamentary groups. i regret this and hope that the rapporteur can reach an agreement with the council soon to have a stable and predictable legal framework before the end of the legislature.
madam president, the decarbonisation of the transport sector is key to meeting the objectives of combating climate change, and we need to act in this sector in a special way because of its difficulty in reducing emissions and its volume, which represents a quarter of the european union. the sector is also a major source of employment in europe and is undergoing a profound technological transformation. ladies and gentlemen, society is demanding that we breathe clean air without pollution, and this is particularly acute in our cities, in the large urban conglomerations. this regulation makes perfect sense in order to promote safer traffic with less polluting vehicles and more advanced technological solutions, while promoting the competitiveness of european industry.

the next item on the agenda is the topical debate (rule 153a) on strengthening the union's resilience to external influences in the upcoming european parliament election campaign (2018/2919 ((rsp)).
mr president, madam president, the interference of external actors in electoral processes and the misuse of metadata are having serious effects on electoral procedures, as they allow both the massive collection of confidential information from the electorate and the distribution of fake news generated to attract and disinform. cambridge analytica killed the privacy of 50 million people, and according to europol's ec3, both clinton and macron's campaigns were attacked. mixing authentic manipulated elements is one strategy to maximize the negative impact of an attack. fake news websites, accounts, and social media are used to spread inaccurate news, designed to appear authentic and harm a candidate or party. in may there are elections to this house. the union must take measures to ensure that no electoral process is subject to criminal interference. public and private actors need to coordinate their actions to prevent such attacks and there is also a need for improved cooperation between agencies. the union needs to curb the misuse of data mining with the european cybersecurity package, which includes pushing for the creation of a european security agency, and must give resources and credibility to those already looking after it, such as europol's european cybercrime centre ec3. the threats to democracy, the sovereignty of states and the fundamental rights of european citizens must be stopped.
mr president, commissioner for security and justice, on 26 may 2019 this european parliament will be elected, representing democratically, directly, 500 million european citizens. and since 2014, the last european parliament election, we have witnessed a series of episodes of criminal interference in electoral processes and consultations and referendums in the member states of the european union. this european parliament, which sends missions to monitor the correctness and credibility of elections abroad, has every reason to be concerned that the fundamental right to political participation and democratic election is not interfered with by a hybrid war of intoxication, cyberterrorism, manipulation or blackmail in any way. it is therefore urgent that we join forces to shape our agenda against cybercrime and for cybersecurity as soon as possible with a european cybersecurity agency and with europol's cybercrime intelligence unit, to ensure that we are absolutely prepared so that the 2019 european parliament elections do not cast the slightest doubt on the credibility of any of the member states of the european union and we are absolutely sure that the result really reflects the will of the europeans and not the will of those who have agreed from some dark and dark workshop of manipulation or re-intoxication outside to condition the composition of this european parliament against the european union and its founding values.
in writing. the next european parliament elections will begin in the coming months and the eu must redouble its efforts to ensure that the fundamental right to political participation and democratic choice is not interfered with by a hybrid war of intoxication, cyber terrorism, manipulation and blackmail in any way. unfortunately, in recent years we have witnessed a number of incidents of criminal interference in electoral processes and consultations and referendums in the member states of the union. the high degree of convergence between the three institutions in this area therefore needs to be reflected in the swift adoption of the measures proposed by the commission, including the establishment of electoral cooperation networks at national and eu level; the launching of guidelines on the application of data protection rules in the electoral context and recommendations on increased transparency in paid online advertising and political communication; the strengthening of cybersecurity; the diligent application of existing electoral rules; and the entry into force of a legislative proposal to allow sanctions to be imposed for the misuse of personal data for electoral purposes.

i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, this report proposes significant progress in the treatment of rail passengers and we hope that it will be an important step towards improving the quality of service. the train must be the means of transport of the future. it is the most sustainable, the safest, the one that allows for greater territorial spinach and accessibility. and so we must encourage its use and make it more attractive to users. some positive aspects are that with this proposal we maximise the information available to the user, ensure that bicycle users can access the train without risk to the safety of other passengers, prioritise relocation without prejudice to compensation and reimbursement in the event of cancellation of a service and ensure an appropriate complaints protocol. but the most important thing is the leap that can be made in the accessibility of the service for vulnerable users. the report proposes that assistance at stations and access to trains be ensured by trained staff, that information be made available in accessible formats and that persons with reduced mobility be given priority in relocation, including with guide animals. however, i would stress that it is not enough to encourage the use of rail to improve passenger rights. it must be promoted as a means of public transport. it must be promoted by public institutions and not be subject to ever-increasing cuts and privatisation processes.
madam president, mrs bulc, i would like to thank you for your time. when did the spanish ave win the battle to the airplane, especially on the main lines, and also increasingly to the road? it was then that, under a socialist government, a female councillor and the head of the ave decided that passengers should be compensated for the least delay and up to 100%, apart from agreeing to give access to the next train if the previous one had been missed. these were fundamental elements of passenger rights that helped the ave to take off and today make it one of the most punctual european trains and one of the most well-received by travellers, although there is always room for improvement, that's for sure. the service for people with accessibility problems has also been strengthened and infrastructure has been built at stations. there's still a lot to do, it's true. sustainable multimodality - with bicycle access to the train - is also needed, but so are urban connections. finally, we do not agree with the attempt to reverse the situation by a misunderstood sense of the protection of the railway sector, by limiting passenger rights. on the contrary, we are in favour of further efforts to guarantee more rights for passengers.
madam president, commissioner, i would like to congratulate you on the work done on this report on railway users' rights, because it is really focused on passengers, because it extends the guarantees and also contains some of the main recommendations of the court of auditors on this matter. because it is not enough to set clear definitions. in addition, it is vital to simplify the procedures for claiming and, if possible, to automate compensation. the first objective is to clarify, to avoid ambiguities which allow companies to evade their responsibilities. it can be improved a great deal if we support amendments which make it clear once and for all what causes of force majeure can and cannot be considered to justify a delay or the cancellation of a service. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. it is committed to more sustainable mobility, always reserving space for bicycles, and the rights of people with disabilities are improved. large stations must be fully adapted. in small towns it is proposed that three hours should be sufficient to request assistance. finally - and this is crucial - in order to improve access to this catalogue of rights and guarantees, a european complaint form and a move towards an automatic compensation system are being considered. it is not reasonable, when it is clear that the passenger must be compensated, for him to ask for what is due him. you have the right to a refund as part of the service including the service you have paid for.

mr president, madam president, president trump's announcement of a possible breach of the intermediate-range nuclear forces (inf) treaty is seriously undermining euro-atlantic security, which is one of the pillars of nato. the inf prohibits the manufacture of ground-launched medium-range missiles, which can reach targets between 500 and 5 500 kilometres. both trump's announcement and russia's alleged failure to comply, developing the novator 9m729 missile, represent a deterioration of the arms control regime in the euro-atlantic space that for decades has fostered peace and stability. in recent years, the union, through the different security strategies presented, as well as its leadership in the negotiations and implementation of the nuclear agreement with iran, has shown its capacity to be a leading international actor in disarmament and non-proliferation policies. tensions between the us and russia over the inf can take us back to the past, when the arms race was a constant source of international danger and tension. to quote gorbachev, "every agreement for nuclear disarmament must be maintained to save the life of the earth". the union must continue to promote non-proliferation policies and establish itself as a leading actor. if the united states and russia want to be irresponsible, the union must be able to act on the international scene to avoid a cold war, or not so cold.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union is able to meet the needs of the people of europe. 80% of care services provided in the european union are provided by informal unpaid carers, 75% of whom are women. this has a lot to do with the problem that exists at the moment, the wage gap and the pension gap. it is scandalous that in the europe of the 21st century women are receiving an average of 45% less in pensions than men. and another revealing fact also drawn from the report is how austerity policies have contributed to the deterioration of public services, so fundamental to achieving this principle of conciliation and co-responsibility. we therefore welcome the report and stress that the requests for progress in reconciling family and working life and in co-responsibility are being met. that is why we are also calling here today for an agreement by the council and for negotiations with this parliament to be possible on the parental leave directive. it is fundamental. it is indispensable. women have spent their entire lives making peace. now we need them to be our partners, to be the men who join this task. and, in addition, this report also refers to the need for the systems for the recognition of social rights and pensions to take care of carers. and that is why i emphasize here initiatives such as that of the spanish government, with its draft budgets, which include the reintegration of women who care for dependent persons into the social security systems. only through these initiatives will we be able to make progress towards a real co-responsibility for the care of dependent persons and children in the european union.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, commissioner, the way europe manages its health services, the way we treat its professionals, will say a lot about what we want for the european union and its future. the care of dependent persons, the elderly and children has traditionally been a task for which women have not been paid or recognised. today, 80% of care services provided in the union are provided by unpaid carers, of whom 75% to 80% are women. the trend in europe is negative: over the last ten years, the time spent by women on care, domestic work and social activities has increased compared to men. this has serious economic and social consequences and is an obstacle to the achievement of the union's gender equality objectives. it's time to change this. it's time we embraced caring for others as a key social task that shapes the level of well-being and even the moral level of a society. it is time for care services to be recognised and regulated for what they are: a european pillar of social rights. both the european institutions and the member states must make an effort in this area: we must define them correctly, so that they include childcare and early childhood education, care for the elderly and also care for people with disabilities. we need to make them accessible and flexible to meet the needs of families with different needs and personal situations. think of single-parent families, the self-employed, shift workers in a profoundly and radically transformed world of work. let us think of a society which must evolve to meet these new challenges, because in a europe which cares, in a europe which protects, in a europe which leaves no one behind, caring must be a respected, safe, transparent, professional and adequately remunerated activity.
on behalf of the green group, mr president, in recent years the lack of sufficiently developed public care and support services for carers has meant that many women have been forced to return to caring. austerity and cuts in public services have done extraordinary damage to equality between men and women. and then, of course, this has repercussions on the pay gap and the pension gap, because many women are forced to leave their jobs to take on caring tasks. it is therefore very important to develop this essential pillar of the welfare state. i am glad that we are adopting this report today, which clearly calls for the development of public services, for clear investment in care services in the member states and for support for professionals, carers and training, and that this is a developed pillar that will allow, once and for all, for an equal society. there will be no equal society in the european union if we do not have public services capable of covering this essential pillar of the welfare state.
mr president, 75% of those engaged in care work in the european union are women. care work, historically carried out by women invisibly in the private sector, is today a source of precariousness in the labour market and yet is essential for the maintenance of life. the care cannot continue to be provided informally at the expense of women's living conditions and health. i therefore call for common sense to remove the reference to informal care. we must professionalize the sector and guarantee labour rights for three reasons: first, because it is a right, for social justice; second, because it is a need of our societies; and third, because it is not only a problem to be solved, but also an opportunity. according to the international trade union conference, in the oecd countries, investing between 2% and 6% could increase employment by up to 8% in many of them. investing in quality care with quality public services can be a great opportunity to create quality jobs and improve the lives of our societies.
in writing. in the eu, three quarters of carers are women. this shows a very unequal situation, which is the result of unjust patriarchal structures and which condemns millions of women to a much more limited access to work than men, not to mention the associated stereotypes that reinforce the idea that we must first of all stay at home and exclusively take care of care tasks. in the face of this, the eu has treaties and a whole series of directives that can be developed and improved in the field of family and work reconciliation and the recognition of rights for carers. we therefore ask the commission to support a programme and a package of concrete measures, including the extension of maternity leave, to promote real equality and reconciliation. we also want the states to get involved by providing quality public services and key infrastructure, such as day centres or day nurseries, with special emphasis on rural areas or those most affected by depopulation. finally, let us not forget to increase the allocation of resources to cohesion policy to strengthen the provision of quality public health care services.

studies, and the findings of the recent ‘fitness check’ on the general food law regulation confirmed this priority. today’s debate is a significant stepping stone on the way to meeting these expectations and to showing that the eu can deliver on our demands, on your demands and on citizens’ demands. allow me to draw your attention to the main features of the commission’s ambitious proposal. i would like to explain briefly how we have pursued the objectives of reinforcing transparency and trust. i believe it is through greater transparency that we will increase citizens’ confidence in the risk assessment system. the new legislation will thus contribute to increasing the legitimacy of the european food safety authority (efsa) and of the commission’s decisions when it accepts or rejects requests for approval. with this goal in mind, the commission has proposed proactive public disclosure of all safety—related data – let me repeat, safety—related data – supporting applications for authorisation, and we have proposed that this be done early in the risk assessment process. early disclosure is essential to ensure maximum transparency and public scrutiny in an effective way, while maintaining a timely and effective risk management process. of course, transparency can also help us to avoid potential bias in science. it is crucial to restore trust in the eu’s evidence—based food safety system and trust in science. let me insist on one important point. postponing transparency until the opinion is published would, as we know from practice today, risk feeding suspicion and controversies. it would not permit a real scientific debate between different views, but would lead to more political controversies – and we have had too many of those recently. as long as the principle of early disclosure is retained, however, its exact timing could be the subject of further consideration. for example, it could coincide with the moment the underlying application is found admissible. this disclosure of studies is also closely linked with two other measures in our proposal: first, the public consultation of submitted studies; and, second, the disclosure of the relevant information in the union register of commissioned studies. these measures will ensure that efsa has at its disposal the broadest relevant scientific evidence possible before it drafts its scientific opinion. and, of course, any rights stemming from the access to documents regulation and the aarhus convention remain intact and will continue to apply. at the same time, i am aware of concerns in relation to the protection of innovation, but i want to reassure you that, when we prepared this proposal, we also had in mind the need to maintain the european union’s high food safety standards together with the competitiveness of the eu food and feed sector. there is no controversy as between food safety standards and competitiveness, and that is why the proposal sets out safeguards for the protection of justifiable, confidential information. it includes a closed positive list of items that may be claimed as confidential. confidentiality can be claimed if the applicant can prove that public disclosure of such information would significantly harm its competitive position. at the same time, the proposal respects existing intellectual property rights, data exclusivity rights and rules on the protection of personal data. these are recognised as key to stimulating innovation, and for the worldwide recognition of eu product safety. furthermore, to assist applicants – most importantly, small and medium-sized enterprises – we have introduced the possibility of efsa providing pre—submission advice. this advice will facilitate a better understanding of the application process and will make life easier for innovators in europe. finally, the proposal also provides for the possibility of commissioning additional studies for verification purposes. this may be done in exceptional circumstances, for example in the event of public controversy or scientific divergence about a product. further to the provisions on transparency, and to ensure the long—term sustainability of efsa’s high level of independent expertise, it is proposed that member states will be represented on the efsa management board. similarly, and without jeopardising efsa’s independence, there is provision for more active involvement by member states in ensuring the presence of experts on efsa’s scientific panels. it has also been recognised that there is a need to improve on our communication of risk. it is important that strong, clear messaging on risks is available to our citizens. to this end, the proposal lays the foundations for a comprehensive and effective risk-communication strategy to ensure that, whether the message comes from the commission, efsa or member states, it will be clear, comprehensive and consistent. the european parliament, the council and the commission are all responsible for maintaining and reinforcing an eu food safety system based on scientific assessments. transparency and risk assessment are therefore a shared duty for all of us. with this proposal, we are, more than ever, playing our part. i would like to thank all those involved, including the rapporteur, ms sommer, and the shadow rapporteur as well as the rapporteurs for opinion, for their active commitment so far – and, i hope, for their continued engagement and dedication in advancing with the commission proposal and defending transparency. who can be against transparency in science? no one. i look forward to a positive outcome in the plenary vote and to the start of the trilogue discussion as soon as the house is ready.
on behalf of the ppe group mr president, commissioner, i would like to start by congratulating mrs sommer on this report and, of course, supporting all her proposals. i understand the aim of the proposal to strengthen transparency in the risk assessment process, but i want to stress as the contact person for the agency that efsa is independent and scientifically sound and that it adheres to the current regulation. however, i sincerely believe that there has been a lack of political ambition to reform the regulation in depth and to update the tasks of efsa which, after almost twenty years, is overburdened with tasks that are far removed from what is strictly food safety. as regards transparency, efsa should be homologated to other union agencies such as ema and echa, i.e. information on applications and baseline studies should be published at the time of the publication of its scientific opinion. i agree that we must strengthen the agency's transparency, but without ideological overtones and without this conditioning the applicants' capacity for innovation. finally, this regulation in force established the rapid alert system, but despite being revised in 2011, we still do not have a harmonised procedure for action by all member states and we have not strengthened the commission's powers in managing alerts. it is not enough to have a simple support manual, as we have today, and this is an opportunity to solve this and to avoid a repeat of the social alarms we have had in the past.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, i would like to thank everyone for the opportunity to contribute to this debate. let me start with digital taxation: i would like to give you a brief overview of the work of the austrian presidency, and i would like to summarise the ecofin council outcome and the next steps, as we see it. all member states agreed that the fair taxation of the digital economy is very topical. we also all agreed that, in the long term, this requires a global solution. it becomes more and more evident that global changes in economic models might require a larger overhaul of agreed international tax rules. if we design specific rules targeting only some of the digital business models, we risk not capturing all and not making the rules future—proof. international rules have to be adapted and this has to be done – preferably in an orderly way – by reaching international agreements with a wide scope, both in terms of ambition and in terms of the number of economies adhering thereto. there are discussions currently ongoing at the level of g20 and the oecd. the european union is actively contributing to these discussions. the g20 has set the oecd the deadline of 2020. i believe this is a realistic deadline, and the oecd should be given a fair chance to negotiate and implement revisions to the international tax framework by that date. keeping in mind the wider global context, it is our firm belief that, when it comes to interim levies, a common eu approach is preferable to unilateral national measures. until now, 11 member states have announced that they have, or shortly will have, a national digital service tax in place. we are convinced that, if we do not reach agreement on the eu interim measure, even more member states might consider taking this path. we could see a proliferation of different national taxes with different rates and scopes. this could lead to the fragmentation of the single market and could harm the competitiveness and growth of the eu economy. in this context, the austrian presidency devoted considerable efforts to the digital service tax directive. all technical and legal aspects of the proposal were examined in great detail. numerous meetings took place at technical, as well as at political levels – most notably at ecofin council meetings on 6 november and 4 december 2018. for the meeting of the ecofin council last week, we prepared the compromise text, which had the broad support of member states. in our view, that compromise was balanced and legally sound, representing elements with the most support. unfortunately, before the ecofin meeting, we could see that we would not have unanimity on the text. during the meeting, two delegations – germany and france – in an effort to constructively contribute to the discussions, suggested that we should continue discussing the directive, but with a narrower scope. we have not yet had in—depth discussions of this new suggestion, since delegations need to study it in their capitals. however, many delegations confirmed their willingness to discuss it. therefore, as the presidency, we will try to take discussions forward on that basis. the incoming romanian presidency is closely associated with these discussions and will be ready to seamlessly take over as from 1 january 2019. last but not least, on the topic of digital taxation, i would also like to thank the honourable rapporteurs, mr tang and mr rosati, for their work on this and we welcome the fact that you will very soon adopt the two reports. on the second topic that you have proposed to discuss today – the need for a majority rule for taxation – i can be very brief. as the treaties currently stand, taxation is subject to unanimity. i am aware of the passerelle clause in the treaty on european union. should there be such an initiative on the table, it would be examined in accordance with the procedure foreseen by the treaties.
member of the commission. the european union is not a party to the treaty of rome, but it is a party to the treaty of rome. i am here to represent my colleague mr moscovici, who is due to meet the italian prime minister in brussels this afternoon. i would like to thank the two rapporteurs, mr tang and mr rosati, with great respect, for two competent and, in my opinion, comprehensive reports which facilitate the work of the commission at european level and which i can largely endorse. that is why the commission presented an initiative in march of this year. we believe that in the digital age, the corporate tax system in the member states is no longer fully up to date in europe and globally. the decomposition works very, very well in the analogue age for products and services, and therefore also the fair allocation of sales, revenues and therefore possible taxes. but in the case of digital services, this is increasingly difficult to do when there is no physical presence and when data from europeans and european events generates sales and revenues, but also taxes, outside europe. this trend will increase. the share of digital services and big data in global gdp is increasing. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the tax system is fair and that the revenue of the public treasury is stabilized. we have therefore made two proposals to ensure fair and efficient taxation. i would like to say at the outset that we are prepared to optimise and develop our proposals. we have made a contribution and are able to work flexibly at any time on further developments with the aim of reaching an agreement. the first is the reform of corporate tax rules to ensure that europe gets a fair share of profits and revenues. and it's about a temporary tax - a temporary tax - targeting the most important digital activities that are currently escaping europe in terms of an increasing amount of revenue. i am glad to see that parliament and the commission are allies on this and other issues. i also thank the presidency for its active role in moderating the council debate, which i believe can be very useful. the two reports - i have mentioned them - show a high level of competence and support the commission's proposals in general. by deciding on these two reports here tomorrow, you will send a clear signal to those member states which are still hesitant to speed up the debate in the council. we think that the franco-german initiative can be helpful here. paris and berlin have proposed to limit the scope to advertising sales in order to reach an agreement by spring next year, with the aim of having a corresponding digital tax come into force on 1 january 2021, but doing everything in time to still reach international solutions at the oecd plus level. the digital tax will enter into force in january 2021 and would expire in 2025, if there is no solution at the international level. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment against the adverse effects of certain substances and preparations is based on the principle of proportionality. the other argument that needs to be seen is that the trade war with the united states, which we want to avoid and have avoided so far, could become a little more likely again. we must make that assessment in the coming months. the paris and berlin proposal is not quite as ambitious as the commission's, but it is an opportunity to reach an agreement. we agreed that the tax should be temporary. we agree that the optimal solution should be of a structural and global nature - that is why the oecd level is the next level of dialogue. and we have to agree that the lack of agreement would lead to a disorderly approach, with 10, 11 or 12 or more national solutions. this would be a fragmentation of the european, and especially the european digital single market. the digital tax dossier shows once again that it is difficult to solve tax problems within the framework of the unanimity principle. we will therefore propose to this house, as announced by president juncker, in the state of the union address, the adoption of a qualified majority in taxation at the beginning of next year. we would gain the ability to act, and we could also get results faster and with a high probability. examples where the majority principle would be useful include the proposed common consolidated corporate tax base, the reform of vat legislation to create a single vat area and the reform of digital taxation. a transition to qualified majority voting would also broaden the scope of tax policy in europe. we believe that taxation can help to achieve general policy objectives in the field of environmental protection or energy policy, in the rural sector, and financial transaction tax, energy tax or climate tax are examples of this. it would also be a democratic advance. in a union of 28 or 27, unanimity is not really practical; it has become cumbersome and counterproductive. we therefore ask the house to take a favourable view of our proposal at the beginning of next year.

mr president, the number of refugee and migrant arrivals in bosnia and herzegovina during 2018 has increased significantly, with more than 22 400 arrivals recorded since the beginning of the year and compared to 755 in 2017. many are trying to move through bosnia and herzegovina to enter the union, crossing croatia. however, others remain in the country. the unhcr estimates that around 6 000 people were present on bosnian territory in mid-november 2018. local communities and international organizations have taken over basic assistance: food, shelter, primary health care. however, the country's capacities are overwhelmed. since june, the union has mobilised over eur 9.2 million in immediate and medium-term assistance. this makes it easier, but not much easier, to access essential services that are far from the migration routes. the western balkans route is mainly used by afghans, pakistanis and syrians. throughout 2018, the migratory pressure on this route has been increasing, which has led to organized crime groups increasing their criminal activity around human trafficking. this is one of the main reasons why europol has identified this region as a priority for increased cooperation. our charter of fundamental rights, the universal declaration of human rights, the 1951 convention relating to the status of refugees and the 1967 protocol commit us to this. and they commit us, fundamentally, from a humanitarian point of view. i applaud the states which signed the global compact on migration in marrakesh. all this commits the european union as a defender of human rights unequivocally.

mr president, the approval of jefta will have tremendous consequences for the citizens. it is the most ambitious treaty negotiated by the european union, but it cannot be debated or amended in national parliaments. this is particularly scandalous because the process has been really opaque and the european commission, in a fit of its supposed transparency, has only consulted the big business lobbies and the corporate lobbies. this is how they manage to impose, as already happened with ceta, the negative list approach to services, severely limiting the powers of governments to manage public services such as health, education and transport, or to encourage their remunicipalization. jefta will grant unprecedented privileges to transnational corporations, including a mechanism that allows them to influence governments through legislation. this is an intolerable reduction of democracy again, of labour rights and of the ability to fight financial speculation, for example. that is why we voted no to jefta.
mr president, the connecting europe facility promotes an energy model at the opposite end of what we need in this time of climate emergency. it promotes an unsustainable centralised model with mega-infrastructures such as the midcat gas pipeline, the tav or, for example, the electricity interconnection of the bay of biscay. far from stopping funding fossil fuels, this mechanism will continue to finance the misnamed natural gas, which will continue to receive billions of euros when we know that its effects on the climate are very, very harmful. nor does this fund put the principle of energy efficiency first, which is what we should be doing by reducing our consumption first rather than promoting infrastructure whose justification is more than doubtful. in addition, the money to finance this mechanism will come from the reduction of the cohesion fund, the main instrument for correcting territorial inequalities within the european union. finally, it is advocating the militarization of transport infrastructure, with the introduction of a pernicious dual use of civil and military: its way of bringing in the military dimension.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, the connecting europe facility promotes an energy model at the opposite end of what we need in this time of global climate emergency. it promotes a centralized and unsustainable model with mega-infrastructures such as gas pipelines like the midcat, or the tav, or the electricity interconnection of the bay of biscay. far from stopping funding fossil fuels, the misnamed natural gas will continue to receive billions of euros, when we know that its effects on the climate are very, very harmful. nor does this fund put forward the principle of energy efficiency, which we should apply by reducing our consumption first rather than promoting mega-infrastructures whose justification is often more than doubtful. in addition, the money to finance the mechanism will come from the reduction of the european cohesion fund, the main instrument for correcting territorial inequalities within the european union. finally, there is a call for the militarization of transport infrastructure, introducing dual use, civil and military. and this is their way of bringing the military dimension into the sectoral and civil policies of the union through the back door. we are in favour of a europe of peace and of the ecological transition. that is why we voted against this mechanism.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, there are more than 6 000 rare diseases affecting 30 million european citizens. they are often chronic and life-threatening. as eurordis says, rare diseases are rare, but rare disease patients are many. there are also many problems they face: among others, lack of access to correct diagnoses and information; social, educational, employment, leisure, etc. consequences; inequality in the availability of treatments and high cost of medicines. the list of problems is very long, but the solutions boil down to providing sufficient resources to implement public health policies. strengthening public health is essential because it is the only guarantee that all patients can have access to diagnoses and treatments under equal conditions and not depending on the financial resources of individuals or families. because this is precisely what creates additional inequality. it is also essential to provide resources for research, and - i repeat - it must be public: we cannot leave the solution of these problems to private research, precisely because of the costs it entails. and also resources for non-medical care: for dependents, family support, social support, for rehabilitation and a long list of others. we have the opportunity to promote these public policies, which are necessary so that patients do not have to suffer, in addition to isolation and vulnerability, inequality and indifference.
i am very pleased that the commissioner has taken this opportunity to express his concern about the situation in the european union. one of the biggest confusions is the concept of rarity. rare diseases are rare, but people with rare diseases are many in europe. i know many families who pay high costs, who have to even campaign in the media to speak out, to ask for money to pay for these treatments. it's hard for these families; they feel alone. one disease may affect only a handful of patients, but another may affect a total of 300 000 people or 10% of the european population. the commission recognised that those affected are particularly isolated and vulnerable. what is important, as the commissioner has said, is to codify, inventory these rare diseases, investigate and extend the centres specialised in european reference networks for rare diseases. and also, for us, we need more funding, possibilities to cooperate across borders, to cooperate across countries and to have these appropriate treatments. i would also like to thank the rapporteur for his report, which is a very good report, and i would also like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done.
